notes.B: Upper molar teeth are removed through the oral cavity; their proximity to the maxillary sinus does not require entering the pterygopalatine fossa.
notes.D: The cavernous sinus is an intracranial venous space and is not the usual target of a transantral pterygopalatine approach.
notes.E: The nasolacrimal duct runs anteriorly from the lacrimal sac to the inferior nasal meatus, outside the pterygopalatine fossa.

questions.stem: The lacrimal gland lies at the:

options.label: C
options.text: Lateral part of the orbital floor

questions.why: The lacrimal gland occupies a shallow depression in the orbital plate of the frontal bone at the superolateral orbit. Its ducts release tears into the superior conjunctival fornix.

notes.A: The inferolateral orbit is near the zygomatic contribution to the orbital floor; the lacrimal gland occupies the superior lateral region.
notes.B: The superomedial orbit contains the trochlea of superior oblique, whereas the lacrimal gland is situated on the lateral side.
notes.C: The lateral orbital floor is formed partly by zygomatic bone and lies below the normal location of the lacrimal gland.
notes.E: The superior orbital fissure is a posterior passage for nerves and veins, not the anterior superolateral lacrimal gland fossa.

questions.stem: The hard palate is formed by the:
questions.why: The palatine processes of the paired maxillae form the anterior portion of the hard palate, while the horizontal plates of the palatine bones complete its posterior part.

notes.A: The sphenoid contributes to the skull base and the zygomatic bone to the cheek and orbit; neither forms the hard palate.
notes.B: The maxilla contributes its palatine process, but the frontal bone forms the forehead and orbital roof rather than the palate.
notes.C: The ethmoid and frontal bones contribute to nasal and orbital structures but do not form the bony roof of the mouth.
notes.E: The palatine bone forms the posterior hard palate through its horizontal plate, while the ethmoid forms nasal and orbital structures.

questions.stem: Which extraocular muscle does NOT arise from the common tendinous ring?
questions.why: Inferior oblique originates anteriorly from the maxillary orbital floor near the nasolacrimal canal, unlike the four rectus muscles, which originate from the common tendinous ring at the orbital apex.

notes.B: Medial rectus originates from the common tendinous ring and inserts on the medial sclera to adduct the eyeball.
notes.C: Lateral rectus originates from the common tendinous ring and abducts the eyeball under abducent nerve control.
notes.D: Inferior rectus originates from the common tendinous ring and primarily depresses the eyeball, with additional adduction and extorsion.
notes.E: The four rectus muscles share the tendinous ring, but inferior oblique has a separate origin on the anterior orbital floor.

questions.stem: The following are enclosed in or embedded in the carotid sheath EXCEPT the:
questions.why: The phrenic nerve descends on the anterior scalene muscle beneath the prevertebral fascial covering, outside the carotid sheath, which encloses the carotid artery, internal jugular vein and vagus.

notes.A: The common carotid artery is enclosed medially within the sheath before dividing into its internal and external branches.
notes.B: The internal jugular vein lies inside the carotid sheath, usually lateral to the common or internal carotid artery.
notes.C: The vagus nerve is enclosed in the sheath posteriorly between the carotid artery and internal jugular vein.
notes.E: Deep cervical lymph nodes lie along the internal jugular vein and may be embedded in or closely associated with the sheath.

questions.stem: The palatine tonsil lies between:
questions.why: The palatine tonsil occupies the tonsillar fossa in the lateral oropharyngeal wall between the palatoglossal arch anteriorly and palatopharyngeal arch posteriorly, formed by their corresponding muscles.

notes.A: Palatoglossus forms the anterior tonsillar pillar, but styloglossus retracts the tongue and does not form the posterior pillar.
notes.B: The superior constrictor contributes to the tonsillar bed, while stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx; neither pair defines the tonsillar pillars.
notes.C: Stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx and styloglossus retracts the tongue, but neither forms the arches enclosing the tonsil.
notes.E: Palatoglossus forms the anterior arch, whereas stylopharyngeus runs deeper and does not form the posterior tonsillar arch.

questions.stem: Salivary stones (sialolithiasis) are most common in the:
questions.why: Most salivary stones occur in the submandibular gland or its duct. Proposed contributors include relatively viscous saliva and a long duct that carries secretions forward and upwards to the floor of the mouth.

notes.A: The parotid gland secretes predominantly watery serous saliva and develops calculi less frequently than the submandibular gland.
notes.C: The sublingual gland drains through multiple short ducts and is an uncommon site of salivary stone formation.
notes.D: The lacrimal gland produces tears rather than saliva, so it is not a site of sialolithiasis.
notes.E: Submandibular stones are much more frequent. The longer duct and more viscous secretion are proposed contributors to this difference.

questions.stem: The lacrimal sac:

options.label: A
options.text: Lies on the floor of the orbit

options.label: B
options.text: Lies at the inferolateral part of the orbit

options.label: C
options.text: Lies at the superomedial part of the orbit

options.label: D
options.text: Lies in the lacrimal fossa at the inferomedial part of the orbit

options.label: E
options.text: Drains into the middle meatus of the nose

questions.why: The lacrimal sac sits in the lacrimal sac fossa on the anterior medial orbital wall near the medial canthus. It drains through the nasolacrimal duct into the inferior nasal meatus.

notes.A: The orbital floor separates the orbit from the maxillary sinus, but the sac occupies the anterior medial orbital wall.
notes.B: The inferolateral orbit is remote from the medial canthus where the lacrimal canaliculi enter the lacrimal sac.
notes.C: The sac lies anteriorly near the medial canthus rather than high on the superomedial orbital wall.
notes.E: The nasolacrimal duct carries tears beneath the inferior concha to the inferior meatus, below the stated drainage site.

questions.stem: The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the nasal cavity through the:
questions.why: The sphenopalatine foramen in the medial boundary of the pterygopalatine fossa leads into the nasal cavity, transmitting the sphenopalatine vessels and posterior superior nasal nerve branches.

notes.A: The nasolacrimal duct connects the lacrimal sac with the inferior nasal meatus rather than the pterygopalatine fossa.
notes.B: The inferior meatus receives the nasolacrimal duct but is not the opening connecting the pterygopalatine fossa to the nose.
notes.D: The superior orbital fissure connects the middle cranial fossa and orbit, not the pterygopalatine fossa and nasal cavity.
notes.E: The infraorbital foramen carries the infraorbital nerve and vessels to the face through the anterior surface of the maxilla.

questions.stem: The medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa is formed by the:

options.label: E
options.text: Perpendicular plate of the palatine bone

questions.why: The perpendicular plate of the palatine bone forms the medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa; the sphenopalatine foramen interrupts this wall to provide access to the nasal cavity.

notes.A: The greater wing of the sphenoid contributes to the superior or posterior boundary rather than forming the medial wall.
notes.B: The lateral pterygoid plate is part of the sphenoid process, whose root contributes to the posterior aspect of the fossa.
notes.C: The medial pterygoid plate is part of the sphenoid pterygoid process; the medial fossa wall is formed by palatine bone.
notes.D: The posterior surface of the maxilla forms the anterior boundary of the fossa rather than its medial wall.

questions.stem: The muscle that rotates the muscular process of the arytenoid forward, adducting the vocal folds, is the:
questions.why: Lateral cricoarytenoid pulls the muscular processes of the arytenoids anterolaterally, rotating their vocal processes medially and closing the membranous portion of the rima glottidis during phonation.

notes.A: Transverse arytenoid draws the arytenoid cartilages together to close the posterior glottis, rather than primarily rotating their muscular processes.
notes.B: Posterior cricoarytenoid rotates the vocal processes laterally and is the only intrinsic muscle that abducts the vocal folds.
notes.D: Thyroarytenoid shortens and relaxes the vocal ligaments, modifying their tension rather than providing the described rotational action.
notes.E: Aryepiglottic muscle narrows the laryngeal inlet during swallowing rather than primarily adducting the vocal folds.

questions.stem: Which structures pass through the jugular foramen?

options.label: E
options.text: Both the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve

questions.why: The jugular foramen transmits the glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves, together with venous drainage including the sigmoid sinus continuing as the internal jugular vein. The hypoglossal nerve uses a separate canal.

notes.A: The foramen transmits cranial nerves as well as the venous channel formed by the continuation of the sigmoid sinus.
notes.B: The vagus passes through the foramen with the glossopharyngeal and accessory nerves, alongside major venous drainage.
notes.C: The hypoglossal nerve leaves through a canal in the occipital bone that is separate from the jugular foramen.
notes.D: This combination includes the hypoglossal nerve, which uses its own canal and does not traverse the jugular foramen.

questions.stem: Features of the soft palate:

options.label: A
options.text: It is attached in front to the hard palate

options.label: B
options.text: It forms part of the boundary of the isthmus of the fauces

options.label: C
options.text: Laterally it is continuous with the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches

options.label: D
options.text: Its main function is to keep the oropharynx closed at all times

options.label: E
options.text: Its posterior border is attached to the pharyngeal wall

notes.A: Its anterior palatine aponeurosis attaches to the posterior margin of the bony hard palate.
notes.B: The soft palate forms the superior boundary of the oropharyngeal isthmus, connecting the mouth to the pharynx.
notes.C: The palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal folds descend from its lateral margins around the tonsillar fossa.
notes.D: The soft palate elevates transiently during swallowing to close the nasopharynx, not the oropharynx continuously.
notes.E: The posterior margin hangs freely into the pharynx and bears the centrally placed uvula.

questions.why: The soft palate is a mobile fibromuscular continuation of the hard palate. It regulates communication between the nasopharynx and oropharynx during swallowing and speech, while its free posterior margin bears the uvula.

questions.stem: Tonsillar tissue closely related to the oropharynx includes the:

notes.A: The lingual tonsil consists of lymphoid nodules on the posterior third of the tongue facing the oropharynx.
notes.B: The tubal tonsil surrounds the pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube in the lateral nasopharynx.
notes.C: The palatine tonsil occupies the lateral oropharyngeal wall between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.
notes.D: The pharyngeal tonsil occupies the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx rather than the oropharynx.

questions.why: Waldeyer’s lymphatic ring surrounds the entrance to the respiratory and digestive tracts. Its palatine and lingual components are associated with the oropharynx, while the tubal and pharyngeal components occupy the nasopharynx.

questions.stem: About the pharynx:

options.label: A
options.text: It lies in front of the upper six cervical vertebrae

options.label: B
options.text: It is separated from the vertebral bodies by the pretracheal fascia

options.label: C
options.text: It is incomplete in front, opening into the nose, mouth and larynx

options.label: D
options.text: Its lateral wall is attached to the ramus of the mandible

questions.why: Its anterior wall is deficient where it opens into the nasal cavity, mouth and larynx.

notes.B: By PREVERTEBRAL fascia (and retropharyngeal space).
notes.D: Not to the ramus.
notes.E: Buccinator is a cheek muscle.

questions.stem: The wall of the pharynx has four layers. Which is NOT one of them?
questions.why: The pharyngeal wall consists of mucosa, pharyngobasilar fascia, skeletal muscle and external buccopharyngeal fascia. The prevertebral fascia lies outside this wall, covering the deep vertebral muscles.

notes.A: The mucous membrane lines the pharyngeal lumen and provides epithelial protection appropriate to its respiratory or digestive region.
notes.B: The pharyngobasilar fascia provides a fibrous supporting layer deep to the mucosa and attaches to the skull base.
notes.C: The constrictors and longitudinal pharyngeal muscles are skeletal muscles that propel food and elevate the pharynx during swallowing.
notes.D: The buccopharyngeal fascia is the external covering of the constrictors and extends forwards over the buccinator.

questions.stem: About the tissue spaces of the neck:

options.label: A
options.text: The prevertebral space lies behind the prevertebral fascia

options.label: B
options.text: The retropharyngeal space lies in front of the prevertebral fascia

options.label: C
options.text: The parapharyngeal space is continuous with the retropharyngeal space

options.label: D
options.text: The upper part of the parapharyngeal space is the infratemporal fossa

options.label: E
options.text: The submandibular space communicates with the sublingual space

notes.A: The prevertebral space lies deep to the prevertebral fascia in relation to the vertebral column and deep muscles.
notes.B: The retropharyngeal space is anterior to the prevertebral fascia, with the alar fascia forming its more immediate posterior boundary.
notes.C: The parapharyngeal and retropharyngeal spaces communicate, allowing infections in the lateral pharyngeal region to spread posteriorly.
notes.D: The parapharyngeal space extends to the skull base but is anatomically distinct from the more lateral infratemporal fossa.
notes.E: The submandibular and sublingual spaces communicate behind mylohyoid, permitting infection to spread between the two regions.

questions.why: Cervical fascial spaces provide pathways for infection. The retropharyngeal space communicates laterally with parapharyngeal regions, while the sublingual and submandibular spaces communicate around the posterior border of mylohyoid.

questions.stem: Structures found in the superficial fascia of the neck include:

notes.A: The transverse cervical nerve runs superficially across sternocleidomastoid to supply the skin of the anterior neck.
notes.B: Platysma lies within the superficial fascia and tenses the skin of the neck during facial expression.
notes.C: The supraclavicular nerves descend in the superficial fascia towards the skin covering the clavicle and shoulder.
notes.D: The suprascapular nerve is a brachial plexus branch that courses deeply towards the scapular notch.
notes.E: The ansa cervicalis lies deep to the investing fascia, commonly on the anterior surface of the carotid sheath.

questions.why: The superficial cervical fascia contains platysma and cutaneous nerves that emerge near the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid. Deeper motor nerves and cervical plexus loops lie beneath the investing fascia.

questions.stem: Extrinsic muscles of the tongue include:

notes.A: Genioglossus originates from the superior mental spine of the mandible and protrudes the tongue.
notes.B: The vertical muscle is intrinsic to the tongue and flattens and broadens it during contraction.
notes.C: Mylohyoid arises from the mandible and forms the muscular floor of the mouth rather than entering the tongue.
notes.D: Styloglossus arises from the styloid process and retracts and elevates the tongue during swallowing.
notes.E: Palatoglossus originates from the palatine aponeurosis and elevates the posterior tongue towards the soft palate.

questions.why: Extrinsic tongue muscles originate outside the tongue and enter it to change its position. Intrinsic muscles instead arise and insert within the tongue, altering its shape.

questions.stem: Origins of the superior constrictor include the:

notes.A: The pharyngeal tubercle anchors the upper end of the posterior raphe and is associated with insertion, not origin.
notes.B: The pterygoid hamulus provides an upper attachment for fibres of the superior pharyngeal constrictor.
notes.C: The lower part of the medial pterygoid plate contributes to the superior constrictor’s origin.
notes.D: The pterygomandibular raphe anchors the superior constrictor posteriorly and buccinator anteriorly, linking pharynx and cheek.
notes.E: The posterior part of the mylohyoid line provides a mandibular origin for fibres of the superior constrictor.

questions.why: Superior constrictor arises from the pterygoid region, pterygomandibular raphe and posterior mylohyoid line. Its fibres converge posteriorly towards the median pharyngeal raphe and pharyngeal tubercle.

questions.stem: Structures passing through the gap between the superior and middle constrictors include:

notes.A: Stylopharyngeus descends from the styloid process and enters between the superior and middle constrictors to elevate the pharynx.
notes.B: Styloglossus passes towards the tongue to retract it and does not enter the pharyngeal wall through this gap.
notes.C: Salpingopharyngeus descends from the auditory tube region within the pharyngeal wall rather than traversing this lateral gap.
notes.D: Palatopharyngeus descends from the soft palate within the pharyngeal wall and does not enter through this gap.
notes.E: The glossopharyngeal nerve accompanies stylopharyngeus through the gap and provides pharyngeal sensory and stylopharyngeal motor innervation.

questions.why: The gap between the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictors allows the stylopharyngeus muscle and glossopharyngeal nerve to enter the pharyngeal wall, linking its longitudinal musculature with its sensory and motor supply.

questions.stem: Origins of the middle constrictor include the:

notes.A: The inferior portion of the stylohyoid ligament gives attachment to fibres of the middle pharyngeal constrictor.
notes.B: The thyrohyoid membrane spans the hyoid and thyroid cartilage but is not an origin of the middle constrictor.
notes.C: The greater horn of the hyoid provides an attachment for the middle constrictor’s broad muscular origin.
notes.D: The lesser horn of the hyoid provides an additional origin near the attachment of the stylohyoid ligament.
notes.E: The median pharyngeal raphe is where the constrictor fibres insert posteriorly, rather than where they originate.

questions.why: The middle constrictor originates from both horns of the hyoid and the lower stylohyoid ligament. Its fibres fan posteriorly to the median pharyngeal raphe and constrict the pharynx during swallowing.

questions.stem: About the pharynx:

options.label: B
options.text: The nasopharynx ends below at the level of C1

options.label: C
options.text: The oropharynx ends at the upper border of the epiglottis

options.label: E
options.text: The hypopharynx is the part above the laryngeal inlet

notes.B: At the soft palate, about C1–C2.
notes.D: Lower border of cricoid.
notes.E: It lies behind and below the inlet (laryngopharynx).

questions.why: The pharynx is about 12-14 cm, the oropharynx ends at the upper border of the epiglottis and the laryngopharynx at C6 (A, C, D true). B is false (the nasopharynx ends at the soft palate, not C1) and E is false (the hypopharynx is the laryngopharynx, not a part above the inlet).

questions.stem: Killian's dehiscence:

options.label: B
options.text: Lies between the superior and inferior constrictors

options.label: D
options.text: Is a weak area in the anterior pharyngeal wall

options.label: E
options.text: Is a site of pharyngeal (Zenker's) diverticulum

notes.A: The two portions of the inferior constrictor meet at the weak area.
notes.B: The superior and inferior constrictors are separated by the middle constrictor, not by this dehiscence.
notes.C: Palatopharyngeus and stylopharyngeus are longitudinal muscles, not the margins of Killian's dehiscence.
notes.D: The weak area lies in the posterior pharyngeal wall, where a pouch can protrude.
notes.E: A Zenker diverticulum is a pulsion pouch that protrudes through this weak area.

questions.why: Killian's dehiscence is a weak posterior area between the oblique thyropharyngeus and transverse cricopharyngeus fibres of the inferior constrictor. Increased intraluminal pressure may force mucosa and submucosa through it.

questions.stem: Structures related to the walls of the nasopharynx:

notes.A: The pharyngeal recess lies posterior to the elevation formed by the auditory tube.
notes.B: The pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube lies on the lateral nasopharyngeal wall.
notes.C: The pharyngeal tonsil occupies the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx.
notes.D: The palatine tonsil occupies the tonsillar fossa in the lateral wall of the oropharynx.
notes.E: The palatopharyngeal arch descends from the soft palate into the oropharynx.

questions.why: The nasopharynx lies behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate. Its lateral walls contain the auditory tube openings, while its roof and posterior wall contain pharyngeal lymphoid tissue.

questions.stem: Muscles of the soft palate include:

notes.A: Tensor veli palatini tenses the palate and assists opening of the auditory tube.
notes.B: Levator veli palatini raises the soft palate to help close the nasopharynx during swallowing.
notes.C: Palatoglossus elevates the posterior tongue and narrows the oropharyngeal isthmus.
notes.D: Palatopharyngeus elevates the pharynx during swallowing and helps position the soft palate.
notes.E: Musculus uvulae shortens and elevates the uvula, helping seal the nasopharynx.

questions.why: The soft-palate muscles coordinate tension and movement during swallowing and speech. Tensor veli palatini receives motor fibres from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, while the others receive vagal fibres through the pharyngeal plexus.

questions.stem: In tonsillectomy, bleeding may come from branches of the:

notes.A: The facial artery supplies the tonsil through its tonsillar and ascending palatine branches.
notes.B: The descending palatine branch of the maxillary artery contributes through its lesser palatine branches.
notes.C: Dorsal lingual branches reach the inferior part of the palatine tonsil.
notes.D: The internal carotid artery gives no cervical branches, although its proximity makes accidental injury dangerous.
notes.E: The ascending pharyngeal artery contributes small branches to the pharyngeal wall and tonsil.

questions.why: The palatine tonsil receives multiple arterial branches, principally the tonsillar branch of the facial artery. Its extensive blood supply and nearby veins explain the risk of bleeding during tonsillectomy.

questions.stem: About the larynx:

options.label: A
options.text: Its upper border is at C3

options.label: B
options.text: Its upper border is related to the common carotid bifurcation

options.label: C
options.text: Its lower border is at C6

options.label: D
options.text: It is joined to the hyoid by the cricohyoid membrane

options.label: E
options.text: The thyroid notch marks the upper end of the laryngeal prominence

notes.A: The superior extent of the adult larynx is approximately at the third cervical vertebra.
notes.B: The carotid bifurcation usually lies near the superior border of the thyroid cartilage, close to the upper larynx.
notes.C: The inferior border of the cricoid cartilage marks the transition to the trachea at about C6.
notes.D: The thyrohyoid membrane connects the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone, not the cricoid cartilage.
notes.E: The superior thyroid notch lies immediately above the laryngeal prominence in the anterior midline.

questions.why: The adult larynx typically spans C3–C6, although its position varies with age and swallowing. The thyroid cartilage forms its anterior prominence and attaches superiorly to the hyoid by the thyrohyoid membrane.

questions.stem: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the:
questions.why: The nasolacrimal duct carries tears from the lacrimal sac to the inferior nasal meatus beneath the inferior concha. This connection explains nasal discharge during crying.

notes.A: The middle meatus receives drainage from the frontal, maxillary and anterior or middle ethmoidal sinuses, rather than tears.
notes.B: The superior meatus receives posterior ethmoidal air cell drainage rather than the nasolacrimal duct.
notes.D: The sphenoethmoidal recess lies above the superior concha and receives drainage from the sphenoidal sinus.
notes.E: The hiatus semilunaris is a groove in the middle meatus involved in sinus drainage rather than tear drainage.

questions.stem: The pterygopalatine fossa connects with the middle cranial fossa through the:
questions.why: Foramen rotundum carries V2.

notes.A: To the face.
notes.B: To the foramen lacerum region.
notes.C: To the nose.
notes.D: To the palate.

questions.stem: Structures passing between the external and internal carotid arteries include the:

notes.A: The styloid process projects downwards between the carotid arteries as part of the styloid apparatus.
notes.B: Stylopharyngeus descends between the carotid arteries towards the lateral pharyngeal wall.
notes.C: Styloglossus passes forwards from the styloid process between the carotid arteries towards the tongue.
notes.D: The glossopharyngeal nerve descends between the carotid arteries on its way towards the pharynx and tongue.
notes.E: The vagus trunk remains within the carotid sheath; its pharyngeal branch may pass between the arteries.

questions.why: As the external carotid artery courses forwards, the styloid apparatus and glossopharyngeal nerve separate it from the internal carotid. The vagus trunk remains inside the carotid sheath alongside the internal carotid.

questions.stem: The following are branches of the external carotid artery EXCEPT:
questions.why: The inferior thyroid artery usually arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the first part of the subclavian artery. The superior thyroid artery, in contrast, usually arises from the external carotid.

notes.B: The superior thyroid artery typically arises near the beginning of the external carotid and supplies the thyroid's upper pole.
notes.C: The facial artery arises from the external carotid and supplies superficial structures of the face and submandibular region.
notes.D: The lingual artery is an anterior branch of the external carotid that supplies the tongue and floor of the mouth.
notes.E: The occipital artery arises posteriorly from the external carotid and supplies the posterior scalp and adjacent muscles.

questions.stem: A pulse felt at the lower border of the mandible just in front of masseter is in the:
questions.why: The facial artery winds around the inferior border of the mandible immediately anterior to masseter. Its superficial position against bone permits palpation or compression at this point.

notes.A: The superficial temporal artery can be palpated anterior to the ear as it crosses the zygomatic arch.
notes.B: The lingual artery runs deep towards the tongue, including a segment deep to hyoglossus, rather than crossing the mandible.
notes.C: The maxillary artery runs deep within the infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae rather than across the mandibular border.
notes.D: The transverse facial artery runs across the cheek below the zygomatic arch, not around the lower mandibular border.

questions.stem: All of the following arteries enter the true pelvis EXCEPT the:
questions.why: The testicular artery descends retroperitoneally towards the deep inguinal ring and travels through the inguinal canal to the scrotum. Unlike the ovarian artery, it does not normally enter the true pelvic cavity.

notes.A: The internal iliac artery descends into the true pelvis and provides the principal arterial supply to pelvic structures.
notes.B: The median sacral artery descends in the midline over the anterior sacrum, entering the pelvic cavity.
notes.C: The superior rectal artery is the continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery and descends into the pelvis to supply the rectum.
notes.D: The ovarian artery passes across the pelvic brim and runs in the suspensory ligament of the ovary to its pelvic destination.

questions.stem: The superior gluteal artery leaves the pelvis through the:
questions.why: The superior gluteal artery is usually a branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery. It exits through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis with the superior gluteal nerve.

notes.B: The lesser sciatic foramen transmits the obturator internus tendon and returning pudendal neurovascular structures, not the superior gluteal artery.
notes.C: The obturator canal carries the obturator nerve and vessels from the pelvis into the medial thigh.
notes.D: The pudendal canal carries internal pudendal vessels and the pudendal nerve along the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa.
notes.E: The sacral foramina carry sacral nerve branches and associated vessels rather than the superior gluteal arterial trunk.

questions.stem: The artery crossing the snuffbox that supplies the scaphoid is the:

notes.A: The ulnar artery passes into the hand on the ulnar side of the wrist rather than crossing the snuffbox.
notes.B: The radial artery provides branches to the scaphoid, many of which enter its distal region and supply it retrogradely.
notes.C: Thenar branches supply the thumb-side palmar muscles; the main vessel crossing the snuffbox is the radial artery.

questions.why: The radial artery crosses the floor of the anatomical snuffbox over the scaphoid and trapezium. Much of the scaphoid receives blood entering distally, making the proximal fragment vulnerable after a waist fracture.

questions.stem: Arteries supplying the thoracic wall include the:

notes.A: The internal thoracic artery gives anterior intercostal branches to the upper intercostal spaces.
notes.B: The inferior epigastric artery principally supplies the anterior abdominal wall, although it anastomoses with the superior epigastric artery.
notes.C: Posterior intercostal arteries supply the intercostal spaces, with most arising directly from the thoracic aorta.
notes.D: The thyrocervical trunk sends branches to the neck and scapula. The upper posterior intercostal supply comes via the costocervical trunk.
notes.E: The suprascapular artery chiefly supplies the scapular region rather than the intercostal muscles.

questions.why: The thoracic wall is supplied chiefly by anterior and posterior intercostal arteries. The internal thoracic and musculophrenic arteries supply anterior intercostal spaces, while the thoracic aorta supplies most posterior spaces.

questions.stem: Features of veins:

options.label: A
options.text: Their lumen becomes larger toward the heart

options.label: B
options.text: They have no elastic lamina in their walls

options.label: C
options.text: Their tunica externa (adventitia) is relatively thicker

options.label: D
options.text: Most have valves to prevent reflux

notes.B: Large veins have elastic fibres; the internal elastic lamina is poorly developed, not absent.
notes.C: It is the thickest layer in veins.
notes.E: They contain blood.

questions.why: Veins widen toward the heart, have a relatively thick adventitia, mostly carry valves and look dark with deoxygenated blood (A, C-E true); B is false because veins do have elastic laminae, only thinner and less defined than in arteries.

questions.stem: Features of arteries:

options.label: A
options.text: Elastic tissue is abundant in the large conducting arteries

options.label: B
options.text: They become smaller from the aorta to the periphery

options.label: C
options.text: Smooth muscle predominates in all arteries

options.label: D
options.text: All have a mesothelial lining of the tunica intima

options.label: E
options.text: They have valves to prevent reflux

notes.A: Elastic lamellae in conducting arteries permit expansion during systole and recoil during diastole.
notes.B: Successive arterial branches generally become smaller in diameter as they approach the capillary beds.
notes.C: Smooth muscle predominates in muscular arteries, whereas elastic arteries contain abundant elastic lamellae.
notes.D: Endothelium lines blood vessels; mesothelium lines serous cavities such as the pleural cavity.
notes.E: Ordinary arteries lack serial valves because pressure gradients drive their flow; semilunar heart valves are at the ventricular outlets.

questions.why: Large elastic arteries accommodate pulsatile ventricular ejection through elastic lamellae, whereas muscular arteries regulate distribution through smooth muscle. All ordinary arterial lumina are lined by endothelium rather than mesothelium.

questions.stem: About the pericardium:

options.label: A
options.text: Its anterior surface forms the posterior boundary of the anterior mediastinum

options.label: B
options.text: The fibrous pericardium around the IVC is attached to the central tendon of the diaphragm

options.label: C
options.text: It has no attachment to the sternum

options.label: D
options.text: Its posterior surface forms the anterior boundary of the posterior mediastinum

options.label: E
options.text: The inner surface of the fibrous pericardium is loosely attached to the parietal serous pericardium

notes.A: The anterior mediastinum lies between the sternum and anterior surface of the fibrous pericardium.
notes.B: The fibrous pericardium blends with the central tendon around the caval opening, anchoring the heart to the diaphragm.
notes.C: Sternopericardial ligaments attach the fibrous pericardium to the posterior surface of the sternum.
notes.D: The posterior mediastinum lies behind the pericardium and in front of the thoracic vertebral column.
notes.E: The parietal serous pericardium is firmly adherent to the fibrous pericardium, rather than loosely attached.

questions.why: The fibrous pericardium surrounds the heart in the middle mediastinum and anchors it to the central tendon and sternum. The parietal serous pericardium adheres to its inner surface.

questions.stem: About the pericardial sac:

options.label: A
options.text: At the arterial end, the two serous layers are continuous with the tunica intima of the vessels

options.label: B
options.text: The transverse sinus separates the aorta and pulmonary trunk from the great veins

options.label: C
options.text: The oblique sinus is a remnant of the sinus venosus

options.label: D
options.text: At the venous end, the parietal serous layer is separated from the visceral layer

options.label: E
options.text: The oblique sinus lies behind the left atrium

notes.A: The serous layers reflect into each other around arterial roots; the tunica intima lines the vessel lumen separately.
notes.B: The transverse sinus lies posterior to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk and anterior to the superior vena cava.
notes.C: The oblique sinus forms between serous reflections around the pulmonary veins and inferior vena cava, rather than from the sinus venosus.
notes.D: The parietal and visceral serous layers remain continuous where they reflect around the venous roots.
notes.E: The oblique sinus is a blind recess posterior to the left atrium between the pulmonary venous reflections.

questions.why: Serous pericardial reflections around arterial and venous roots create the transverse and oblique sinuses. The visceral and parietal layers are continuous at these reflections, enclosing a potential fluid-filled cavity.

questions.stem: Described surfaces of the heart include:

notes.A: The posterior base is formed mainly by the left atrium and receives the pulmonary veins.
notes.B: The sternocostal surface faces the anterior thoracic wall and is formed largely by the right ventricle.
notes.C: The diaphragmatic surface rests on the diaphragm and consists chiefly of the left ventricle with part of the right ventricle.
notes.D: The left pulmonary surface faces the left lung and is formed mainly by the left ventricle.
notes.E: A distinct medial surface is not part of the standard anatomical description of the heart.

questions.why: Cardiac surfaces are named according to their anatomical relationships: sternocostal, diaphragmatic and pulmonary surfaces, with the posterior base largely formed by the left atrium. No standard medial surface is described.

questions.stem: Features of the sternocostal surface of the heart:

notes.A: The anterior interventricular groove separates the ventricular surfaces and contains the anterior interventricular vessels.
notes.B: The coronary sulcus separates atria from ventricles, with portions visible on the anterior surface.
notes.C: The right auricle projects anteriorly from the right atrium beside the ascending aorta.
notes.D: The inferior vena cava enters the right atrium from below. Its opening is inside the atrium.
notes.E: The coronary sinus runs in the posterior coronary sulcus and drains into the right atrium.

questions.why: The sternocostal surface faces the sternum and costal cartilages and is formed mainly by the right ventricle. It displays anterior coronary grooves and the auricles rather than posterior venous structures.

questions.stem: Features of the diaphragmatic (inferior) surface of the heart:

options.label: D
options.text: The posterior interventricular branch of the right coronary artery

notes.A: The left atrium forms the base (posterior).
notes.B: The apex is at the left end of the sternocostal and diaphragmatic surfaces; texts usually describe it separately.

questions.why: The diaphragmatic (inferior) surface carries the posterior interventricular branch of the right coronary artery (D true); the apex is on the sternocostal aspect and the great vessels arise from the base, so the other options are false.

questions.stem: Features inside the adult right atrium:

notes.A: The pulmonary veins normally open into the left atrium and carry oxygenated blood from the lungs.
notes.B: The coronary sinus opens into the right atrium near the inferior vena cava and tricuspid orifice.
notes.C: The infundibulum is the smooth right ventricular outflow tract leading to the pulmonary valve.
notes.D: The limbus is the raised margin around the fossa ovalis on the right atrial side of the interatrial septum.
notes.E: Chordae tendineae connect atrioventricular valve cusps to papillary muscles within the ventricles.

questions.why: The right atrium receives systemic and coronary venous blood and contains the fossa ovalis with its raised limbus. Pulmonary venous openings belong to the left atrium, while chordae and infundibulum belong to ventricles.

questions.stem: Parts of the conducting system lying in the interventricular septum:

notes.B: They spread through the ventricular walls.
notes.D: In the interatrial septum.
notes.E: In the right atrial wall at the SVC.

questions.why: The bundle of His and its right and left bundle branches run in the interventricular septum (A, C true); the Purkinje fibres ramify through the ventricular walls, and the AV and SA nodes lie in the atrial walls, so B, D and E are false.

questions.stem: Capillary networks are found in all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.why: The epidermis consists of avascular stratified squamous epithelium. Its living cells obtain oxygen and nutrients by diffusion from capillaries in the underlying dermis rather than from vessels within the epidermis.

notes.A: The conjunctival connective tissue contains capillary networks that supply its overlying epithelium.
notes.B: The suprarenal gland has extensive capillary and sinusoidal networks that support hormone secretion into blood.
notes.D: Hepatic sinusoids are specialised discontinuous capillary channels that exchange substances with hepatocytes.
notes.E: Cortical bone contains blood vessels within central and perforating canals that nourish the mineralised tissue.

questions.stem: About capillaries:

options.label: B
options.text: Capillaries in the CNS are continuous

options.label: D
options.text: Fenestrated capillaries are abundant in the skin

options.label: E
options.text: Sinusoids are the same as fenestrated capillaries

questions.why: Most central nervous system capillaries have continuous endothelium with tight junctions and restricted transcytosis. This specialised endothelial barrier helps maintain the stable extracellular environment required by neurones.

notes.A: Continuous capillaries lack endothelial fenestrations; fenestrated capillaries have pores that facilitate exchange.
notes.C: Pulmonary alveolar capillaries have continuous endothelium forming part of the thin air–blood barrier.
notes.D: Skin capillaries are predominantly continuous, whereas fenestrated capillaries are typical of endocrine and absorptive organs.
notes.E: Sinusoids have wider channels and discontinuous endothelial or basal lamina features, unlike ordinary fenestrated capillaries.

questions.stem: The following arteries can be felt clinically EXCEPT:
questions.why: The deep palmar arterial arch lies deep to the long flexor tendons near the metacarpal bases. Its depth and overlying tissues prevent routine clinical palpation as a superficial pulse.

notes.A: The radial artery is palpable at the anterior wrist just lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon.
notes.B: The superficial temporal artery is palpable where it crosses the zygomatic arch anterior to the ear.
notes.C: The facial artery is palpable where it winds around the mandible immediately anterior to masseter.
notes.E: Dorsalis pedis is palpable on the dorsum of the foot, usually lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.

questions.stem: Branches of the first part of the subclavian artery include:

notes.A: The vertebral artery arises from the first part and ascends towards the cervical transverse foramina.
notes.B: The superior thoracic artery usually arises from the first part of the axillary artery, beyond the first rib.
notes.C: The internal thoracic artery arises from the first part and descends along the internal anterior thoracic wall.
notes.D: The thyrocervical trunk originates from the first part and supplies cervical and scapular structures through its branches.
notes.E: The thoracodorsal artery usually branches from the subscapular artery, which arises from the axillary artery.

questions.why: The first part of the subclavian artery lies medial to anterior scalene and normally gives the vertebral artery, internal thoracic artery and thyrocervical trunk. The costocervical origin varies by side.

questions.stem: About the electrocardiogram:

options.label: A
options.text: A prolonged PR interval suggests delay in the SA node

options.label: B
options.text: The T wave is ventricular repolarization

options.label: C
options.text: The ST segment lies between ventricular depolarization and repolarization

options.label: D
options.text: An abnormal QRS mostly indicates left atrial disease

options.label: E
options.text: An absent or abnormal P wave suggests AV node dysfunction

notes.A: A prolonged PR interval indicates delayed atrioventricular conduction, commonly at the atrioventricular node, rather than delayed sinoatrial firing.
notes.B: The T wave reflects the electrical recovery of the ventricular myocardium following depolarisation.
notes.C: The segment between the QRS complex and T wave represents the interval when most ventricular myocardium remains depolarised.
notes.D: QRS abnormalities generally reflect ventricular activation, conduction or myocardial changes rather than isolated left atrial disease.
notes.E: An absent or abnormal P wave usually reflects altered atrial activation or rhythm, not necessarily atrioventricular node dysfunction.

questions.why: The electrocardiogram records electrical activity: the P wave reflects atrial depolarisation, the QRS complex ventricular depolarisation and the T wave ventricular repolarisation. Intervals and segments help localise conduction abnormalities.

questions.stem: Auscultation areas:

options.label: A
options.text: Aortic: right 2nd intercostal space by the sternum

options.label: B
options.text: Pulmonary: left 2nd space by the sternum

options.label: C
options.text: Tricuspid: lower left sternal border (4th–5th space)

options.label: D
options.text: Mitral: left 5th space by the sternum

options.label: E
options.text: Apex beat: left 5th space just medial to the midclavicular line

notes.A: The aortic area is at the right second intercostal space immediately adjacent to the sternum.
notes.B: The pulmonary area is at the left second intercostal space immediately adjacent to the sternum.
notes.C: Tricuspid sounds are best heard near the lower left sternal border, typically the fourth or fifth intercostal space.
notes.D: Mitral sounds are best heard at the cardiac apex near the left fifth intercostal space and midclavicular line.
notes.E: The normal apex beat is usually felt in the left fifth intercostal space at or just medial to the midclavicular line.

questions.why: Valve sounds are heard best at characteristic chest-wall sites rather than directly over their anatomical positions. The aortic and pulmonary areas lie superiorly, while tricuspid and mitral areas lie more inferiorly.

questions.stem: End arteries are found in the:

notes.A: Renal segmental arteries lack effective intersegmental arterial communications, so occlusion can cause a segmental infarct.
notes.B: Splenic segmental branches have limited effective collateral connections, making their territories susceptible to infarction.
notes.C: The penis receives communicating arterial branches, rather than being a classic example of end-arterial supply.
notes.D: The stomach has abundant arterial communications along both curvatures, providing collateral routes for blood flow.
notes.E: The central retinal artery supplies the inner retina with little effective collateral circulation.

questions.why: An end artery supplies a territory without sufficient collateral arterial flow to sustain it after occlusion. Renal and splenic segmental arteries and the central retinal artery illustrate this vulnerability.

questions.stem: Arteriovenous anastomoses are found in the:
questions.why: Arteriovenous anastomoses for thermoregulation are plentiful in the skin of the digits, lips and nose and at the anorectal junction; the axilla is not a classic site, so D is false.

questions.stem: Arterial supply of the leg and foot:

options.label: A
options.text: The fibular (peroneal) artery supplies the anterior compartment

options.label: B
options.text: The plantar arteries are terminal branches of the posterior tibial

options.label: C
options.text: Dorsalis pedis continues the anterior tibial artery

options.label: D
options.text: Posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis are the only palpable arteries in the leg and foot

options.label: E
options.text: The plantar arch is formed mainly by the lateral plantar artery

notes.A: Lateral and posterior compartments.
notes.D: The popliteal can also be felt.

questions.why: The posterior tibial gives the plantar arteries, dorsalis pedis continues the anterior tibial, and the lateral plantar forms most of the plantar arch (B, C, E true). A is false (the fibular artery supplies the lateral and posterior compartments) and D is false (other leg arteries are also palpable).

questions.stem: Structures in the subcutaneous tissue of the thigh include the:

options.label: C
options.text: Saphenous opening (as a gap in the deep fascia)

notes.A: The great saphenous vein ascends superficially along the medial thigh before entering the femoral vein.
notes.B: The small saphenous vein usually ascends the posterior calf and terminates in the popliteal vein.
notes.C: The saphenous opening is a gap in fascia lata, which is deep to the subcutaneous tissue.
notes.D: The superficial epigastric artery ascends in superficial fascia towards the lower anterior abdominal wall.
notes.E: The superficial external pudendal artery crosses the superficial medial thigh towards the external genitalia.

questions.why: Superficial veins and cutaneous arterial branches run within the thigh subcutaneous tissue. The saphenous opening, by contrast, is a defect in the underlying deep fascia lata.

questions.stem: True or false: The deep palmar arch is mainly the continuation of the ulnar artery.
questions.why: The deep palmar arch is formed predominantly by the radial artery and completed by the deep branch of the ulnar artery. The superficial arch is predominantly ulnar.

notes.A: The ulnar artery chiefly forms the superficial palmar arch; its deep branch contributes to the deep arch.

questions.stem: True or false: The axillary vein begins at the lower border of teres major.
questions.why: At the inferior border of teres major, the basilic vein continues as the axillary vein, receiving the brachial veins. The axillary vein becomes subclavian at the lateral border of the first rib.

notes.B: The lower border of teres major is the conventional landmark for the beginning of the axillary vein.

questions.stem: True or false: The femoral canal lies medial to the femoral artery but lateral to the femoral vein.
questions.why: The femoral sheath contains the artery laterally, the vein centrally and the femoral canal medially. The canal allows expansion of the adjacent femoral vein and contains loose tissue and lymphatics.

notes.A: The canal lies medial to both femoral vessels, rather than between the artery and vein.

questions.stem: True or false: The paraumbilical veins run with the ligamentum teres and drain into the left branch of the portal vein.
questions.why: Paraumbilical veins accompany the ligamentum teres within the falciform ligament and communicate with the left portal vein. Their connections to superficial abdominal veins provide a portosystemic collateral pathway.

notes.B: Paraumbilical veins accompany the round ligament to the left portal system and can carry flow towards superficial abdominal veins in portal hypertension.

questions.stem: True or false: The internal thoracic artery ends by dividing into the superior epigastric and anterior intercostal arteries.
questions.why: Near the sixth intercostal space, the internal thoracic artery divides into the musculophrenic and superior epigastric arteries. Anterior intercostal branches arise along the internal thoracic and musculophrenic routes.

notes.A: Anterior intercostal arteries are segmental branches. The internal thoracic artery ends by giving the superior epigastric and musculophrenic branches.

questions.stem: True or false: The diaphragm receives most of its blood from branches of the internal thoracic artery.
questions.why: The paired inferior phrenic arteries provide major arterial supply to the inferior surface of the diaphragm. Superior phrenic, intercostal and internal thoracic branches supplement the diaphragmatic circulation.

notes.A: Internal thoracic branches contribute through the musculophrenic and pericardiacophrenic arteries, but do not constitute the principal supply.

questions.stem: True or false: The pulmonary valve lies behind the right border of the sternum at the 3rd costal cartilage.
questions.why: The pulmonary valve projects behind the medial end of the left third costal cartilage near the sternum. Its sound is heard best in the left second intercostal space.

notes.A: The pulmonary valve has a left-sided surface projection, not one at the right third costal cartilage.

questions.stem: True or false: During ventricular systole, eversion of the AV valve cusps into the atria is prevented by the papillary muscles.
questions.why: During ventricular contraction, papillary muscles tense the chordae tendineae attached to atrioventricular valve cusps. This prevents the closed cusps from prolapsing into the atria under ventricular pressure.

notes.B: Papillary muscle contraction stabilises the valve cusps through the chordae tendineae rather than opening the valves.

questions.stem: True or false: The AV bundle (of His) lies in the interatrial septum.
questions.why: The atrioventricular bundle penetrates the fibrous cardiac skeleton and courses at the superior interventricular septum before dividing. The atrioventricular node, rather than the bundle, occupies the inferior atrial septal region.

notes.A: The bundle of His reaches the interventricular septum; the atrioventricular node is in the atrial septal region.

questions.stem: True or false: The cardiac veins do not have names matching the arteries they accompany.
questions.why: E.g. great cardiac vein with the LAD, middle cardiac vein with the posterior interventricular artery.

questions.stem: True or false: The conus artery is one of the first branches of the right coronary artery.
questions.why: The conus branch commonly arises early from the right coronary artery and supplies the right ventricular outflow tract. In some individuals it arises separately from the right aortic sinus.

notes.B: The conus artery typically branches near the origin of the right coronary artery to supply the infundibulum.

questions.stem: True or false: The right ascending lumbar vein joins the right subcostal vein to form the hemiazygos vein.
questions.why: The right ascending lumbar and right subcostal veins commonly unite to form the azygos vein. Their left-sided counterparts contribute to the hemiazygos vein, with variations in both origins.

notes.A: The right-sided union contributes to the azygos vein, whereas the hemiazygos vein originates on the left.

questions.stem: True or false: The posterior cerebral artery is a terminal branch of the internal carotid artery.
questions.why: In the usual arterial pattern, the basilar artery terminates by dividing into the posterior cerebral arteries. The internal carotid artery normally terminates as the anterior and middle cerebral arteries.

notes.A: The posterior cerebral artery normally arises from the basilar artery, although a fetal-type carotid supply is a recognised variant.

questions.stem: True or false: At the confluence of sinuses, the straight sinus usually continues as the left transverse sinus.
questions.why: The superior sagittal usually turns right, the straight sinus left.

questions.stem: True or false: Branches of both the femoral and internal pudendal arteries supply the scrotum.
questions.why: Scrotal skin receives anterior scrotal branches from the external pudendal arteries and posterior scrotal branches from the internal pudendal artery. This differs from the arterial supply of the testes themselves.

notes.B: The femoral artery supplies anterior scrotal skin through external pudendal branches, and the internal pudendal supplies posterior skin.

questions.stem: Structures lying below (in the concavity of) the arch of the aorta include the:

notes.A: The pulmonary trunk divides beneath the aortic arch into right and left pulmonary arteries.
notes.B: The arch passes superior to the left lung root as it continues into the descending thoracic aorta.
notes.C: The ligamentum arteriosum joins the aortic isthmus to the left pulmonary artery immediately beneath the arch.
notes.D: The left vagus nerve crosses the lateral arch; its recurrent laryngeal branch loops beneath the arch.
notes.E: The left phrenic nerve crosses the lateral aspect of the arch anterior to the vagus nerve.

questions.why: The aortic arch curves over the left lung root and pulmonary arterial bifurcation. The ligamentum arteriosum links the arch and pulmonary artery, while the phrenic and vagus nerves cross its lateral aspect.

questions.stem: The groups of axillary lymph nodes include:

notes.A: Central nodes receive lymph from the pectoral, humeral and subscapular axillary groups.
notes.B: Humeral nodes lie near the axillary vein and drain most lymph from the upper limb.
notes.C: Supraclavicular nodes are located in the lower neck, beyond the axillary nodal groups.

questions.why: Axillary nodes are organised into pectoral, subscapular, humeral, central and apical groups. Most lymph from the upper limb and breast passes through these groups before reaching the subclavian lymphatic trunk.

questions.stem: Lymphatic drainage of the chest wall:

options.label: A
options.text: Most of the skin and subcutaneous tissue of the thorax drains to the parasternal nodes

options.label: B
options.text: Above the umbilicus, superficial lymph drains to the pectoral (anterior) axillary nodes

options.label: C
options.text: The deep chest wall drains to the axillary nodes

options.label: D
options.text: Superficial lymph of the breast can reach the supraclavicular nodes

options.label: E
options.text: Lymph from the back of the thorax drains to the superficial inguinal nodes

notes.A: Most superficial thoracic lymph reaches axillary rather than parasternal nodes.
notes.B: Pectoral axillary nodes receive lymph from the superficial anterior thoracic wall and the supraumbilical region of the anterior abdominal wall.
notes.C: Deep intercostal tissues drain chiefly to intercostal and parasternal nodes rather than superficial axillary pathways.
notes.D: Breast lymph can reach supraclavicular nodes through apical axillary and other communicating lymphatic pathways.
notes.E: Superficial lymph from the upper back generally reaches subscapular axillary nodes rather than superficial inguinal nodes.

questions.why: Superficial chest-wall lymph drains mainly to axillary nodes, while deeper intercostal tissues drain towards parasternal and intercostal nodes. Breast lymph may also reach supraclavicular nodes via higher nodal pathways.

questions.stem: Tissues WITHOUT lymphatic vessels include:

notes.A: Rich in lymphatics.
notes.B: The lips have a rich lymphatic drainage to the submental and submandibular nodes.
notes.C: Endomysium, around individual muscle fibres, is classically taught as lacking lymphatics, which run instead in the perimysium.

questions.why: Lymphatics are absent from CNS, bone marrow, cornea, cartilage, epidermis and endomysium.

questions.stem: Lymphatic capillaries are:
questions.why: Lymphatic capillaries are blind-ended with overlapping endothelial flaps and an absent or incomplete basal lamina, making them very permeable; they are neither fenestrated nor continuous, so only B is true.

questions.stem: The lymphatic system contains:

notes.A: The conventional named trunks include paired jugular, subclavian, bronchomediastinal and lumbar trunks, as well as the intestinal trunk.
notes.B: The thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct represent the two conventional main collecting pathways.
notes.C: The human body contains several hundred lymph nodes, commonly estimated at approximately six hundred.

questions.why: Lymph converges through regional trunks into two principal collecting ducts, with considerable anatomical variation in their termination. Hundreds of lymph nodes filter lymph along these regional drainage pathways.

questions.stem: Lymph from which organs may enter the thoracic duct directly without passing through nodes?

notes.A: Some thyroid lymph vessels drain straight into the thoracic duct.
notes.B: Some oesophageal lymph vessels drain straight into the thoracic duct.
notes.C: Liver lymph passes through hepatic and coeliac nodes first.

questions.why: Some vessels from the thyroid and oesophagus drain straight into the thoracic duct.

questions.stem: Primary lymphoid organs include:

notes.A: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs where mature lymphocytes encounter antigens carried in lymph.
notes.B: Red bone marrow produces lymphocyte precursors and provides the site of B-cell development and maturation.
notes.C: The thymus provides the specialised environment for T-cell maturation and selection.

questions.why: Primary lymphoid organs provide environments for lymphocyte development and antigen-independent maturation. B lymphocytes mature in the bone marrow, while T-cell precursors migrate to the thymus for maturation and selection.

questions.stem: About lymphatic drainage:

options.label: A
options.text: Lymph from the right half of the head and neck enters the right lymphatic duct

options.label: B
options.text: The superficial nodes of the upper limb include the lateral axillary group

options.label: C
options.text: Efferents from subpyloric nodes go to the para-aortic nodes

options.label: D
options.text: The jugulodigastric node is a deep cervical node draining the head

options.label: E
options.text: Lymph from the breast mostly enters the lateral axillary group

notes.A: The right jugular trunk can join the right lymphatic duct or empty independently at the right venous angle.
notes.B: Humeral axillary nodes are deep within the axilla and receive lymph from superficial and deep upper-limb vessels.
notes.C: Subpyloric nodes drain towards hepatic and coeliac nodal pathways rather than directly to the lumbar nodes.
notes.D: The jugulodigastric node belongs to the upper deep cervical chain and receives lymph from pharyngeal structures.
notes.E: Most breast lymph reaches the pectoral axillary group, not the humeral group that principally drains the arm.

questions.why: Regional lymphatic drainage follows characteristic nodal pathways before entering the major lymphatic trunks. Most breast lymph drains to pectoral axillary nodes, while head and neck lymph passes through cervical nodes.

questions.stem: Components of Waldeyer's ring include:

notes.A: The palatine tonsils lie in the lateral oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.
notes.B: The lingual tonsil comprises lymphoid nodules at the posterior part of the tongue.
notes.C: The jugulodigastric node is a deep cervical lymph node that receives tonsillar drainage, not tonsillar tissue.
notes.D: Submental nodes drain structures such as the chin and lower lip rather than forming the pharyngeal lymphoid ring.
notes.E: Tubal tonsillar tissue surrounds the pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube in the nasopharynx.

questions.why: Waldeyer’s ring is a collection of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue around the entrance to the respiratory and digestive tracts. It includes pharyngeal, tubal, palatine and lingual tonsillar tissue.

questions.stem: About the superficial inguinal lymph nodes:

options.label: A
options.text: The proximal group lies horizontally below the inguinal ligament

options.label: B
options.text: The distal group lies vertically along the great saphenous vein

options.label: C
options.text: The lateral nodes of the proximal group drain the external genitalia

options.label: D
options.text: The medial nodes of the proximal group drain the anterior abdominal wall below the umbilicus

options.label: E
options.text: The distal group receives almost all superficial lymphatics of the lower limb

notes.A: The horizontal group lies parallel to and just inferior to the inguinal ligament.
notes.B: The vertical group lies along the terminal great saphenous vein in the proximal thigh.
notes.C: External genital skin generally drains to medial horizontal nodes, while lateral nodes receive gluteal and lateral abdominal drainage.
notes.D: The medial horizontal group receives superficial lymph from the lower anterior abdomen. Lateral abdominal territories may drain to the lateral horizontal nodes.
notes.E: Most superficial lower-limb lymph reaches the vertical group, except some vessels accompanying the small saphenous vein.

questions.why: Superficial inguinal nodes comprise a horizontal group below the inguinal ligament and a vertical group beside the great saphenous vein. They drain superficial lower-limb, lower abdominal and perineal territories.

questions.stem: About the relations of the spleen:

options.label: A
options.text: Its long axis lies along the 10th rib

options.label: B
options.text: Its lower pole rests on the phrenicocolic ligament

options.label: C
options.text: It has no contact with the large intestine

options.label: D
options.text: The concave area between the notched superior border and hilum is the gastric impression

options.label: E
options.text: The area behind the hilum is the renal impression

notes.A: The long splenic axis runs approximately along the tenth rib, between the ninth and eleventh ribs.
notes.B: The phrenicocolic ligament forms a supporting shelf beneath the inferior aspect of the spleen.
notes.C: The colic impression on the visceral surface is related to the left colic flexure.
notes.D: The gastric impression occupies the broad concavity between the hilum and superior border.
notes.E: The renal impression lies posterior to the hilum and contacts the upper left kidney.

questions.why: The spleen lies in the left hypochondrium with its long axis approximately parallel to the tenth rib. Its visceral surface bears impressions from the stomach, left kidney and colonic flexure.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman has a growing malignant swelling on her back (upper trunk). Which nodes should be examined for metastasis?
questions.why: Superficial lymph from the upper posterior trunk generally drains to the subscapular axillary nodes. These lie along the posterior axillary fold and pass lymph to central and apical nodes.

notes.A: Superficial inguinal nodes receive lymph chiefly from the lower trunk, perineum and superficial lower limb.
notes.B: Pectoral axillary nodes primarily receive lymph from the anterior thoracic wall and breast.
notes.C: External iliac nodes receive deep inguinal and pelvic drainage. Upper-back skin generally drains through the axilla.
notes.E: Deep cervical nodes principally drain head and neck structures rather than the upper posterior thoracic wall.

questions.stem: True or false: In the trunk, the superficial lymphatic vessels accompany the arteries.
questions.why: Superficial lymphatic collectors generally accompany superficial veins in the subcutaneous tissues. Deep lymphatic vessels more often accompany major arteries and veins supplying or draining deeper structures.

notes.A: Superficial lymphatics are associated with superficial veins, while deep lymphatics accompany deeper neurovascular bundles.

questions.stem: True or false: The thoracic duct begins at the upper end of the cisterna chyli at about T12.
questions.why: When a cisterna chyli is present, its upper end continues as the thoracic duct near the thoracolumbar junction. The duct enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus at approximately T12, while the reservoir's level varies.

notes.B: The cisterna chyli continues into the thoracic duct near the aortic hiatus when this lymphatic reservoir is present.

questions.stem: Which condition is most likely to compromise breathing by compressing the trachea?
questions.why: The thyroid gland lies immediately anterior and lateral to the upper trachea. Enlargement, especially with retrosternal extension, can narrow or displace the tracheal lumen and compromise airflow.

notes.B: A thoracic aortic aneurysm can compress the intrathoracic trachea. Thyroid enlargement is a common cause of compression in the lower neck.
notes.C: Aortic coarctation is a narrowing of the aortic lumen rather than a typical compressive mass.
notes.D: A retropharyngeal abscess can obstruct the upper airway by bulging into the pharynx rather than primarily compressing the trachea.
notes.E: Horner syndrome reflects interrupted sympathetic innervation and is not itself a mass that compresses the airway.

questions.stem: About the superior thoracic aperture:

options.label: B
options.text: Its posterior border is the body of T1

options.label: C
options.text: Its anterior border is the upper border of the manubrium

options.label: D
options.text: Its lateral borders are the outer borders of the first ribs

options.label: E
options.text: Its anterior border is higher than its posterior border

questions.why: Bounded by T1, the first ribs and cartilages, and the upper border of the manubrium; it slopes downward and FORWARD.

notes.A: It slopes down and forward.
notes.B: T1 only.
notes.D: The INNER borders.
notes.E: Lower than.

questions.stem: About the inferior thoracic aperture:

options.label: B
options.text: Its posterior border is lower than its anterior border

options.label: C
options.text: Its posterior border is the lower two thoracic vertebrae

options.label: D
options.text: Its lateral borders are formed by ribs 11 and 12 only

options.label: E
options.text: Its anterior border is the costal margins only

questions.why: The inferior thoracic aperture is bounded posteriorly by T12 and anteriorly by the xiphisternal region. Its posterior boundary lies lower than its anterior boundary, with the diaphragm closing the opening.

notes.A: The inferior aperture slopes downwards posteriorly because its vertebral boundary lies below the anterior boundary.
notes.C: The posterior boundary is formed by the twelfth thoracic vertebra rather than two vertebral bodies.
notes.D: The lateral boundaries are formed by the costal margins as well as the eleventh and twelfth ribs.
notes.E: The anterior boundary is the xiphisternal region, with the costal margins forming anterolateral boundaries.

questions.stem: All of the following about the mediastinum are correct EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: The inferior mediastinum is larger than the superior mediastinum

options.label: B
options.text: The superior mediastinum communicates with all the other subdivisions

options.label: C
options.text: The posterior mediastinum communicates with the middle mediastinum through the superior mediastinum

options.label: D
options.text: The superior mediastinum continues up into the neck

options.label: E
options.text: Tracheal position in the jugular notch is a guide to mediastinal shift

questions.why: The anterior, middle and posterior parts communicate only through the superior mediastinum, not with each other directly.

notes.A: True.
notes.B: True.
notes.D: True.
notes.E: True.

questions.stem: The contents of the anterior mediastinum include the following EXCEPT:

options.label: B
options.text: Branches of the internal thoracic artery

questions.why: The anterior mediastinum is the narrow space between the sternum and fibrous pericardium. It contains connective tissue, lymph nodes, thymic tissue and small mediastinal vessels rather than vagal branches.

notes.A: Sternopericardial ligaments connect the fibrous pericardium to the sternum across the anterior mediastinum.
notes.B: Small mediastinal branches of the internal thoracic artery supply tissues within the anterior mediastinum.
notes.C: Thymic tissue or its fatty remnant is found in the anterior and superior mediastinum.
notes.E: Anterior mediastinal lymph nodes receive lymph from nearby mediastinal structures and connective tissues.

questions.stem: Which lies in the superior mediastinum?

options.label: C
options.text: The upper part of the azygos vein entering the IVC

questions.why: The aortic arch lies above the transverse thoracic plane within the superior mediastinum. It connects the ascending and descending aorta and gives rise to the major arteries supplying the head and upper limbs.

notes.B: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve passes around the right subclavian artery near the root of the neck.
notes.C: The azygos arch lies in the superior mediastinum and enters the superior vena cava. The option names the inferior vena cava instead.
notes.D: The pulmonary trunk bifurcation lies near the transverse thoracic plane beneath the aortic arch in the middle mediastinal region.
notes.E: The right subclavian artery is a terminal branch of the brachiocephalic trunk near the right sternoclavicular joint.

questions.stem: About the pleura, which is NOT correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The pulmonary pleura is also called visceral pleura

options.label: B
options.text: Visceral and parietal pleura are continuous at the lung root

options.label: C
options.text: The right and left pleural cavities communicate through the posterior mediastinum

options.label: D
options.text: Parietal pleura lies on the endothoracic fascia

options.label: E
options.text: In pleurisy the visceral pleura may adhere to the parietal

questions.why: The right and left pleural cavities are separate potential spaces, each enclosed by its own continuous serous membrane. The mediastinum separates the two cavities rather than providing a normal communicating passage.

notes.A: Visceral or pulmonary pleura adheres closely to the lung surface and extends into its fissures.
notes.B: The visceral layer is continuous with parietal pleura at its reflection around the root of the lung.
notes.D: The endothoracic fascia lies between costal parietal pleura and the inner thoracic wall.
notes.E: Inflammation of pleural surfaces can produce fibrous adhesions joining the visceral and parietal layers.

questions.stem: Which is NOT part of the parietal pleura?
questions.why: Pulmonary pleura is the visceral layer that covers the lung and follows its fissures. The parietal layer is named according to the thoracic region that it lines.

notes.A: The cupula is cervical parietal pleura extending above the first rib into the root of the neck.
notes.B: Mediastinal pleura forms the parietal covering of the lateral mediastinum and reflects at the lung root.
notes.C: Diaphragmatic pleura is the parietal layer over the diaphragm except where the mediastinum intervenes.
notes.D: Costal pleura forms the parietal lining of the internal rib surfaces and intercostal spaces.

questions.stem: About pleural aspiration and drainage:

options.label: A
options.text: The needle is passed just above the upper border of the rib below

options.label: B
options.text: The 7th space or below is always chosen

options.label: C
options.text: The midclavicular line is preferred because it is simpler

options.label: D
options.text: The tube is left open to air

options.label: E
options.text: The patient holds a deep breath during the procedure

questions.why: The main intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the costal groove of the rib above. Pleural aspiration uses the route above a rib to reduce injury to the main bundle, with ultrasound to identify a suitable site.

notes.B: The appropriate intercostal space depends on the indication, anatomy and imaging rather than a fixed seventh-space threshold.
notes.C: The access site is selected according to the intended pleural procedure and imaging, not simply because a midclavicular approach is convenient.
notes.D: A pleural drain connects to a closed drainage system to prevent unrestricted air entry into the pleural cavity.
notes.E: A sustained deep inspiration is not a routine requirement for pleural fluid aspiration or drainage.

questions.stem: About the lungs, which is NOT correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The left and right lungs are similar but not identical

options.label: B
options.text: They are covered by visceral pleura except at the hilum

options.label: C
options.text: The region where bronchi and vessels enter is the root

options.label: D
options.text: The right lung is larger than the left

options.label: E
options.text: The main and lobar bronchi lie outside the lung

questions.why: Lobar bronchi are intrapulmonary; only the main bronchi are extrapulmonary.

notes.A: True.
notes.B: True.
notes.C: True (hilum/root).
notes.D: True.

questions.stem: About the lung roots, which is NOT correct?

options.label: B
options.text: The phrenic nerve lies in front of them

options.label: C
options.text: The vagus lies in front of them

options.label: D
options.text: The SVC is related to the right root only

options.label: E
options.text: The azygos vein arches over the right root only

questions.why: The vagus nerve descends posterior to the root of each lung, whereas the phrenic nerve descends anterior to it. This relationship is a useful landmark when studying the mediastinal surface.

notes.A: The hila and roots are situated approximately opposite the fifth to seventh thoracic vertebral levels.
notes.B: The phrenic nerve runs between mediastinal pleura and fibrous pericardium anterior to the lung root.
notes.D: The superior vena cava is a right-sided mediastinal structure related to the anterior aspect of the right lung root.
notes.E: The azygos arch curves above the right lung root before entering the superior vena cava.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a feature of the mediastinal surface of the right lung?
questions.why: The lingula is a projection of the left superior lobe below the cardiac notch. It corresponds roughly to the right middle lobe and is absent from the right lung.

notes.B: The azygos vein arches over the right lung root and produces a groove on its mediastinal surface.
notes.C: The oesophagus is related to the posterior part of the right mediastinal lung surface and may leave an impression.
notes.D: The right superior lobar bronchus lies above the right pulmonary artery at the hilum and is termed eparterial.
notes.E: The superior vena cava is a right-sided mediastinal relation that produces an impression anterior to the hilum.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a feature of the mediastinal surface of the left lung?
questions.why: The eparterial bronchus is the right superior lobar bronchus, which branches above the right pulmonary artery. On the left, the pulmonary artery arches superior to the bronchus at the hilum.

notes.A: The cardiac notch is an indentation of the anterior left lung border that accommodates the heart.
notes.B: The arch and descending thoracic aorta leave impressions on the mediastinal surface of the left lung.
notes.D: The lingula is a tongue-like part of the left superior lobe beneath the cardiac notch.
notes.E: The lower thoracic oesophagus can leave an impression near the inferior part of the left mediastinal lung surface.

questions.stem: About the fissures and lobes of the lungs:

options.label: A
options.text: The oblique fissure is present in the right lung only

options.label: B
options.text: The horizontal fissure is present in both lungs

options.label: C
options.text: The superior lobe lies above and behind the oblique fissure

options.label: D
options.text: The middle lobe is present only in the right lung

options.label: E
options.text: The inferior lobe touches the anterior thoracic wall

questions.why: The right lung has three lobes (including the middle lobe) with oblique and horizontal fissures, while the left has only an oblique fissure and two lobes, so the middle lobe being right-sided only is correct.

notes.A: Both lungs.
notes.B: Right only.
notes.C: Above and IN FRONT.
notes.E: It is mainly posterior and inferior.

questions.stem: About bronchi and bronchopulmonary segments:

options.label: A
options.text: The left main bronchus gives off three lobar bronchi

options.label: B
options.text: Division of lobar into segmental bronchi occurs outside the lung

options.label: C
options.text: A segment is the area supplied by a lobar bronchus

options.label: D
options.text: There are more segmental bronchi in the right lung than the left

options.label: E
options.text: Each segmental bronchus has two branches of the pulmonary artery
