questions.why: The right lung conventionally has ten bronchopulmonary segments, while the left often has eight or nine because some segments share bronchi. Each segment is supplied by a segmental bronchus and pulmonary arterial branch.

notes.A: The left main bronchus supplies two lobes through superior and inferior lobar bronchi.
notes.B: Lobar bronchi divide into segmental bronchi within the lung, supplying subdivisions of their respective lobes.
notes.C: A lobar bronchus supplies a lobe; a bronchopulmonary segment is supplied by a segmental bronchus.
notes.E: A segmental pulmonary arterial branch normally accompanies each segmental bronchus, although arterial branching patterns vary.

questions.stem: Regarding the respiratory tract:

options.label: A
options.text: The whole lower respiratory tract lies below the larynx

options.label: B
options.text: The trachea and all bronchi and bronchioles have the same structure

options.label: C
options.text: The epithelium of the trachea resembles that of the intrapulmonary bronchi

options.label: D
options.text: The tracheobronchial tree ends at the segmental bronchi

questions.why: Both have ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells.

notes.A: The larynx is usually counted as part of the lower tract.
notes.B: Cartilage and glands are lost distally.
notes.D: It continues to bronchioles.
notes.E: They have cartilage plates.

questions.stem: Which is a muscle of expiration in active (forced) breathing?
questions.why: During forced expiration, abdominal wall muscles contract to raise intra-abdominal pressure and push the diaphragm upwards. This reduces thoracic volume, increasing alveolar pressure and driving air out.

notes.A: The scalene muscles elevate and stabilise the upper ribs during inspiration rather than forcing air out.
notes.B: External intercostals generally elevate the ribs during inspiration and help maintain thoracic wall stability.
notes.C: Diaphragmatic contraction increases vertical thoracic diameter during inspiration; relaxation permits the dome to rise during expiration.
notes.E: Sternocleidomastoid assists deep inspiration by elevating the sternum when the head and neck are stabilised.

questions.stem: All of the following about thoracic movements are correct EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: In inspiration all three diameters increase

options.label: B
options.text: Transverse diameter increases by the bucket-handle movement of the ribs

options.label: C
options.text: In expiration the diaphragm is dome-shaped

options.label: D
options.text: Vertical diameter changes are due to diaphragmatic movement

options.label: E
options.text: Ankylosis of the manubriosternal joint affects mainly the transverse diameter

questions.why: During pump-handle movement, the sternum and anterior ends of the ribs rise and move forwards, increasing the chest's anteroposterior diameter. Transverse expansion chiefly results from the bucket-handle movement of the ribs.

notes.A: Inspiration enlarges the thorax vertically, transversely and anteroposteriorly through coordinated diaphragmatic and rib movements.
notes.B: Bucket-handle elevation of the ribs moves their lateral portions outward, increasing the transverse diameter.
notes.C: As the diaphragm relaxes during expiration, its domes rise towards the thoracic cavity.
notes.D: Diaphragmatic descent increases the vertical diameter during inspiration, while ascent reduces it during expiration.

questions.stem: Which can NOT normally be seen on a PA chest radiograph?
questions.why: Normal uncalcified costal cartilage is poorly distinguished on a plain chest radiograph because its attenuation resembles surrounding soft tissue. Calcification with age can make portions of the cartilage visible.

notes.A: The air-filled tracheal lumen produces a radiolucent central column against the mediastinal soft tissues.
notes.C: The diaphragmatic domes form visible curved interfaces between aerated lung and the abdominal soft tissues.
notes.D: The aortic arch creates the aortic knuckle, a visible contour of the left superior mediastinum.
notes.E: The main bronchi may be recognised as air-filled branching structures near the central pulmonary hila.

questions.stem: In thoracocentesis in the midaxillary line, the needle passes through all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.why: The target of thoracocentesis is the pleural space between the parietal and visceral layers. Entering visceral pleura would penetrate the lung surface rather than remaining within the intended space.

notes.A: Serratus anterior overlies the lateral thoracic wall and may be traversed in a midaxillary approach.
notes.B: The internal intercostal muscle forms an intermediate layer of the lateral intercostal wall.
notes.C: Parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall and must be crossed to enter the pleural cavity.
notes.E: Endothoracic fascia lies deep to the intercostal layers and superficial to the parietal pleura.

questions.stem: True or false: In pleural aspiration, the needle passes through the intercostal space close to the upper border of the rib below.
questions.why: The main intercostal neurovascular bundle occupies the costal groove along the lower edge of the upper rib. The route above the rib below reduces injury risk, while ultrasound identifies an appropriate site for pleural aspiration.

notes.B: The upper border of the lower rib is preferred over the lower border of the upper rib, where the main bundle runs.

questions.stem: The rectosigmoid junction lies in front of the:
questions.why: The rectum conventionally begins in front of the third sacral vertebra, where the sigmoid mesocolon ends and the three longitudinal muscle bands spread into a continuous outer layer.

notes.B: The prostate is related to the anterior wall of the lower male rectum, not its upper junction with the sigmoid colon.
notes.C: The obturator foramen lies in the anterolateral bony pelvis rather than at the posterior rectosigmoid junction.
notes.D: The urinary bladder lies anterior to the rectum and does not define its upper vertebral level.
notes.E: The pararectal fossae are peritoneal depressions beside the rectum, not the landmark defining its origin.

questions.stem: The caudate lobe of the liver lies:

options.label: A
options.text: Between the gallbladder and the fissure for the ligamentum teres

options.label: B
options.text: Between the IVC and the fissure for the ligamentum venosum

options.label: C
options.text: At the back of the left lobe

options.label: E
options.text: Between the left lobe and the quadrate lobe

questions.why: The caudate lobe is on the visceral surface of the liver, posterior to the porta hepatis. It lies between the groove for the inferior vena cava and fissure for the ligamentum venosum.

notes.A: The quadrate lobe lies between the gallbladder fossa and the ligamentum teres fissure, anterior to the porta hepatis.
notes.C: The caudate lobe is a distinct posterior region rather than simply the back of the anatomical left lobe.
notes.D: The anterosuperior diaphragmatic surface is smooth and does not contain the principal landmarks of the caudate lobe.
notes.E: The porta hepatis separates the caudate lobe posteriorly from the quadrate lobe anteriorly.

questions.stem: A man has an ischioanal abscess. The roof of the ischioanal fossa is formed by:

notes.A: It forms part of the anterior recess boundary, not the roof.
notes.B: The roof (apex) is where levator ani arises from the obturator fascia.

questions.why: The fossa is wedge-shaped: lateral wall obturator internus fascia; medial/superior wall levator ani; they meet at the roof.

questions.stem: Anatomical differences between internal and external haemorrhoids:

options.label: A
options.text: Internal haemorrhoid mucosa has visceral (GVA) innervation, external has somatic (GSA)

options.label: B
options.text: Internal involve the superior rectal veins; external involve the middle rectal veins

options.label: C
options.text: Bleeding from external haemorrhoids is more profuse than from internal

notes.A: Visceral sensory innervation above the pectinate line contrasts with inferior rectal nerve supply below it.
notes.B: External haemorrhoids involve the external plexus draining through inferior rectal veins, not primarily the middle rectal veins.
notes.C: Internal haemorrhoids characteristically produce bright red rectal bleeding, whereas external haemorrhoids are especially associated with painful thrombosis.

questions.why: The pectinate line distinguishes the visceral sensory territory above from somatic sensory territory below. Internal haemorrhoids arise above this line and commonly bleed painlessly; thrombosed external haemorrhoids can be markedly painful.

questions.stem: About the vestibule of the mouth:

options.label: A
options.text: It is bounded internally by the teeth and gums (dental arches)

options.label: B
options.text: It always communicates with the oral cavity proper

options.label: C
options.text: It opens to the exterior through the isthmus of the fauces

options.label: D
options.text: The front and infratemporal surfaces of the maxilla can be felt with a finger in the vestibule

options.label: E
options.text: The parotid duct opens opposite the 3rd lower molar

notes.B: Even with the teeth clenched, through the gap behind the last molars.
notes.C: It opens through the ORAL FISSURE; the isthmus of the fauces joins the mouth to the oropharynx.
notes.E: It opens opposite the upper 2nd molar.

questions.why: The vestibule lies between the lips/cheeks and the dental arches, its outer wall overlying the maxilla (A, D true); B is false (with the teeth closed it communicates with the oral cavity only behind the last molar), C is false (it opens externally at the oral fissure, not the fauces) and E is false (the parotid duct opens opposite the 2nd UPPER molar).

questions.stem: About the lips:

options.label: A
options.text: The line of contact of closed lips is at the cutting edge of the lower incisors

options.label: B
options.text: The vertical groove on the external surface of the upper lip is the philtrum

options.label: C
options.text: The angle of the mouth lies in front of the 1st premolar

options.label: D
options.text: The main muscle of the lips is orbicularis oris

options.label: E
options.text: The inner (mucosal) surface of the lips contains abundant sebaceous glands

notes.A: The classical surface landmark for the oral fissure is the upper incisal edge, with variation according to posture and dentition.
notes.B: The philtrum is the vertical midline groove on the external surface of the upper lip.
notes.C: The oral commissure usually lies just anterior to the first premolar, although its level varies with facial and dental anatomy.
notes.D: Orbicularis oris surrounds the oral fissure and contributes to closing and protruding the lips.
notes.E: Labial mucosa contains minor salivary glands; ectopic sebaceous glands may occur but are not its principal glandular component.

questions.why: The lips consist of a muscular core of orbicularis oris covered by skin externally and mucosa internally. Their external landmarks include the philtrum and oral commissures, whose relationship to the teeth varies.

questions.stem: About the cheeks:

options.label: A
options.text: They form the lateral wall of the vestibule and are continuous in front with the lips

options.label: B
options.text: Their principal muscle (buccinator) arises posteriorly from the pterygomandibular raphe

options.label: C
options.text: They are often unaffected in facial nerve paralysis

options.label: D
options.text: Structurally the lip resembles the cheek

options.label: E
options.text: The principal muscle of the cheek is masseter

notes.A: The cheeks bound the vestibule laterally and merge with the lips at the corners of the mouth.
notes.B: Buccinator takes origin partly from the pterygomandibular raphe, which also provides attachment for the superior pharyngeal constrictor.
notes.C: Facial nerve paralysis weakens buccinator, allowing food to collect between the cheek and teeth.
notes.D: Both cheek and lip have external skin, a muscular core and an internal mucosal lining.
notes.E: Masseter elevates the mandible outside the cheek wall; buccinator is the principal muscle of the cheek itself.

questions.why: The cheek is the muscular lateral boundary of the vestibule, with buccinator supporting the mucosa and keeping food between the teeth. Like the lips, it has skin externally and oral mucosa internally.

questions.stem: About the gingivae (gums):

options.label: C
options.text: Their epithelium is stratified squamous, mostly parakeratinized

options.label: D
options.text: They are attached to the enamel

notes.A: Attached gingiva lacks a distinct submucosa and is firmly connected to the underlying periosteum.
notes.B: The gingiva covers the alveolar process and surrounds the tooth neck, superficial to the coronal part of the periodontal attachment.
notes.C: The exposed gingival surface is commonly covered by keratinised or parakeratinised stratified squamous epithelium.
notes.D: At a healthy tooth with no attachment loss, junctional epithelium adheres to the enamel near the cemento-enamel junction.
notes.E: Cementoblasts deposit cementum on the tooth root, whereas gingiva develops as specialised oral mucosa.

questions.why: Gingiva is masticatory mucosa surrounding the teeth. Attached gingiva is firmly bound to underlying tissue, and the junctional epithelium provides the epithelial attachment at the tooth surface.

questions.stem: About the oral cavity proper:

options.label: A
options.text: It is limited below by the dorsum of the tongue

options.label: B
options.text: It communicates with the exterior through the oral fissure

options.label: C
options.text: The sublingual space is part of it

options.label: D
options.text: The frenulum of the tongue divides the sublingual region into right and left parts

options.label: E
options.text: The soft palate forms its posterosuperior wall

notes.A: The tongue occupies much of the cavity, while its underlying muscular floor is formed chiefly by mylohyoid.
notes.B: The oral fissure communicates with the vestibule, which in turn communicates with the oral cavity proper.
notes.C: The sublingual space lies immediately beneath the floor-of-mouth mucosa and contains the sublingual gland and related structures.
notes.D: The lingual frenulum marks the midline of the visible floor of the mouth, with a sublingual fold on each side.
notes.E: The soft palate forms the posterior portion of the roof and participates in separating the oral and nasal pharyngeal passages.

questions.why: The oral cavity proper lies inside the dental arches and has a muscular floor formed principally by mylohyoid beneath the tongue. The hard and soft palate form its roof.

questions.stem: About human teeth:

options.label: A
options.text: There are five deciduous teeth in each half of each jaw

options.label: B
options.text: The deciduous set has no premolars, whereas each permanent quadrant has two

options.label: C
options.text: The part of the tooth above the gingiva is the clinical crown

options.label: D
options.text: The junction of enamel and cementum on the dentine surface is the cervix (neck)

options.label: E
options.text: The dentine of the anatomical crown is covered by cementum

notes.A: Each deciduous quadrant contains two incisors, one canine and two molars, totalling five teeth.
notes.B: Premolars occur in permanent dentition and replace deciduous molars during the transition to adult teeth.
notes.C: The clinical crown is the exposed part of the tooth, so its extent depends on gingival level.
notes.D: The cemento-enamel junction demarcates the anatomical neck between the enamel-covered crown and cementum-covered root.
notes.E: Enamel covers crown dentine; cementum instead covers the root dentine and provides periodontal ligament attachment.

questions.why: The deciduous dentition contains twenty teeth, while the complete permanent dentition has thirty-two. The anatomical crown is enamel-covered; the clinical crown denotes the portion visible above the gingival margin.

questions.stem: Bony attachments of the extrinsic muscles of the tongue include the:

notes.A: Styloglossus arises from the styloid process and retracts and elevates the sides of the tongue.
notes.B: Genioglossus arises from the superior mental spine of the mandible and principally protrudes the tongue.
notes.C: Hyoglossus arises from the body and greater horn of the hyoid and depresses the tongue.
notes.D: The pterygoid process anchors muscles such as the pterygoids, not the standard extrinsic tongue muscles.
notes.E: Palatoglossus arises from the soft palate rather than directly from the bony hard palate.

questions.why: Extrinsic tongue muscles originate outside the tongue and move it as a whole. Genioglossus, hyoglossus and styloglossus arise from bone, while palatoglossus arises from the palatine aponeurosis.

questions.stem: Human dentition is:

notes.A: Homodont dentition consists of broadly similar teeth, unlike the differentiated human incisors, canines and posterior teeth.
notes.B: Diphyodont dentition has two successive generations of teeth, represented by the deciduous and permanent sets.
notes.C: Haplodont teeth have a simple conical form, unlike the complex cusped posterior teeth of humans.
notes.D: Heterodont dentition contains different tooth classes adapted for cutting, tearing and grinding food.
notes.E: Polyphyodont dentition involves repeated generations of replacement teeth, rather than the two human sets.

questions.why: Human teeth are heterodont because they have distinct shapes adapted for different functions, and diphyodont because deciduous dentition is followed by permanent dentition. These terms describe separate aspects of dental organisation.

questions.stem: Parts of the stomach include the:

notes.A: The cardia surrounds the gastro-oesophageal opening where food enters the stomach from the oesophagus.
notes.B: The incisura angularis is a notch on the lesser curvature that helps mark the boundary between the body and pyloric part.
notes.C: The body forms the large central region between the fundus and the pyloric part of the stomach.
notes.D: An isthmus is a narrow connecting region in other organs and is not a standard major gastric division.
notes.E: The term ampulla describes dilated regions such as the rectal ampulla, not a standard division of the stomach.

questions.why: The stomach is divided into cardia, fundus, body and pyloric part, with the last subdivided into antrum and canal. Named notches and openings are landmarks rather than separate major regions.

questions.stem: About the peritoneum:

options.label: A
options.text: A fold passing between the stomach and another organ is an omentum

options.label: B
options.text: A fold attaching the intestine to the posterior abdominal wall is a mesentery

options.label: C
options.text: A fold connecting one organ to another (or to the wall) is a peritoneal ligament

options.label: D
options.text: Visceral peritoneum is more pain-sensitive than parietal

notes.A: Omenta extend from the stomach or proximal duodenum to other abdominal structures, as in the lesser and greater omenta.
notes.B: A mesentery is a double peritoneal fold suspending intestinal structures from the abdominal wall and transmitting their vessels.
notes.C: A peritoneal ligament is a fold joining an organ to another organ or to the abdominal wall.
notes.D: Parietal peritoneum has somatic innervation and is sensitive to local irritation, while visceral sensation chiefly responds to stretch and chemical stimuli.
notes.E: Peritoneal surfaces are lined by mesothelium, whereas endothelium lines blood and lymphatic vessels.

questions.why: Peritoneal folds suspend and connect abdominal viscera while providing pathways for vessels, lymphatics and nerves. The peritoneum itself is a serous membrane with a mesothelial lining and differing visceral and parietal sensory supply.

questions.stem: About the peritoneal cavity:

options.label: A
options.text: It communicates with the exterior only in the female

options.label: B
options.text: The supracolic compartment includes the subphrenic spaces

options.label: C
options.text: An abscess in the right subphrenic space cannot spread to the left subphrenic space

options.label: D
options.text: The left infracolic space communicates freely with the right medial paracolic gutter

options.label: E
options.text: The right medial paracolic gutter drains directly into the rectovesical pouch

notes.A: The uterine tubes communicate with the peritoneal cavity, providing a potential route through the female reproductive tract.
notes.B: The subphrenic spaces lie between diaphragm and liver within the supracolic region of the greater sac.
notes.C: The falciform ligament limits direct subphrenic spread but does not prevent all communication between the two regions.
notes.D: The small-intestinal mesenteric root divides the infracolic spaces, while the left space opens inferiorly into the pelvis.
notes.E: The usual named right paracolic gutter is lateral to the ascending colon and communicates with the pelvis inferiorly.

questions.why: The transverse mesocolon divides the greater sac into supracolic and infracolic regions. Peritoneal reflections partly restrict fluid movement, but communicating gutters allow fluid to spread between abdominal and pelvic spaces.

questions.stem: About the omental bursa (lesser sac):

options.label: A
options.text: Its superior recess is larger than its inferior recess

options.label: B
options.text: It communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen

options.label: C
options.text: Its anterior relations include the quadrate lobe of the liver

options.label: D
options.text: It extends into the greater omentum

options.label: E
options.text: Its posterior relations include the left suprarenal gland

notes.A: The traditional unfused inferior recess is more extensive; fusion of the omental layers can markedly reduce it in adults.
notes.B: The epiploic foramen provides the normal connection between the omental bursa and the greater sac.
notes.C: The caudate lobe is related to the superior part of the bursa, rather than the quadrate lobe.
notes.D: The inferior recess can extend between the layers of the greater omentum before their variable fusion.
notes.E: The left suprarenal gland is among the posterior relations of the bursa, separated by intervening peritoneum.

questions.why: The lesser sac lies behind the stomach and communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen. Inferior extension into the greater omentum varies with fusion of its peritoneal layers.

questions.stem: Boundaries of the lesser sac:

options.label: A
options.text: On the left: the spleen and the splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament

options.label: B
options.text: On the right: the posterior layer of the right coronary ligament

options.label: D
options.text: Behind: peritoneum covering the diaphragm and pancreas

options.label: E
options.text: In front: the lesser omentum and stomach

notes.A: The splenic recess extends leftwards between peritoneal folds related to the spleen, including the splenorenal ligament.
notes.B: The right coronary ligament reflects around the bare area of the liver, rather than defining the right boundary of the lesser sac.
notes.C: The transverse mesocolon is related to the inferior boundary of the main lesser sac in the usual adult arrangement.
notes.D: The posterior wall includes peritoneum over the pancreas and diaphragm, separating these structures from the cavity.
notes.E: The posterior gastric surface and lesser omentum form much of the anterior boundary of the omental bursa.

questions.why: The lesser sac is bounded anteriorly by the stomach and lesser omentum and posteriorly by peritoneum covering retroperitoneal structures. It extends leftwards towards the spleen and communicates rightwards through the epiploic foramen.

questions.stem: Organs completely (intraperitoneally) covered by peritoneum include the:

notes.A: The spleen is invested by visceral peritoneum except at its hilum, where its vascular structures enter.
notes.B: The urinary bladder is predominantly subperitoneal, with its superior surface covered by reflected peritoneum.
notes.C: The vermiform appendix is intraperitoneal and is suspended by its vascular mesoappendix.
notes.D: Most of the duodenum is secondarily retroperitoneal, with only its proximal portion freely mobile and peritoneally invested.
notes.E: The gallbladder surface attached to the liver lacks a complete serosal covering, unlike a freely invested intraperitoneal organ.

questions.why: Intraperitoneal organs are invested by visceral peritoneum except at attachments such as a hilum or mesentery. The gallbladder and bladder have substantial uncovered surfaces, and most of the duodenum is secondarily retroperitoneal.

questions.stem: Organs PARTIALLY covered by peritoneum include the:

notes.A: The sigmoid colon is conventionally intraperitoneal and suspended by its sigmoid mesocolon.
notes.B: The liver has uncovered regions including its bare area, porta hepatis and gallbladder attachment.
notes.C: The ovary projects into the peritoneal cavity. Specialised ovarian surface epithelium covers its free surface.
notes.D: Only the proximal duodenum is freely intraperitoneal; most of the remainder is fixed against the posterior abdominal wall.
notes.E: Peritoneum covers the uterine fundus and portions of the body but does not completely surround the cervix.

questions.why: Peritoneal investment varies according to an organ’s attachments and position. The liver has a bare area, most of the duodenum is retroperitoneal, and the uterus is only partly covered by reflected peritoneum.

questions.stem: About the duodenum:

options.label: B
options.text: Its first 2.5 cm is freely mobile

notes.A: The combined four duodenal parts measure approximately 25 cm in the standard gross anatomy description.
notes.B: The proximal duodenal cap is mobile and differs from the predominantly retroperitoneal distal duodenum.
notes.C: The horizontal third part is conventionally about 10 cm long in the standard four-part description.
notes.D: The descending second part is commonly described as approximately 7.5 cm long in this teaching scheme.
notes.E: The ascending fourth part is conventionally about 2.5 cm long, although measured lengths vary between individuals.

questions.why: The duodenum has four parts that curve around the pancreatic head. Its usual teaching length is approximately 25 cm, with the proximal bulb being mobile and most remaining segments fixed retroperitoneally.

questions.stem: About the jejunum and ileum:

options.label: A
options.text: The jejunum is shorter (2/5) than the ileum (3/5)

options.label: B
options.text: The jejunum has a thicker wall than the ileum

options.label: C
options.text: Occlusion of a vasa recta may cause infarction of a segment in the jejunum but not in the ileum

options.label: E
options.text: In the jejunum, mesenteric fat is thin and does not reach the gut wall

notes.A: The conventional length proportions are two-fifths jejunum and three-fifths ileum, excluding the duodenum.
notes.B: The jejunum has more prominent circular folds and a thicker wall than the distal ileum.
notes.C: Straight mesenteric vessels supply discrete territories in both regions. The greater number of ileal arcades does not guarantee collateral flow beyond a blocked straight vessel.
notes.D: Both jejunum and ileum are intraperitoneal and receive their vascular supply through the small-intestinal mesentery.
notes.E: Jejunal mesenteric fat typically stops short of the intestinal border, leaving translucent windows between vessels.

questions.why: The jejunum occupies the proximal two-fifths of the mobile small intestine and generally has a thicker wall, longer vasa recta and less mesenteric fat than the ileum. Both regions are suspended by mesentery.

questions.stem: The root of the mesentery crosses the:

notes.A: The horizontal third duodenal part is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric vessels and mesenteric root.
notes.B: The mesenteric root crosses the abdominal aorta as it descends obliquely to the right.
notes.C: The inferior vena cava lies behind the mesenteric attachment along its course across the posterior abdominal wall.
notes.D: The right ureter descends retroperitoneally behind the attachment of the small-intestinal mesentery.
notes.E: The right gonadal vessels descend along the posterior abdominal wall and are crossed by the mesenteric root.

questions.why: The small-intestinal mesenteric root extends obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure towards the right iliac fossa. Its short attachment crosses major retroperitoneal structures while the free edge supports the mobile jejunum and ileum.

questions.stem: About the large intestine:

options.label: B
options.text: Its longitudinal muscle is gathered into taeniae coli

options.label: D
options.text: The appendices epiploicae are small fat-filled peritoneal tags

options.label: E
options.text: The taeniae run from the appendix to the sigmoid colon

notes.A: The colonic lumen contains an abundant microbial community that participates in fermentation and other metabolic processes.
notes.B: The outer longitudinal muscle of the colon is concentrated into three bands called the taeniae coli.
notes.C: Haustra are sacculations of the colonic wall associated with the arrangement and tone of its longitudinal muscle.
notes.D: Appendices epiploicae are small fat-containing peritoneal projections attached to the external surface of the colon.
notes.E: The taeniae converge at the appendiceal base and continue along the colon until they broaden at the rectosigmoid junction.

questions.why: The colon is distinguished by three longitudinal muscle bands, haustra and fat-filled appendices epiploicae. Its luminal microbiota also participate in fermentation of material not digested by human enzymes.

questions.stem: About the vermiform appendix:

options.label: A
options.text: Its average length is about 9 cm

options.label: B
options.text: Its base is where the taeniae coli converge

options.label: D
options.text: Its base lies below the ileocaecal orifice

notes.A: Appendiceal length varies considerably, with approximately 9 cm representing a traditional average in gross anatomy.
notes.B: The three caecal taeniae converge at the base of the appendix and provide a reliable anatomical landmark.
notes.C: The mesoappendix suspends the appendix and contains its principal arterial and venous supply.
notes.D: The appendiceal base opens into the caecum inferior to the ileocaecal orifice.
notes.E: The retrocaecal position places the appendiceal tip behind the caecum and is commonly described as the most frequent position.

questions.why: The appendix is a blind-ended tube arising from the caecum below the ileocaecal opening. Its base is relatively constant, but the direction of its tip varies and is commonly retrocaecal.

questions.stem: About the rectum:

options.label: A
options.text: It begins at the level of S4

options.label: B
options.text: It ends at the level of the tip of the coccyx

options.label: D
options.text: It has no mesentery anywhere along its length

options.label: E
options.text: Its ampulla is its upper part

notes.A: The rectosigmoid junction is conventionally located at the third sacral vertebra rather than the fourth.
notes.B: The anorectal junction lies near the tip of the coccyx, anterior to it where puborectalis encircles the bowel.
notes.C: The rectum is generally approximately 12–15 cm long, rather than a fixed length of 20 cm.
notes.D: The rectum lacks a free suspensory peritoneal mesentery, although its surrounding mesorectal connective tissue carries vessels and lymphatics.
notes.E: The ampulla is the dilated distal portion of the rectum, which accommodates faeces before defaecation.

questions.why: The rectum extends from approximately S3 to the anorectal junction at the pelvic floor. It is usually around 12–15 cm long, with its lower part dilated into the rectal ampulla.

questions.stem: Peritoneal relations of the rectum:

options.label: A
options.text: Its whole surface is covered by peritoneum

options.label: B
options.text: Only its anterior surface is covered throughout

options.label: C
options.text: Its upper third is covered in front and at the sides

options.label: D
options.text: Its middle third is covered in front only

options.label: E
options.text: Its lower third has no peritoneal covering

notes.A: The posterior rectal surface and distal rectum are uncovered, so the entire organ is not intraperitoneal.
notes.B: The lateral surfaces of the upper rectum have peritoneum, and even the anterior covering ends at the lower rectum.
notes.C: The upper rectum is covered by peritoneum on its anterior and lateral surfaces but not posteriorly.
notes.D: The middle rectum retains an anterior peritoneal covering as the lateral reflection recedes.
notes.E: The lower rectum lies below the peritoneal reflection and is surrounded by pelvic connective tissue.

questions.why: Peritoneum covers progressively less of the rectum as it descends. The conventional upper, middle and lower thirds have anterior and lateral, only anterior, and no peritoneal covering respectively.

questions.stem: Regarding the anal canal:

options.label: A
options.text: It begins at the anorectal junction

options.label: B
options.text: The anal columns contain terminal branches of the superior rectal artery and vein

options.label: C
options.text: The lower ends of the anal columns are joined by the anal valves

options.label: D
options.text: The line formed by the anal valves is the pectinate line

options.label: E
options.text: Its smooth (circular) muscle forms the internal anal sphincter

notes.B: Of the SUPERIOR, not inferior, rectal vessels.

questions.why: The anal canal begins at the anorectal junction; its anal columns are joined below by anal valves forming the pectinate line, and its circular smooth muscle thickens into the internal anal sphincter (A, C, D, E true); B is keyed false.

questions.stem: About the tongue:

options.label: A
options.text: The sulcus terminalis divides the dorsum into anterior one-third and posterior two-thirds

options.label: B
options.text: The apex of the sulcus terminalis points backwards and is at the foramen caecum

options.label: C
options.text: Macroglossia is due to hypertrophy of the lingual muscles

options.label: D
options.text: The foramen caecum marks the origin of the parotid duct

options.label: E
options.text: Movement of the tip is restrained by the frenulum

questions.why: The V-shaped sulcus terminalis points back to the foramen caecum, origin of the thyroglossal duct.

notes.A: Anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third.
notes.C: It has many causes (e.g. hypothyroidism, amyloid, acromegaly).
notes.D: It marks the origin of the THYROGLOSSAL duct.
notes.E: The frenulum limits the movement of the whole tongue, not just the tip.

questions.stem: About the lingual papillae:

options.label: A
options.text: Fungiform papillae are relatively few in number

options.label: B
options.text: Filiform papillae are concentrated at the margins

options.label: C
options.text: Foliate papillae are concentrated around the foramen caecum

options.label: D
options.text: Vallate papillae are concentrated at the tip

options.label: E
options.text: Most taste buds are on filiform papillae

questions.why: Fungiform papillae are scattered among the much more numerous filiform papillae, particularly near the tip and margins of the tongue. They contain taste buds and have a rounded, mushroom-like profile.

notes.B: Filiform papillae cover much of the anterior dorsum and provide mechanical friction, rather than being confined mainly to the margins.
notes.C: Foliate papillae form folds on the posterolateral tongue rather than encircling the foramen caecum.
notes.D: Vallate papillae form a row immediately anterior to the sulcus terminalis, not at the tip.
notes.E: Filiform papillae are mechanical papillae and lack taste buds; gustatory receptors occur in other papillae.

questions.stem: About the salivary glands:

options.label: A
options.text: About 5 L of saliva is produced daily

options.label: C
options.text: The sublingual glands produce the least of the three major glands

options.label: D
options.text: The three major glands produce saliva of the same composition

options.label: E
options.text: The submandibular gland has equal numbers of mucous and serous cells

questions.why: Sublingual glands make about 5%; submandibular about 70% at rest; parotid about 25%.

notes.A: About 1–1.5 L a day.
notes.B: The submandibular produces most at rest.
notes.D: Composition differs (serous vs mucous).
notes.E: It is mainly serous.

questions.stem: About the salivary ducts:

options.label: A
options.text: The parotid duct arises from the medial border of the gland

options.label: B
options.text: The parotid duct pierces masseter to open into the mouth

options.label: C
options.text: The submandibular duct arises from the deep part of the gland

options.label: D
options.text: The sublingual gland has the largest duct

options.label: E
options.text: The sublingual ducts cannot be shown radiographically

questions.why: The submandibular duct arises from the deep part of the gland and travels forwards in the floor of the mouth. It opens at the sublingual caruncle beside the lingual frenulum.

notes.A: The parotid duct emerges from the anterior border of the gland before crossing the lateral surface of masseter.
notes.B: The parotid duct crosses masseter superficially and turns medially to pierce buccinator before entering the oral vestibule.
notes.D: The sublingual gland drains mainly through multiple small ducts rather than having the largest major salivary duct.
notes.E: The sublingual gland commonly drains through multiple small ducts. Conventional sialography may miss these ducts, but their visibility depends on the imaging technique.

questions.stem: About the oesophagus:

options.label: B
options.text: It begins in the midline at the level of C4

options.label: C
options.text: As it descends it first deviates to the right

options.label: D
options.text: It pierces the diaphragm at T8

options.label: E
options.text: In the neck, the retropharyngeal space lies in front of it

questions.why: The adult oesophagus is approximately 25 cm long, extending from the pharyngoesophageal junction at C6 to the gastric cardia near T11. Its length varies with body size.

notes.B: The oesophagus originates at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, approximately C6 rather than C4.
notes.C: The cervical oesophagus is usually directed slightly to the left of the midline as it descends.
notes.D: The oesophagus passes through the muscular oesophageal hiatus at T10, whereas the caval opening is at T8.
notes.E: The retropharyngeal and related retrovisceral spaces lie posterior to the pharynx and oesophagus rather than anteriorly.

questions.stem: About the oesophagus:

options.label: A
options.text: In the thorax it passes through the superior and posterior mediastina

options.label: B
options.text: Its abdominal part is about 4 cm long

options.label: C
options.text: Its left border is continuous with the lesser curvature

options.label: D
options.text: The left vagal trunk lies on its posterior surface

options.label: E
options.text: Its left border makes an obtuse angle with the fundus

questions.why: The thoracic oesophagus descends through the superior mediastinum before passing into the posterior mediastinum below the transverse thoracic plane. It enters the abdomen through the oesophageal hiatus.

notes.B: The abdominal oesophagus is usually only about one to two centimetres long before joining the stomach.
notes.C: The right oesophageal border is continuous with the lesser curvature, while the left border meets the gastric fundus.
notes.D: The left vagus supplies most fibres of the anterior vagal trunk, while the right vagus contributes mainly to the posterior trunk.
notes.E: The left oesophageal border forms with the fundus an acute angle called the cardiac notch.

questions.stem: About the oesophageal constrictions, all are correct EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: The first constriction is at C4

options.label: B
options.text: The first constriction is about 15 cm from the incisor teeth

options.label: C
options.text: The second is where the arch of the aorta crosses it

options.label: D
options.text: The second is about 22.5 cm from the incisor teeth

options.label: E
options.text: The diaphragmatic constriction is about 40 cm from the incisor teeth

questions.why: The upper oesophageal constriction is at the pharyngoesophageal junction near C6, where the cricopharyngeus surrounds the passage at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage.

notes.B: The cricopharyngeal narrowing is encountered approximately 15 cm from the upper incisor teeth during endoscopy.
notes.C: The arch of the aorta crosses the oesophagus and produces one of its normal thoracic impressions.
notes.D: The aortic impression lies roughly 22–25 cm from the upper incisors, with variation between individuals.
notes.E: The diaphragmatic narrowing is encountered near 38–40 cm from the incisors, depending on body size.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the liver?

options.label: A
options.text: It is anatomically divided into right and left lobes by the ligamentum venosum

options.label: B
options.text: Its inferior border is notched by the ligamentum teres

options.label: C
options.text: Its right surface includes the bare area

options.label: D
options.text: Its inferior border separates the anterior from the posterior surface

options.label: E
options.text: The fundus of the gallbladder projects above the inferior border

questions.why: The round ligament of the liver occupies a fissure extending from the umbilical region to the visceral surface. Its course produces a notch in the sharp inferior border.

notes.A: The falciform ligament marks the lobar division on the diaphragmatic surface. The fissure for ligamentum venosum forms only part of the boundary on the visceral side.
notes.C: The bare area lies mainly on the posterosuperior aspect of the right lobe, where coronary reflections bound its direct contact with the diaphragm.
notes.D: The sharp inferior border separates the anterior diaphragmatic surface from the visceral surface rather than the posterior aspect.
notes.E: The gallbladder fundus commonly extends inferior to the liver margin near the right ninth costal cartilage.

questions.stem: The peritoneal fold joining the liver to the anterior abdominal wall is the:
questions.why: The falciform ligament is a double layer of peritoneum connecting the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm. Its free inferior edge contains the ligamentum teres.

notes.B: The triangular ligaments are lateral peritoneal reflections attaching the liver to the diaphragm on either side.
notes.C: The coronary ligament is reflected between the liver and diaphragm and defines margins of the bare area.
notes.D: The hepatogastric ligament forms part of the lesser omentum between the liver and lesser curvature of the stomach.
notes.E: The ligamentum teres is the fibrous remnant of the fetal umbilical vein within the falciform ligament.

questions.stem: The surfaces of the liver include the following EXCEPT:
questions.why: Described surfaces: diaphragmatic (anterior, superior, posterior, right) and visceral.

notes.A: Described.
notes.B: Described.
notes.C: Described.
notes.D: Described.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a peritoneal fold?
questions.why: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum is a fibromuscular structure supporting the duodenojejunal flexure. Despite its common name, ligament of Treitz, it is not simply a double layer of peritoneum.

notes.B: The hepatogastric ligament is a double peritoneal layer connecting the liver with the lesser gastric curvature.
notes.C: The mesoappendix is a peritoneal mesentery carrying the appendicular vessels to the vermiform appendix.
notes.D: The gastrosplenic ligament is a peritoneal fold carrying short gastric and left gastro-omental vessels between stomach and spleen.
notes.E: The falciform ligament is a double peritoneal reflection connecting the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm.

questions.stem: The right subphrenic space is bounded above by the:

options.label: B
options.text: Superior (anterior) layer of the coronary ligament

options.label: C
options.text: Posterior layer of the coronary ligament

questions.why: It lies between the diaphragm and the liver, limited behind/above by the upper layer of the coronary ligament and on the left by the falciform ligament.

notes.A: Its left boundary.
notes.C: Bounds the hepatorenal pouch.
notes.D: Left side.
notes.E: Lesser omentum.

questions.stem: All of the following about the root of the mesentery are correct EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: The right infracolic space lies on its right side

options.label: B
options.text: It runs down from right to left at about 45°

options.label: C
options.text: It crosses the 3rd part of the duodenum

questions.why: The mesenteric root runs obliquely downwards and to the right from the duodenojejunal flexure to the right iliac region. Its direction is opposite to a course from right to left.

notes.A: The root separates the infracolic compartment into right and left spaces, with the right space on its right side.
notes.C: The horizontal third part of the duodenum lies posterior to the root of the small intestinal mesentery.
notes.D: The mesenteric root passes across the anterior surface of the right psoas major as it approaches the right iliac region.
notes.E: The inferior vena cava is among the retroperitoneal structures crossed by the small intestinal mesenteric root.

questions.stem: All of the following about the left paracolic gutter are correct EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: It lies beside the descending colon

options.label: B
options.text: It is limited above by the phrenicocolic ligament

options.label: C
options.text: It communicates freely with the pelvis

options.label: E
options.text: It is limited below by the attachment of the sigmoid mesocolon

questions.why: The left lateral paracolic gutter extends down alongside the descending colon into the pelvic peritoneal cavity. Its superior communication is restricted by the phrenicocolic ligament, but it is not normally sealed inferiorly.

notes.A: The left paracolic gutter is the peritoneal channel lateral to the descending colon along the abdominal wall.
notes.B: The phrenicocolic ligament forms a barrier to upward spread of fluid from the left paracolic gutter into the left subphrenic region.
notes.C: The inferior opening of the left paracolic gutter permits peritoneal fluid to descend into the pelvic cavity.
notes.D: The gutter passes across the pelvic brim as it continues from the abdominal compartment towards the pelvis.

questions.stem: About the visceral surface of the liver:

options.label: A
options.text: The porta hepatis separates the caudate lobe from the quadrate lobe

options.label: B
options.text: The IVC groove lies medial to the caudate lobe

options.label: C
options.text: The colic impression is on the left lobe

options.label: D
options.text: The gastric impression is on the right lobe

options.label: E
options.text: The gallbladder fossa forms the medial border of the quadrate lobe

questions.why: The porta hepatis is the transverse fissure on the visceral surface through which hepatic ducts, vessels and nerves pass. It separates the caudate lobe posteriorly from the quadrate lobe anteriorly.

notes.B: The inferior vena cava groove lies on the right of the caudate lobe, while the ligamentum venosum fissure lies on its left.
notes.C: The colic impression lies on the visceral surface of the right lobe near the right colic flexure.
notes.D: The gastric impression is on the visceral surface of the left lobe where it relates to the stomach.
notes.E: The gallbladder fossa forms the right boundary of the quadrate lobe and the round ligament fissure forms the left boundary.

questions.stem: Conditions directly associated with the stomach include:

notes.A: A congenital diaphragmatic defect can permit abdominal viscera, including the stomach, to enter the thorax.
notes.B: A hiatus hernia involves migration of part of the stomach through the oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm.
notes.C: Pyrosis is the burning sensation commonly caused by reflux of acidic gastric contents into the oesophagus.

questions.why: Displacement of the stomach through diaphragmatic openings and reflux of its acidic contents are distinct anatomical and functional problems. Both can affect the upper gastrointestinal tract.

questions.stem: Functions of the extrahepatic biliary apparatus include:

options.label: B
options.text: Regulating discharge of bile into the duodenum

options.label: C
options.text: Regulating production of bile in the liver

notes.A: The gallbladder stores bile and absorbs water and electrolytes to increase its concentration between meals.
notes.B: The sphincter of Oddi and gallbladder contraction regulate delivery of bile into the duodenal lumen.
notes.C: Hepatocytes and intrahepatic duct cells produce and modify bile. The extrahepatic biliary apparatus mainly stores, concentrates and conveys the fluid.

questions.why: The extrahepatic biliary system transports bile from the liver, stores and concentrates it in the gallbladder, and regulates delivery to the duodenum. Hepatocytes produce bile within the liver.

questions.stem: The extrahepatic biliary apparatus includes the:

notes.A: The right and left hepatic ducts drain their respective hepatic territories and unite to form the common hepatic duct.
notes.B: The cystic duct connects the gallbladder neck to the common hepatic duct, allowing bile to enter or leave the gallbladder.
notes.C: Bile canaliculi are tiny intrahepatic channels formed between adjacent hepatocytes and are not extrahepatic ducts.

questions.why: Bile flows from intrahepatic canaliculi into progressively larger ducts, then through the hepatic ducts and extrahepatic biliary passages. The gallbladder communicates with this system via the cystic duct.

questions.stem: About the extrahepatic biliary apparatus:

options.label: A
options.text: Right and left hepatic ducts unite to form the bile duct

options.label: B
options.text: The cystic duct joins the common hepatic duct to form the bile duct

options.label: C
options.text: The bile duct joins the pancreatic duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla

notes.A: The right and left hepatic ducts unite as the common hepatic duct before the cystic duct joins it.
notes.B: The junction of the cystic duct and common hepatic duct marks the beginning of the common bile duct.
notes.C: The common bile duct and main pancreatic duct usually unite at the hepatopancreatic ampulla before opening into the duodenum.

questions.why: The common hepatic duct forms from the right and left hepatic ducts, then joins the cystic duct to form the common bile duct. The latter usually unites with the main pancreatic duct.

questions.stem: Terms used for parts of the gallbladder:

notes.A: Antrum is a standard subdivision of the pyloric stomach, not a conventional anatomical part of the gallbladder.
notes.B: The rounded fundus is the blind distal end of the gallbladder and may project below the liver margin.
notes.C: The gallbladder neck is a standard division. Hartmann's pouch refers to variable widening near the junction of the neck and body.

questions.why: The gallbladder consists of a fundus, body and neck, which continues into the cystic duct. Hartmann’s pouch is a variable outpouching near the infundibulum or neck.

questions.stem: Terms used for parts of the pancreas:

notes.A: The pancreatic head lies within the C-shaped curve of the duodenum on the right side of the abdomen.
notes.B: The elongated central portion of the pancreas is called the body, not the trunk in standard anatomical nomenclature.
notes.C: Rostrum is not a conventional subdivision of the pancreas; its left extremity is termed the tail.

questions.why: The pancreas is divided into head, neck, body and tail, with the uncinate process projecting from the head. These anatomical terms describe its relationship to adjacent vessels and organs.

questions.stem: About the pancreatic duct system:

options.label: A
options.text: The accessory duct lies above the main duct

options.label: B
options.text: The main pancreatic duct begins in the tail

options.label: C
options.text: The ampulla of Vater is the major duodenal papilla

notes.A: The accessory pancreatic duct generally courses superior to the terminal main duct and opens at the minor duodenal papilla.
notes.B: The main pancreatic duct begins in the tail and receives tributaries as it runs towards the pancreatic head.
notes.C: The ampulla is a ductal junction or dilation, whereas the major duodenal papilla is the mucosal elevation bearing its opening.

questions.why: The main pancreatic duct drains the gland from tail towards head and usually joins the bile duct. The accessory duct, when patent, drains through the minor papilla above the major papilla.

questions.stem: Arteries supplying the pancreas come from the:

notes.A: The splenic artery gives pancreatic branches along the superior border and supplies much of the pancreatic body and tail.
notes.B: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the head through the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery and its anastomoses.
notes.C: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies distal colonic and upper rectal territories rather than the pancreas.

questions.why: The pancreatic body and tail receive branches of the splenic artery, while the head receives pancreaticoduodenal arcades connecting the coeliac and superior mesenteric territories. The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut.

questions.stem: Surgical approaches to the body of the pancreas (on the floor of the lesser sac) include:

options.label: A
options.text: Through the greater omentum along the greater curvature

options.label: C
options.text: Through the anterior wall of the epiploic foramen

notes.A: The gastrocolic portion of the greater omentum can be opened to expose the lesser sac anterior to the pancreas.
notes.B: The transverse mesocolon provides an alternative anatomical approach to the region of the pancreatic body.
notes.C: The anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen contains the portal triad in the hepatoduodenal ligament and is not a standard access route.

questions.why: The pancreatic body lies retroperitoneally behind the lesser sac. Surgical exposure may be obtained through the gastrocolic ligament or transverse mesocolon, depending on the intended operation.

questions.stem: About the pancreas:

options.label: A
options.text: It has a head, body and tail but no neck

options.label: C
options.text: The uncinate process is part of the lower head

notes.A: The pancreatic neck links the head and body and lies in front of the junction of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.
notes.B: The pancreas is approximately 12–15 cm long in many adults, although its dimensions vary between individuals.
notes.C: The uncinate process projects medially from the inferior part of the pancreatic head, usually behind the superior mesenteric vessels.

questions.why: The elongated pancreas extends from the duodenal curve towards the splenic hilum. Its head, neck, body and tail are recognisable subdivisions, and its uncinate process projects from the inferior head.

questions.stem: Arteries that may be divided in partial gastrectomy with gastroduodenal anastomosis include the:

notes.A: They supply the duodenum and head of pancreas, which are kept.
notes.D: If the upper stomach is removed.
notes.E: Preserved.

questions.why: In a partial gastrectomy the left gastric, right gastroepiploic and short gastric arteries to the resected stomach are divided (B-D true); the pancreaticoduodenal and gastroduodenal arteries are preserved to keep the duodenal stump and pancreas perfused, so A and E are false.

questions.stem: Deciduous teeth correctly matched with approximate eruption times:

notes.A: The lower central incisors commonly erupt first at around six to ten months, with the upper pair following.
notes.B: Lateral incisors usually erupt after central incisors, and the lower lateral incisors may emerge several months into the second year.
notes.C: Primary canines commonly erupt during the second year of life after the first primary molars.
notes.D: The first primary molars typically emerge early in the second year, before the canines and second primary molars.
notes.E: Second primary molars complete the sequence, with reference charts giving ranges of about 23–31 months below and 25–33 months above.

questions.why: Eruption usually begins with the lower central incisors and ends with the second primary molars before or around age three. The listed ages are teaching approximations, and upper and lower teeth have different reference ranges.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old heavy drinker has severe epigastric pain and vomits blood. His symptom is:

notes.A: Haemoptysis is expectoration of blood from the respiratory tract during coughing, rather than vomiting of blood.
notes.B: Haematemesis describes blood expelled by vomiting, commonly associated with an oesophageal, gastric or duodenal source.
notes.C: Haemothorax refers to accumulation of blood in the pleural cavity rather than bleeding through the mouth.
notes.D: A haematoma is a localised collection of blood within tissue or another confined anatomical space.
notes.E: Haemoperitoneum describes blood within the peritoneal cavity rather than the gastrointestinal lumen.

questions.why: Haematemesis is the passage of blood by vomiting, commonly from the oesophagus, stomach or duodenum. Coughing up blood is haemoptysis, so the route of expulsion distinguishes the two symptoms.

questions.stem: Possible anatomical sources of his vomited blood include:

options.label: C
options.text: A duodenal ulcer eroding the gastroduodenal artery

options.label: D
options.text: Ruptured oesophageal varices from cirrhosis and portal hypertension

notes.A: Unlikely and not suggested by the history.

questions.why: Haematemesis commonly comes from a bleeding gastric ulcer, a duodenal ulcer eroding the gastroduodenal artery, ruptured oesophageal varices or gastritis (B-E true); a strangulated hiatus hernia is not a typical source, so A is false.

questions.stem: About the mouth:

options.label: A
options.text: Its posterior limit is the palatoglossal arch

options.label: B
options.text: The space between the lips/cheeks and the teeth is the vestibule

options.label: C
options.text: The floor of the mouth is formed by hyoglossus

options.label: D
options.text: The red margin of the lips has no hair follicles

options.label: E
options.text: The oral cavity is lined by stratified squamous epithelium, keratinized in places (gums, hard palate)

notes.A: The palatoglossal arches mark the lateral boundaries of the oropharyngeal isthmus at the posterior opening of the mouth.
notes.B: The oral vestibule lies external to the dental arches and internal to the lips and cheeks.
notes.C: Mylohyoid forms the principal muscular diaphragm of the mouth floor, whereas hyoglossus is an extrinsic tongue muscle.
notes.D: The vermilion zone of the lips lacks hair follicles and has superficial capillary loops contributing to its red colour.
notes.E: The hard palate and gingiva have masticatory stratified squamous epithelium, generally keratinised or parakeratinised for resistance to friction.

questions.why: The oral cavity is divided by the dental arches into vestibule and cavity proper. Its muscular floor supports the tongue, and its lining varies according to mechanical demands.

questions.stem: Parts of a tooth include:

notes.A: Dentine forms the bulk of the tooth and surrounds the pulp cavity beneath the enamel or cementum.
notes.B: The anatomical crown is the enamel-covered region, whereas the clinical crown is the part visible above the gingiva.
notes.C: Enamel is a highly mineralised tissue covering the anatomical crown and resisting the stresses of mastication.
notes.D: The dental pulp contains loose connective tissue, nerves and blood vessels within the central pulp chamber and root canals.
notes.E: Cementum covers the root dentine and provides attachment for periodontal ligament fibres anchoring the tooth in its socket.

questions.why: A tooth has an anatomical crown and root, with dentine forming most of its structure. Enamel covers the crown, cementum covers the root, and vascular connective tissue occupies the pulp cavity.

questions.stem: The dental formula in each half-jaw of an adult is:

notes.A: The normal permanent quadrant contains two incisors and one canine, not three incisors and two canines.
notes.B: Two incisors, one canine, two premolars and three molars form the standard complete adult quadrant.
notes.C: A complete adult quadrant has three molars including the wisdom tooth, although third molars may be absent.
notes.D: The permanent quadrant has two incisors and two premolars rather than one incisor and three premolars.
notes.E: The permanent dentition contains two premolars per quadrant, so a formula with three premolars is incorrect.

questions.why: A complete permanent dentition has eight teeth per quadrant: two incisors, one canine, two premolars and three molars. This gives a total of 32 teeth when third molars are present.

questions.stem: About adult teeth:

options.label: B
options.text: At occlusion the upper incisors overlap the lower (they do not meet edge to edge)

options.label: C
options.text: Premolars have buccal and lingual cusps

options.label: D
options.text: The upper first molar is larger than the lower

options.label: E
options.text: The lower first molar has five cusps

notes.A: Incisors are chisel-shaped; canines are conical.
notes.D: The LOWER first molar is usually the larger.

questions.why: At occlusion the upper incisors overlap the lower, premolars have buccal and lingual cusps, and the lower first molar has five cusps (B, C, E true); A is false (the canine crown is pointed, not chisel-like) and D is false (the lower first molar is the larger).

questions.stem: About the deciduous dentition:

options.label: B
options.text: Eruption is complete by about 2½–3 years

options.label: C
options.text: There are more deciduous teeth than permanent teeth

options.label: D
options.text: All deciduous teeth are shed and replaced

options.label: E
options.text: Deciduous molars are replaced by permanent premolars

notes.A: Primary tooth eruption usually starts near six months of age, most often with the lower central incisors.
notes.B: The second primary molars typically complete eruption by approximately two and a half to three years.
notes.C: The primary dentition has 20 teeth, compared with 32 in a complete permanent dentition.
notes.D: Normally, primary teeth exfoliate as their roots resorb and permanent successors erupt, although individual teeth may be retained.
notes.E: Permanent premolars replace the primary molars, while permanent molars erupt behind the primary dentition without predecessors.

questions.why: The primary dentition has 20 teeth that are normally shed as permanent successors erupt. Premolars succeed the primary molars, and permanent molars emerge behind them without primary predecessors.

questions.stem: About the oesophagus:

options.label: A
options.text: Its upper end is at C4

options.label: B
options.text: Its lower end is at T11

options.label: D
options.text: Its abdominal part is about 1–2 cm long

options.label: E
options.text: At T7 it deviates to the right and crosses behind the descending aorta

notes.A: The oesophagus begins at the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage around the sixth cervical vertebral level.
notes.B: The gastro-oesophageal junction is generally situated near T11, inferior to the diaphragmatic hiatus at T10.
notes.C: The adult oesophagus has an approximate length of 25 cm, with variation according to individual body dimensions.
notes.D: The portion between the oesophageal hiatus and gastric cardia is short, usually around one to two centimetres.
notes.E: In the lower thorax the oesophagus deviates leftwards and passes anterior to the descending thoracic aorta.

questions.why: The oesophagus runs from the cricoid cartilage at C6 to the gastric cardia near T11, traversing the neck, thorax and a short abdominal segment. Its course shifts leftward towards the diaphragm.

questions.stem: Distances along the oesophagus from the incisor teeth:

options.label: B
options.text: Crossing of the aortic arch: about 22 cm

options.label: C
options.text: Crossing of the left main bronchus: about 27 cm

options.label: D
options.text: Passage through the diaphragm: about 38 cm

options.label: E
options.text: Entry into the cardia: about 40 cm

notes.A: The cricopharyngeal narrowing at the upper oesophageal sphincter is approximately 15 cm from the upper incisors.
notes.B: The aortic arch produces an impression on the oesophagus around 22–25 cm from the upper incisors.
notes.C: The left main bronchus produces another thoracic impression approximately 25–28 cm from the incisors.
notes.D: The diaphragmatic impression is in the high thirties to about 40 centimetres from the incisors, depending on body size and landmark definition.
notes.E: The gastric cardia follows the short abdominal segment of the oesophagus, so it lies slightly distal to the diaphragmatic impression.

questions.why: Normal oesophageal impressions provide approximate endoscopic landmarks measured from the upper incisors. Their distances vary with body size, and the aortic and bronchial impressions may be described together.

questions.stem: Relations of the oesophagus:

options.label: A
options.text: In the superior mediastinum the trachea lies in front of it for its whole length there

options.label: B
options.text: In the posterior mediastinum it is crossed in front by the RIGHT bronchus

options.label: C
options.text: In the posterior mediastinum the thoracic duct lies behind it

options.label: D
options.text: The hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins lie in front of it

options.label: E
options.text: Below the cricoid it lies in front of the prevertebral fascia

notes.A: The trachea lies anterior to the oesophagus throughout their shared course within the superior mediastinum.
notes.B: The left main bronchus, rather than the right, crosses anterior to the oesophagus and produces a normal impression.
notes.C: The thoracic duct ascends posterior to the oesophagus in the posterior mediastinum before crossing towards the left.
notes.D: The hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins cross towards the azygos vein posterior to the oesophagus.
notes.E: The cervical oesophagus lies anterior to the prevertebral fascia and associated retrovisceral connective tissue spaces.

questions.why: The oesophagus has changing mediastinal relations as it descends. It initially lies behind the trachea, then passes behind the left main bronchus and anterior to several posterior mediastinal structures.

questions.stem: About peritoneal compartments:

options.label: A
options.text: The transverse mesocolon divides supracolic from infracolic compartments

options.label: B
options.text: The falciform ligament subdivides the supracolic compartment

options.label: C
options.text: The hepatorenal pouch is closed above by the coronary ligament (inferior layer)

options.label: D
options.text: On the left, the hepatorenal pouch communicates with the omental bursa

options.label: E
options.text: The left subhepatic space is the lesser sac

notes.D: Through the epiploic foramen.
notes.E: In some descriptions the lesser sac is called the left posterior subhepatic space.

questions.why: All are true: the transverse mesocolon separates the supracolic from the infracolic compartment, the falciform ligament subdivides the supracolic space, the hepatorenal pouch is closed above by the coronary ligament and communicates on the left with the lesser sac, and the left subhepatic space is the lesser sac.

questions.stem: About the root of the mesentery of the small intestine:

options.label: A
options.text: It runs downward from left to right

options.label: B
options.text: It crosses the 3rd part of the duodenum

notes.A: The mesenteric attachment descends obliquely from the left side of L2 towards the right sacroiliac joint region.
notes.B: The root of the small intestinal mesentery crosses anterior to the horizontal third part of the duodenum.
notes.C: The inferior vena cava lies behind the mesenteric root along its course towards the right iliac fossa.
notes.D: The mesenteric root crosses the right psoas major as it descends towards the right iliac region.
notes.E: The right ureter lies behind the mesenteric root along its course across the right posterior abdominal wall.

questions.why: The root of the small intestinal mesentery extends from the duodenojejunal flexure to the right iliac region. Along this oblique course it crosses major retroperitoneal vessels and right-sided structures.

questions.stem: About the paracolic gutters:

options.label: A
options.text: The left (lateral) paracolic gutter is closed above by the phrenicocolic ligament

options.label: B
options.text: The right paracolic gutter leads up to the hepatorenal pouch

options.label: C
options.text: Fluid in the right infracolic compartment drains directly to the pelvis

options.label: D
options.text: Fluid in the left infracolic compartment can reach the pelvis

options.label: E
options.text: Fluid in the hepatorenal pouch can track to the pelvis along the right paracolic gutter

notes.A: The phrenicocolic ligament limits superior communication between the left paracolic gutter and the left subphrenic space.
notes.B: The right paracolic gutter communicates superiorly with the right subhepatic region, including the hepatorenal recess.
notes.C: The oblique mesenteric root restricts direct inferior drainage from the right infracolic space into the pelvis.
notes.D: The left infracolic space has inferior continuity with the pelvic peritoneal cavity, allowing fluid to track downwards.
notes.E: Fluid in the hepatorenal recess can descend along the right paracolic gutter towards the pelvis.

questions.why: The paracolic gutters are channels for peritoneal fluid between abdominal and pelvic spaces. The oblique root of the small intestinal mesentery restricts drainage from the right infracolic compartment more than from the left.

questions.stem: Boundaries of the epiploic foramen:

options.label: A
options.text: It lies at the right border of the lesser sac

options.label: B
options.text: Above: the caudate process of the liver

options.label: C
options.text: Below: the 1st part of the duodenum

options.label: D
options.text: Behind: the IVC covered by peritoneum

options.label: E
options.text: In front: the free right border of the lesser omentum

notes.A: The epiploic foramen opens at the right side of the lesser sac behind the hepatoduodenal ligament.
notes.B: The caudate process of the liver forms the superior boundary of the opening into the lesser sac.
notes.C: The superior first part of the duodenum forms the inferior boundary of the epiploic foramen.
notes.D: The inferior vena cava covered by peritoneum forms the posterior boundary of the epiploic foramen.
notes.E: The free right border of the lesser omentum contains the portal vein, proper hepatic artery and bile duct.

questions.why: The epiploic foramen provides the normal communication between the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs. Its boundaries are important because the portal triad lies in the free anterior margin of the lesser omentum.

questions.stem: About the duodenum:

options.label: A
options.text: It is about 10 inches (25 cm) long

options.label: B
options.text: Its first part is about 5 cm

options.label: C
options.text: The 3rd part is twice as long as the 1st

options.label: D
options.text: The 4th part is about one third the length of the 2nd

options.label: E
options.text: Half of the 1st part is intraperitoneal

notes.A: The duodenum is conventionally about 25 cm long, although measured length differs among individuals.
notes.B: The superior first part of the duodenum is approximately 5 cm long from the pylorus to the superior flexure.
notes.C: The horizontal third part is conventionally around 10 cm long, approximately twice the length of the first part.
notes.D: The ascending fourth part is traditionally estimated at 2.5 cm, compared with about 7.5 cm for the descending part.
notes.E: Only the proximal two to two and a half centimetres of the first part retain the usual mobility and peritoneal investment.

questions.why: The four duodenal parts form a C-shaped loop around the pancreatic head. Conventional approximate lengths are 5, 7.5, 10 and 2.5 cm, with the proximal portion retaining mobility.

questions.stem: About the position of the duodenum:

options.label: A
options.text: The 1st part lies at the level of L1

options.label: B
options.text: The 2nd part lies to the LEFT of L2

options.label: D
options.text: The 4th part lies at the right of L2

notes.A: The superior duodenal part begins at the pylorus near the transpyloric plane at approximately L1.
notes.B: The descending second part passes along the right side of the upper lumbar vertebrae beside the pancreatic head.
notes.C: The horizontal third part crosses anterior to the aorta and inferior vena cava near the L3 vertebral level.
notes.D: The ascending fourth part passes to the left of the aorta towards the duodenojejunal flexure near L2.
notes.E: The third part is conventionally described as about 10 cm long, exceeding the usual 7.5 cm estimate for the second part.

questions.why: The duodenum begins near L1, descends on the right to approximately L3, crosses the midline and ascends to the duodenojejunal flexure on the left. Its horizontal third part is conventionally the longest.

questions.stem: Structures crossed by the 3rd (horizontal) part of the duodenum include the:

notes.A: The right psoas major lies posterior to the right portion of the horizontal duodenum.
notes.B: The right ureter descends on psoas major behind the horizontal part of the duodenum.
notes.C: The inferior vena cava lies behind the horizontal duodenum on the right of the aorta.
notes.D: The right gonadal vessels descend on the posterior abdominal wall behind the horizontal duodenum.
notes.E: The abdominal aorta lies posterior to the horizontal duodenum, opposite the superior mesenteric artery anteriorly.

questions.why: The horizontal duodenum crosses the posterior abdominal wall from right to left near L3. The superior mesenteric vessels cross anterior to it, explaining the possibility of compression between the artery and aorta.

questions.stem: The stomach normally occupies the following regions:

notes.A: The distal gastric body and pyloric region commonly occupy part of the epigastrium.
notes.B: The liver and gallbladder occupy most of the right hypochondrium. The distal stomach is normally nearer the midline.
notes.C: The lower portion of the stomach may extend into the umbilical region, especially when distended.
notes.D: The stomach can descend below its upper abdominal position when full, but the central rather than the left lumbar region is its usual downward extension.
notes.E: The fundus and much of the gastric body occupy the left hypochondriac region.

questions.why: The stomach normally lies mainly in the epigastric and left hypochondriac regions, but its lower portion may extend into the umbilical region. Its position varies with posture, filling and body build.

questions.stem: About the stomach:

options.label: A
options.text: The gastro-oesophageal junction is at T10

options.label: B
options.text: The pylorus lies at L1 (transpyloric plane)

options.label: C
options.text: The gastro-oesophageal junction is to the left of the midline

options.label: D
options.text: The pylorus is about 40 cm from the incisor teeth

options.label: E
options.text: The greater curvature lies below the umbilicus

notes.A: The gastro-oesophageal junction is typically near T11, while T10 corresponds to the oesophageal opening of the diaphragm.
notes.B: The pylorus commonly lies near the transpyloric plane at L1 when the stomach is relatively empty and the patient supine.
notes.C: The cardia lies to the left of the median plane where the oesophagus enters the stomach.
notes.D: The distance of approximately 40 cm from the incisors describes the cardia rather than the more distal pylorus.
notes.E: The greater curvature is usually above the umbilicus but may descend further when the stomach is distended.

questions.why: The gastric cardia is usually near T11, below the oesophageal hiatus at T10. The pylorus is commonly near L1 in the supine position, but gastric landmarks move with distension and posture.

questions.stem: About the parts of the stomach:

options.label: A
options.text: The cardia is the region around the oesophageal opening

options.label: B
options.text: The fundus projects above the level of the cardia

options.label: C
options.text: The body lies between the fundus and the pyloric antrum

options.label: D
options.text: The angular notch lies at the middle of the lesser curvature

options.label: E
options.text: The pyloric antrum lies between the angular notch and the pyloric canal

notes.A: The cardia is the small gastric region immediately surrounding the opening of the oesophagus.
notes.B: The fundus is the dome of the stomach projecting superior to the level of the cardiac opening.
notes.C: The body forms the largest gastric region between the fundus and the distal pyloric part.
notes.D: The angular notch occurs towards the distal lesser curvature at the transition from body to pyloric part.
notes.E: The pyloric antrum extends from the angular notch towards the narrower pyloric canal before the pylorus.

questions.why: The stomach comprises the cardia, fundus, body and pyloric part. The angular notch on the lesser curvature helps distinguish the distal pyloric region from the body.

questions.stem: About the histology of the stomach:

options.label: A
options.text: Neuroendocrine G and D cells are abundant in the pyloric part

options.label: B
options.text: Parietal cells are abundant in the pyloric part

options.label: C
options.text: Chief cells predominate in the fundus and body

options.label: D
options.text: Mucus-secreting cells are present in all regions

options.label: E
options.text: Solitary lymphoid nodules may be found in the pyloric part

notes.B: In the fundus and body.

questions.why: G and D cells are abundant in the pylorus, chief cells predominate in the fundus and body, mucous cells occur throughout, and lymphoid nodules may appear in the pylorus (A, C-E true); B is false because parietal (acid-secreting) cells are concentrated in the fundus and body, not the pylorus.

questions.stem: About the jejunum and ileum:

options.label: A
options.text: They are the mobile part of the small intestine

options.label: B
options.text: The jejunum is shorter than the ileum

options.label: C
options.text: The jejunum has a wider lumen than the ileum

options.label: D
