notes.B: Effacement shortens the cervical canal as its tissue is taken up into the lower uterine segment.
notes.A: Cervical tissue thins with effacement while the external opening widens to permit passage of the presenting part.
notes.C: The descending presenting part can press the anterior bladder against the rigid pubic symphysis.
notes.D: The perineal body lies at the posterior vaginal opening and stretches as the presenting part reaches the outlet.
notes.E: The rectum lies behind the vagina and may be compressed by the presenting part during descent.

questions.why: During labour the cervix shortens and thins as the opening widens. As the presenting part descends, it can press on the bladder and rectum and stretch the pelvic outlet.

questions.stem: Nucleus ambiguus supplies all of the following muscles EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: The intrinsic muscles of the larynx

questions.why: The nucleus ambiguus supplies branchial motor fibres to the larynx and most muscles of the pharynx and palate through the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves. Tensor veli palatini receives trigeminal motor fibres.

notes.A: Vagal fibres from the nucleus ambiguus supply the intrinsic laryngeal muscles through the superior and recurrent laryngeal branches.
notes.B: Stylopharyngeus receives branchial motor fibres carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve from the nucleus ambiguus.
notes.C: Vagal fibres to the pharyngeal plexus activate the constrictor muscles during the pharyngeal phase of swallowing.
notes.D: Palatoglossus receives vagal motor fibres through the pharyngeal plexus and helps narrow the opening to the oropharynx.

questions.stem: Nucleus ambiguus sends fibres into all of the following EXCEPT the:

options.label: D
options.text: Cranial root of the accessory nerve

questions.why: The spinal part of the accessory nerve originates in the cervical spinal cord and supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. The nucleus ambiguus in the medulla supplies branchial motor fibres carried chiefly by glossopharyngeal and vagal pathways.

notes.A: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries branchial motor fibres from the nucleus ambiguus to the stylopharyngeus muscle.
notes.B: The vagus carries fibres from the nucleus ambiguus to muscles of the palate, pharynx and larynx.
notes.D: The medullary fibres traditionally called the cranial accessory root join vagal pathways to the pharynx and larynx.
notes.E: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is a vagal branch carrying branchial motor fibres to most intrinsic laryngeal muscles.

questions.stem: Constriction of the RIGHT pupil when light shines into the LEFT eye needs all of the following EXCEPT the:
questions.why: The consensual reflex: left optic nerve → both pretectal nuclei → both Edinger–Westphal nuclei → oculomotor nerves → ciliary ganglia. The right optic nerve carries light from the right eye only.

notes.A: The afferent limb.
notes.B: Relays to both EW nuclei.
notes.C: The efferent limb to the right pupil.
notes.E: Sends preganglionic fibres to the right pupil.

questions.stem: The same consensual light reflex (light in the left eye, right pupil constricts) does NOT need the:
questions.why: Reflex fibres leave the optic tract for the pretectal area before the lateral geniculate body; the optic radiation and cortex are not involved.

notes.A: Needed (afferent).
notes.B: Needed.
notes.D: Needed (efferent to the right eye).
notes.E: Its crossing nasal fibres reach the opposite pretectal area.

questions.stem: A vascular lesion of the primary visual cortex (area 17) on one side typically causes:

options.label: E
options.text: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

questions.why: Posterior cerebral artery occlusion gives contralateral homonymous hemianopia; the macula is spared because its cortex has a dual supply (MCA and PCA).

notes.A: Needs bilateral damage.
notes.B: Needs lateral lesions at the chiasm.
notes.C: Chiasm compression.
notes.D: Typical of optic tract or radiation lesions, without macular sparing.

questions.stem: A pituitary adenoma pressing upward typically causes:

options.label: E
options.text: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

questions.why: An expanding pituitary adenoma can compress the optic chiasm above the sella. Nasal retinal fibres cross in its centre and carry information from the temporal visual fields, producing bitemporal loss.

notes.A: Complete loss of sight in one eye usually occurs with severe damage to its retina or optic nerve before the chiasm.
notes.B: Binasal loss would involve the uncrossed temporal retinal fibres at both lateral edges of the chiasm.
notes.D: A homonymous defect affects the same side of the visual field in both eyes and localises behind the chiasm.
notes.E: Macular sparing can accompany an occipital lesion in which the central visual representation remains intact.

questions.stem: Bitemporal hemianopia indicates a lesion of the:

options.label: B
options.text: Central part of the optic chiasma

options.label: C
options.text: Lateral part of the optic chiasma

questions.why: The nasal halves of both retinae receive light from the temporal visual fields. Their axons decussate in the centre of the optic chiasm, so a central lesion can remove both temporal hemifields.

notes.A: Each optic nerve carries input from one eye, so its injury causes monocular visual loss or a monocular field defect.
notes.C: The lateral chiasm carries uncrossed temporal retinal fibres, which represent the nasal field of the eye on that side.
notes.D: An optic tract carries the opposite visual hemifield from both eyes, making its loss homonymous.
notes.E: An optic radiation conveys one contralateral hemifield to the occipital cortex, so its lesions produce homonymous defects.

questions.stem: The nucleus of the tractus solitarius receives all of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: Taste from the anterior two-thirds via the chorda tympani

options.label: B
options.text: Taste from the posterior third via the glossopharyngeal nerve

options.label: C
options.text: Taste from the epiglottis via the vagus

options.label: D
options.text: General sensation from the anterior two-thirds via the lingual nerve

options.label: E
options.text: Visceral sensation from organs supplied by the vagus

questions.why: The solitary nucleus receives taste and visceral afferents. Touch, pain and temperature from the anterior tongue instead enter trigeminal pathways via the lingual nerve, a branch of the mandibular division.

notes.A: Chorda tympani fibres carry taste from most of the anterior tongue and project centrally to the rostral solitary nucleus.
notes.B: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste from the posterior tongue and circumvallate papillae to the gustatory region of the nucleus.
notes.C: The internal laryngeal branch of the vagus carries epiglottic taste afferents towards the solitary nucleus.
notes.E: The caudal part of the solitary nucleus receives vagal afferents from thoracic and abdominal organs.

questions.stem: About the pupillary light reflex:

options.label: A
options.text: Its efferent limb runs in the optic nerve

options.label: B
options.text: It is relayed through the inferior colliculi

notes.A: The optic nerve carries afferent input from the illuminated eye. Oculomotor parasympathetic fibres start the efferent limb.
notes.B: The pretectal area relays the reflex in the midbrain. The inferior colliculus chiefly relays auditory information.
notes.C: Bilateral pretectal output lets illumination of one eye produce direct constriction in that eye and consensual constriction in the other.

questions.why: Retinal signals travel in the optic nerve to pretectal nuclei, which project to both Edinger–Westphal nuclei. Parasympathetic fibres travel with each oculomotor nerve, allowing one light stimulus to constrict both pupils.

questions.stem: Specialised parts of a chemical synapse include:

notes.A: The presynaptic membrane has release sites where vesicles fuse and discharge neurotransmitter in response to calcium entry.
notes.B: The synaptic cleft is the extracellular gap through which transmitter diffuses before reaching the receiving cell.
notes.C: The postsynaptic membrane contains receptors that convert transmitter binding into an electrical or biochemical response.

questions.why: At a chemical synapse, an electrical signal triggers transmitter release from one cell. The transmitter crosses a narrow extracellular gap and binds receptors that change the activity of the receiving cell.

questions.stem: Non-encapsulated cutaneous receptors include:

notes.A: Ruffini corpuscles have elongated connective tissue specialisations around endings that respond to sustained skin stretch.
notes.B: Free endings branch among tissue cells without a capsule and can signal pain, temperature or other stimuli.
notes.C: Merkel cell–neurite complexes lie near the basal epidermis and signal sustained indentation and fine spatial detail.

questions.why: Free nerve endings lack a specialised capsule. A Merkel disc is an expanded sensory nerve ending associated with a Merkel cell in the basal epidermis, without the capsule typical of a corpuscle.

questions.stem: Correctly matched cutaneous receptors:

options.label: B
options.text: Free nerve endings → pain, temperature and crude touch

options.label: C
options.text: Meissner corpuscle → fine touch and two-point discrimination

notes.A: Pacinian corpuscles respond strongly to high-frequency vibration and rapidly changing pressure in deeper tissue.
notes.B: Different populations of free endings signal tissue injury, warming or cooling, and aspects of poorly localised touch.
notes.C: Meissner corpuscles respond to light moving touch in hairless skin and contribute to fine tactile discrimination.

questions.why: Cutaneous receptors are tuned to different stimuli. Free endings include thermal and nociceptive sensors, while encapsulated mechanoreceptors such as Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles transduce distinct patterns of skin deformation.

questions.stem: Fibres carrying SENSORY information from skeletal muscle include:

options.label: A
options.text: Myelinated fibres from annulospiral and flower-spray endings of muscle spindles

options.label: B
options.text: Small gamma fibres to intrafusal fibres

options.label: C
options.text: Large alpha fibres to extrafusal fibres

notes.A: Myelinated group Ia and II afferents carry signals from primary annulospiral and secondary flower-spray endings in the spindle.
notes.B: Gamma motor axons contract the ends of intrafusal fibres, adjusting spindle sensitivity during changes in muscle length.
notes.C: Alpha motor axons activate extrafusal fibres, which generate the main force of skeletal muscle contraction.

questions.why: Muscle spindles encode muscle length and its rate of change. Primary and secondary spindle afferents carry that information to the spinal cord, while motor fibres adjust intrafusal tension or drive muscle contraction.

questions.stem: In a horizontal section of the cerebrum, the external capsule:

options.label: A
options.text: Lies between the claustrum and the lentiform nucleus

options.label: C
options.text: Separates the lentiform nucleus from the caudate nucleus

notes.C: The anterior limb of the internal capsule separates the caudate head from the lentiform nucleus.
notes.A: The putamen forms the lateral part of the lentiform nucleus and borders the external capsule medially.
notes.B: The claustrum is a thin grey sheet on the lateral side of the external capsule.

questions.why: The external capsule is a narrow sheet of white matter lateral to the putamen and medial to the claustrum. The extreme capsule is the separate white sheet between the claustrum and insula.

questions.stem: Features of the anterior surface of the medulla oblongata include:

options.label: C
options.text: The spinal roots of the accessory nerve

notes.C: Spinal accessory rootlets arise along the lateral upper cervical cord and ascend into the skull through the foramen magnum.
notes.A: The anterior median fissure runs in the midline between the two ventral pyramids and is interrupted near their decussation.
notes.B: The pyramids contain descending corticospinal fibres and form paired elevations on the ventral surface of the medulla.

questions.why: The ventral medulla presents two corticospinal pyramids separated by the anterior median fissure. The roots of the spinal accessory nerve arise from the upper cervical cord.

questions.stem: The nucleus ambiguus:

options.label: A
options.text: Is a column of large motor neurons in the medulla

options.label: C
options.text: Gives motor fibres to the glossopharyngeal nerve

notes.C: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries motor fibres from the nucleus ambiguus to the stylopharyngeus muscle.
notes.A: Large motor neurons in the ventrolateral medulla form the longitudinal column called nucleus ambiguus.
notes.B: Damage weakens pharyngeal or laryngeal muscles, which can impair bolus propulsion and the protection of the airway during swallowing.

questions.why: The nucleus ambiguus is a medullary column of branchial motor neurons. Its fibres travel in glossopharyngeal and vagal pathways to muscles used in swallowing and phonation.

questions.stem: The quadrigeminal plate (corpora quadrigemina) relates to the:

notes.B: The interpeduncular fossa lies on the ventral surface of the midbrain between the cerebral peduncles.
notes.C: The longitudinal fissure divides the cerebral hemispheres and is separate from the dorsal surface of the midbrain.
notes.A: The quadrigeminal plate forms the tectum, which lies behind the cerebral aqueduct at the dorsal midbrain surface.

questions.why: The corpora quadrigemina are four elevations on the dorsal midbrain. The paired superior colliculi participate in visual orienting, while the paired inferior colliculi form part of the auditory pathway.

questions.stem: About the optic nerve and visual pathway:

options.label: A
options.text: The optic nerve is formed by myelinated axons of retinal ganglion cells

options.label: B
options.text: In the chiasm, fibres from the TEMPORAL half of each retina cross

options.label: C
options.text: Fibres leaving the lateral geniculate body form the optic tract

options.label: D
options.text: Optic tract fibres pass through the internal capsule to the visual cortex

options.label: E
options.text: The optic radiation runs from the medial geniculate body

questions.why: Axons of retinal ganglion cells collect at the optic disc and continue as the optic nerve. They are unmyelinated within the retina and acquire oligodendrocyte myelin behind the lamina cribrosa.

notes.B: Nasal retinal fibres decussate at the chiasm. The optic tract on the same side carries the temporal retinal fibres.
notes.C: The optic tract reaches the lateral geniculate body. Its relay neurons give rise to the optic radiation.
notes.D: The optic radiation passes through retrolenticular white matter to the visual cortex after synapsing in the lateral geniculate body.
notes.E: The medial geniculate body relays auditory signals. The optic radiation arises in the lateral geniculate body.

questions.stem: A tumour compressing the RIGHT side of the optic chiasm (uncrossed fibres) produces:

options.label: E
options.text: Complete blindness of the right eye

questions.why: At the right lateral edge of the optic chiasm, uncrossed fibres carry signals from the temporal retina of the right eye. This retinal region receives images from the right eye's nasal field.

notes.A: Bitemporal hemianopia results from damage to crossing fibres from both nasal retinal halves at the centre of the chiasm.
notes.B: Binasal hemianopia requires disruption of uncrossed temporal retinal fibres on both sides, a rare pattern.
notes.D: Left nasal field loss involves temporal retinal fibres from the left eye, which remain on the left side of the chiasm.
notes.E: Complete right-eye blindness requires much more extensive loss of right-eye input, classically from a severe right optic nerve lesion.

questions.stem: All of the following are features of frontal lobe lesions EXCEPT:

options.label: D
options.text: Inability to turn the eyes to the opposite side

questions.why: Receptive aphasia typically follows damage to the dominant posterior temporal language network. Frontal lesions can instead disturb voluntary movement, gaze control, behaviour or speech production, depending on the site.

notes.A: Damage to the precentral motor cortex can produce contralateral weakness with upper motor neuron signs.
notes.B: Disruption of descending motor pathways in the frontal lobe can produce increased tone after the acute phase.
notes.D: A destructive frontal eye field lesion can impair voluntary conjugate gaze towards the opposite side.
notes.E: Prefrontal damage can alter judgement, initiative, inhibition and behaviour, producing a noticeable personality change.

questions.stem: Which Brodmann areas are in the frontal lobe?
questions.why: Brodmann areas 44 and 45 occupy the pars opercularis and pars triangularis of the inferior frontal gyrus. In the dominant hemisphere they form a core part of Broca’s language region.

notes.B: Areas one and two are parts of primary somatosensory cortex on the parietal postcentral gyrus.
notes.C: Areas 41 and 42 lie in the superior temporal auditory region, including cortex on the transverse temporal gyri.
notes.D: Areas 17 and 18 are primary and adjacent visual areas in the occipital lobe.
notes.E: Area five lies in the superior parietal lobule and contributes to somatosensory association.

questions.stem: All of the following are features of parietal lobe lesions EXCEPT:
questions.why: Classic expressive aphasia localises to the dominant inferior frontal language region and adjacent pathways. Parietal lesions more typically affect cortical sensation, skilled movement or functions such as calculation and writing.

notes.A: Damage around the dominant angular gyrus can cause Gerstmann syndrome, including acalculia, agraphia and finger agnosia.
notes.B: The postcentral cortex processes fine spatial discrimination, which may be impaired on the opposite side after a parietal lesion.
notes.D: Parietal sensory damage can prevent identification of an object by touch despite enough primary sensation to feel it.
notes.E: Dominant parietal lesions can disrupt programming of learned movements, producing apraxia despite preserved basic strength.

questions.stem: All of the following are associated with occipital lobe lesions EXCEPT:
questions.why: Severe anterograde amnesia is associated with damage to hippocampal and related medial temporal circuits needed to establish new memories. Occipital lesions primarily disrupt visual fields or higher visual processing.

notes.A: A focal lesion in retinotopic occipital cortex can cause a local field defect, called a scotoma.
notes.B: Cerebral achromatopsia can follow damage to the ventral occipitotemporal network involved in colour perception.
notes.C: Prosopagnosia can follow damage to ventral occipitotemporal regions, particularly a right-sided network specialised for recognising faces.
notes.D: Injury to visual association cortex can prevent recognition of objects despite enough elementary vision to see them.

questions.stem: All of the following are associated with temporal lobe lesions EXCEPT:
questions.why: Astereognosis usually localises to the contralateral parietal somatosensory network. Temporal lesions can instead affect memory, understanding of language or auditory recognition, with the particular deficit depending on lesion location.

notes.A: Medial temporal structures, including the hippocampus, are needed to form new declarative memories.
notes.B: Damage around the dominant posterior superior temporal region can impair language comprehension and produce fluent, poorly meaningful speech.
notes.C: Temporal auditory association damage can prevent recognition of sounds even when basic hearing remains.
notes.E: Bilateral damage to primary auditory cortices in the superior temporal lobes can produce cortical deafness.

questions.stem: All of the following characterize lower motor neuron lesions EXCEPT:
questions.why: Clonus consists of rhythmic stretch-induced contractions due to exaggerated reflex activity after an upper motor neuron lesion. Lower motor neuron damage disrupts the motor limb of the reflex arc and reduces reflex activity.

notes.A: A damaged lower motor axon interrupts the reflex arc's efferent limb, so the corresponding tendon reflex decreases or disappears.
notes.B: Loss of motor input to the muscle reduces resting tone in the affected distribution.
notes.C: Denervated muscle fibres undergo pronounced wasting over time because they lose their normal neural input.
notes.D: Paralysis is flaccid when the final motor pathway to the muscle is interrupted.

questions.stem: All of the following characterize upper motor neuron lesions EXCEPT:
questions.why: Fibrillations and fasciculations suggest denervation of muscle fibres or motor units. An established upper motor neuron lesion more typically produces spasticity, brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response.

notes.A: After the acute phase, loss of descending control can cause weakness with velocity-dependent resistance to passive movement.
notes.B: The muscle remains connected to lower motor neurons, so wasting is generally less marked than after denervation.
notes.C: Reduced descending inhibition can make tendon reflexes brisk and can allow repetitive stretch responses.
notes.E: In an adult, an extensor plantar response is a sign of dysfunction in the corticospinal pathway.

questions.stem: Tests of cerebellar function include all of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: B
options.text: Romberg test (when used to separate sensory ataxia)

questions.why: The Trendelenburg test assesses whether the hip abductors stabilise the pelvis during single-leg stance. Cerebellar assessment focuses on coordinated gait and limb movements, with sensory testing helping distinguish causes of ataxia.

notes.A: Tandem walking challenges balance and may reveal gait instability due to cerebellar dysfunction.
notes.B: The Romberg manoeuvre compares stance with eyes open and closed, helping distinguish sensory dependence from persistent cerebellar instability.
notes.D: Targeted finger-to-nose movement can reveal an intention tremor or difficulty judging distance in a cerebellar lesion.
notes.E: Moving the heel along the opposite shin tests coordination of the lower limb and may reveal cerebellar dysmetria.

questions.stem: The main features of cerebellar dysfunction include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.why: Cerebellar disease impairs timing, calibration and coordination without usually causing primary paralysis. Limb findings from a cerebellar hemisphere lesion are generally ipsilateral, while midline disease more often affects stance and gait.

notes.B: Ataxia is impaired coordination that can make gait unsteady or limb movements irregular.
notes.C: Cerebellar involvement can disturb the timing and force of speech movements, producing dysarthria.
notes.D: Dysmetria is a failure to judge movement distance, so the limb overshoots or undershoots a target.
notes.E: Dysdiadochokinesia is difficulty performing rapid alternating movements smoothly and rhythmically.

questions.stem: Destruction of the entire postcentral gyrus may cause all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.why: Hemiplegia needs the precentral (motor) gyrus.

notes.B: Sensory loss.
notes.C: Sensory.
notes.D: Sensory.
notes.E: Parietal.

questions.stem: All of the following about the postcentral gyrus boundaries are correct EXCEPT:
questions.why: The postcentral gyrus occupies the strip between the central and postcentral sulci. The supramarginal gyrus belongs to the inferior parietal lobule farther posteriorly, curving around the end of the lateral sulcus.

notes.A: The longitudinal fissure separates the cerebral hemispheres and borders the superior end of the postcentral gyrus.
notes.B: The central sulcus separates the postcentral sensory cortex from the precentral motor cortex in front of it.
notes.C: The postcentral sulcus marks the posterior limit of the postcentral strip and separates it from parietal association cortex.
notes.E: The inferior end of the postcentral region approaches the lateral sulcus, which separates it from the temporal lobe.

questions.stem: Destruction of the entire inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere causes:
questions.why: The dominant inferior frontal gyrus includes the opercular and triangular parts of Broca’s region. Damage here and in nearby networks can disrupt speech production, leading to effortful, nonfluent language.

notes.A: Anosmia is loss of smell and more commonly implicates the olfactory apparatus or its central projections.
notes.B: Contralateral lower facial weakness arises from damage to the face area of the precentral gyrus or its descending corticobulbar fibres.
notes.D: Apraxia is impaired performance of learned actions and can result from disruption of a wider parietofrontal network.
notes.E: Agnosia is failure to recognise a familiar stimulus despite adequate primary sensation, usually after association cortex damage.

questions.stem: All of the following about split-brain (corpus callosotomy) patients are correct EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: Communication between the hemispheres is impaired

options.label: B
options.text: They cannot name an object seen only by the right hemisphere

options.label: C
options.text: They develop a personality change like the "Boston crowbar" case

options.label: D
options.text: They cannot name an object felt only by the left hand

options.label: E
options.text: They may seem confused in some tasks

questions.why: Corpus callosotomy interrupts major connections between the cerebral hemispheres and can dissociate what each hemisphere can report. Phineas Gage’s reported behavioural change followed a frontal injury, a different anatomical mechanism.

notes.A: The corpus callosum carries interhemispheric fibres, so complete section reduces transfer of sensory and other information between hemispheres.
notes.B: In typical left language dominance, an object shown exclusively to the right hemisphere cannot be named through the usual left-sided language network.
notes.D: Without vision, an object felt in the left hand is represented initially on the right and may be inaccessible to left-sided language areas.
notes.E: When a laboratory task isolates information in one hemisphere, the patient's verbal report and actions may appear inconsistent.

questions.stem: All of the following about syringomyelia are true EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: It interrupts the crossing spinothalamic fibres

options.label: B
options.text: It causes bilateral segmental loss of pain and temperature

options.label: C
options.text: Touch, vibration and position sense are often spared

questions.why: An enlarging spinal cord syrinx can affect nearby anterior horn cells and descending motor pathways. These injuries can respectively reduce reflexes at the level of the cavity or increase them below it.

notes.A: A centrally placed cavity can interrupt the pain and temperature axons that cross in the anterior white commissure.
notes.B: Involvement of crossing fibres on both sides can cause bilateral loss of pain and temperature in affected segments.
notes.C: Dorsal column fibres can remain intact early, preserving vibration and joint position sense despite loss of pain and temperature.
notes.D: An extensive syrinx can injure descending motor tracts, leading to severe weakness of the lower limbs.

questions.stem: In a horizontal section, structures between the globus pallidus and the insula include all EXCEPT the:
questions.why: The internal capsule lies medial to the lentiform nucleus. Going laterally from the globus pallidus towards the insula, one passes through putamen, external capsule, claustrum and then extreme capsule.

notes.B: The external capsule is the thin sheet of white matter between the putamen and claustrum.
notes.C: The putamen is the lateral part of the lentiform nucleus, immediately lateral to the globus pallidus.
notes.D: The claustrum is a thin sheet of grey matter between the external and extreme capsules.
notes.E: The extreme capsule is the white matter layer between the claustrum and overlying insular cortex.

questions.stem: True or false: The cranial dura is anatomically different from the spinal dura.
questions.why: Cranial dura has a periosteal layer and a meningeal layer, which separate to form dural venous sinuses. The spinal dural sac continues the meningeal layer and is separated from the vertebral canal by a true epidural space.

notes.B: A real epidural compartment containing fat and veins separates spinal dura from vertebral periosteum.

questions.stem: True or false: The opercula include the gyrus rectus.
questions.why: The frontal, parietal and temporal opercula form lips around the lateral sulcus and overlie the insula. The gyrus rectus lies on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe medial to the olfactory sulcus.

notes.A: The gyrus rectus is on the underside of the frontal lobe rather than on a lip covering the insula.

questions.stem: True or false: The thalamus can be seen in the floor of the lateral ventricle.
questions.why: The superior surface of the thalamus contributes to the floor of the body of the lateral ventricle. It lies medial to the caudate nucleus, with the stria terminalis running along their interval.

notes.B: The superior thalamic surface forms part of the ventricular floor alongside the groove for the stria terminalis.

questions.stem: True or false: The interventricular foramen (of Monro) is closely related to the crus of the fornix.
questions.why: The interventricular foramen links each lateral ventricle with the third ventricle. Its anterior margin is closely related to a column of the fornix, while the anterior thalamus lies posteriorly.

notes.A: The crura lie posteriorly near the hippocampi and converge into the body before the fornix divides into anterior columns.

questions.stem: True or false: A lesion of the splenium of the corpus callosum causes alien hand syndrome.
questions.why: Splenium lesions cause alexia without agraphia; alien hand follows anterior callosal or frontal lesions.

questions.stem: True or false: In raised intracranial pressure, cingulate (subfalcine) herniation may compress the superior petrosal sinus.
questions.why: Subfalcine herniation moves the cingulate gyrus under the free edge of the falx cerebri. It can compress the anterior cerebral or pericallosal vessels near the displaced medial hemisphere.

notes.A: The superior petrosal sinus runs along the petrous ridge, away from the falcine edge beside the displaced cingulate gyrus.

questions.stem: True or false: In transcalvarial herniation, brain tissue is squeezed through the foramen magnum.
questions.why: Transcalvarial herniation is displacement of swollen brain through a defect in the skull vault. At the foramen magnum, downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils is termed tonsillar herniation.

notes.A: The foramen magnum lies at the skull base. Downward movement of the cerebellar tonsils through it defines a different herniation pattern.

questions.stem: True or false: The corpora quadrigemina are seen on the ventral surface of the midbrain.
questions.why: The superior and inferior colliculi form the four elevations of the tectum on the posterior midbrain. The cerebral peduncles and intervening fossa are seen on the ventral surface.

notes.A: The cerebral peduncles form ventral prominences. The colliculi lie behind the cerebral aqueduct on the dorsal side.

questions.stem: True or false: A pontine lesion may present as a contralateral cranial nerve palsy.
questions.why: Brainstem lesions give IPSILATERAL cranial nerve palsy with contralateral hemiplegia.

questions.stem: True or false: The primary motor cortex is Brodmann areas 6 and 8.
questions.why: Brodmann area 4 in the precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex. Area 6 includes premotor and supplementary motor areas, while area 8 includes the frontal eye field.

notes.A: Area 6 helps plan movement and area 8 includes gaze control. The chief primary cortical motor area is area 4.

questions.stem: True or false: In the dominant hemisphere, Broca's area is on the superior temporal gyrus.
questions.why: The pars opercularis and pars triangularis of the dominant inferior frontal gyrus make up the classical Broca region. The posterior superior temporal cortex is traditionally associated with language comprehension.

notes.A: The superior temporal gyrus includes posterior auditory and language comprehension regions, while Broca’s region lies in the inferior frontal gyrus.

questions.stem: True or false: Agraphaesthesia suggests a lesion of the frontal lobe.
questions.why: Agraphaesthesia is failure to identify a figure traced on the skin despite sufficient primary sensory input. It usually points to impaired contralateral parietal processing of the spatial pattern.

notes.A: The parietal cortex combines tactile signals needed to recognise the traced figure, whereas frontal motor regions chiefly organise movement.

questions.stem: True or false: Bitemporal hemianopia suggests compression of the midline optic chiasma.
questions.why: Nasal retinal fibres from both eyes cross at the centre of the optic chiasm. They carry the temporal visual fields, so a central compressive lesion can produce bitemporal hemianopia.

notes.B: The crossing nasal fibres carry temporal field information from each eye, so central chiasmal compression can affect both temporal fields.

questions.stem: The fornix links the mammillary bodies to the hippocampus. Its parts include the:

notes.A: The body divides anteriorly into paired columns, with postcommissural fibres continuing towards the mammillary bodies.
notes.B: The crura converge beneath the corpus callosum to form the body of the fornix.
notes.C: The hippocampal commissure contains fibres passing between the two sides at the level of the crura.
notes.D: Each crus curves beneath the splenium as a continuation of the fimbria before joining the body.
notes.E: The fimbria forms where axons from the hippocampal surface collect along its medial edge.

questions.why: Hippocampal fibres gather in the fimbria and continue into the paired crura. The crura join the body, which divides into columns projecting towards targets including the mammillary bodies.

questions.stem: Ptosis with the left eye turned outward (abducted) suggests a lesion of the:
questions.why: Oculomotor palsy weakens the muscle that elevates the upper eyelid and most extraocular muscles. A functioning lateral rectus and superior oblique then pull the eye outwards and usually downwards.

notes.A: Trochlear palsy weakens superior oblique and can cause vertical diplopia, while the upper lid elevator remains innervated.
notes.B: Abducent palsy weakens lateral rectus, so the affected eye has difficulty moving outwards and may rest medially.
notes.D: Loss of cervical sympathetic output causes mild ptosis and miosis, with the main extraocular motor nerves still working.
notes.E: The facial nerve supplies orbicularis oculi. Its palsy impairs eyelid closure, with the upper lid elevator and extraocular muscles intact.

questions.stem: Which extraocular muscle is supplied by the abducent nerve?
questions.why: The abducent nerve supplies the lateral rectus, which moves the eye laterally. The trochlear nerve supplies the superior oblique, and the oculomotor nerve supplies most of the other orbital muscles.

notes.A: The medial rectus adducts the eye and receives motor fibres from the oculomotor nerve.
notes.B: The superior rectus helps elevate the eye and is supplied by the superior division of the oculomotor nerve.
notes.C: The inferior rectus primarily depresses the eye and is supplied by the inferior division of the oculomotor nerve.
notes.D: The levator raises the upper eyelid and receives motor fibres through the superior division of the oculomotor nerve.

questions.stem: Which of the following nerves does NOT supply the tongue?
questions.why: The spinal accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. The tongue receives trigeminal, facial, glossopharyngeal and vagal sensory fibres, while hypoglossal and vagal pathways provide its motor supply.

notes.A: The lingual branch of the mandibular nerve carries touch, pain and temperature from most of the anterior tongue.
notes.B: Chorda tympani fibres of the facial nerve join the lingual nerve and carry taste from most of the anterior tongue.
notes.C: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste and general sensation from the posterior tongue and supplies the circumvallate papillae.
notes.D: The vagus carries sensation near the epiglottis and supplies palatoglossus through the pharyngeal plexus.

questions.stem: A permanently dilated pupil points to involvement of the:
questions.why: Parasympathetic fibres in the oculomotor nerve ultimately activate the sphincter pupillae. Injury to these fibres can prevent constriction and leave the pupil dilated and poorly reactive.

notes.A: Optic nerve damage blocks afferent light signals from that eye. The pupil can still constrict when the other eye receives a stimulus.
notes.B: Interruption of cervical sympathetic fibres causes a small pupil because these fibres normally activate the pupillary dilator.
notes.C: The ophthalmic nerve mainly provides sensory input from the eye and forehead. It does not carry the preganglionic pupillary constrictor fibres.
notes.E: The facial nerve supplies eyelid closure through orbicularis oculi and carries secretomotor fibres to the lacrimal gland.

questions.stem: A lesion of the lingual nerve just after it is joined by the chorda tympani could cause each of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: B
options.text: Sensory loss from the lower teeth

options.label: C
options.text: Loss of taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue

options.label: E
options.text: Sensory loss from the mucosa of the floor of the mouth

questions.why: After chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve, the combined nerve carries taste, oral sensation and salivary parasympathetic fibres. Sensory fibres from the lower teeth travel separately through the inferior alveolar nerve.

notes.A: Sublingual secretomotor fibres ultimately reach the gland from the submandibular ganglion by travelling with branches of the lingual nerve.
notes.C: Anterior tongue taste travels in chorda tympani fibres that temporarily run with the lingual nerve.
notes.D: Chorda tympani fibres reach the submandibular ganglion via the lingual nerve before postganglionic fibres supply the gland.
notes.E: The lingual nerve supplies the mucosa of the floor of the mouth as part of its general sensory distribution.

questions.stem: The nerve to mylohyoid is correctly described by each of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: It contains fibres of the mandibular nerve

options.label: B
options.text: It lies in the mylohyoid groove of the mandible

options.label: C
options.text: It supplies the anterior belly of digastric

options.label: E
options.text: It runs partly with the submental artery

questions.why: The mylohyoid nerve leaves the inferior alveolar nerve just before the latter enters the mandibular foramen. It travels down the mylohyoid groove to supply mylohyoid and the anterior digastric belly.

notes.A: The inferior alveolar nerve arises from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve and gives off the mylohyoid branch.
notes.B: The mylohyoid groove runs below the mandibular foramen and carries the nerve towards the floor of the mouth.
notes.C: The anterior digastric belly receives the mylohyoid nerve, while the posterior belly receives a facial nerve branch.
notes.E: The submental artery supplies the region beneath mylohyoid and accompanies the nerve for part of its course.

questions.stem: A doctor places his fingers over a patient's eyelids and asks her to keep her eyes closed while he tries to open them. This tests the:

options.label: B
options.text: Motor root of the trigeminal nerve

questions.why: Firm eyelid closure tests orbicularis oculi, a facial expression muscle supplied by the facial nerve. Weakness lets an examiner open the eyelids more easily despite the patient's effort.

notes.B: Trigeminal motor fibres activate jaw muscles and mylohyoid. The trigeminal nerve provides sensory input to the corneal reflex.
notes.C: The abducent nerve supplies lateral rectus and moves the eye outwards without closing the lid.
notes.D: The trochlear nerve supplies superior oblique and helps depress the adducted eye without closing the lid.
notes.E: The superior division of the oculomotor nerve supplies the levator, which actively raises the upper lid.

questions.stem: The recurrent laryngeal nerve:

options.label: A
options.text: Runs in the groove between the oesophagus and the trachea

options.label: B
options.text: Enters the larynx through the cricothyroid membrane

options.label: C
options.text: Is a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve

options.label: E
options.text: A, B and C are correct

questions.why: The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends towards the larynx beside the trachea and oesophagus, commonly in their intervening groove. It reaches the larynx deep to the inferior constrictor.

notes.B: The recurrent nerve passes deep to the inferior constrictor. The thyrohyoid membrane is pierced by the internal laryngeal nerve.
notes.C: Both recurrent laryngeal nerves are branches of the vagus, looping around a vessel before ascending.
notes.D: The external laryngeal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid. The recurrent nerve supplies the other intrinsic muscles.
notes.E: The combination is incorrect because the nerve enters deep to the inferior constrictor and arises from the vagus.

questions.stem: The cell bodies of the fibres carrying taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue lie in the:
questions.why: Taste afferents from most of the anterior tongue pass in the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve. Their cell bodies lie in the geniculate ganglion before central processes reach the brainstem.

notes.A: The superior cervical ganglion contains sympathetic postganglionic neurons supplying structures in the head and neck.
notes.B: The trigeminal ganglion contains cell bodies for general sensation from the tongue through the lingual nerve.
notes.D: The otic ganglion is a parasympathetic relay for secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland.
notes.E: The submandibular ganglion contains parasympathetic neurons for salivary secretion, while sensory taste cell bodies lie in the geniculate ganglion.

questions.stem: A lesion compressing the contents of the right jugular foramen might cause:

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of pain from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue

options.label: C
options.text: Sensory loss over the zygomatic bone

options.label: D
options.text: Inability to elevate the soft palate

options.label: E
options.text: Inability to turn the chin upward and to the right

questions.why: The glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves pass through the jugular foramen. Damage to the vagus there can weaken elevation of the palate by interrupting motor fibres to levator veli palatini.

notes.A: The lingual nerve carries pain signals from the anterior tongue and belongs to the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
notes.B: Tongue protrusion depends on genioglossus and the hypoglossal nerve, which passes through its own canal.
notes.C: Skin over the zygomatic prominence receives maxillary trigeminal branches that pass through the orbit and zygomatic bone.
notes.E: Right sternocleidomastoid helps rotate the face to the left. Turning the chin right relies mainly on the left muscle.

questions.stem: A tumour infiltrating the foramen ovale might cause all of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: B
options.text: Sensory loss from the skin of the lower lip

options.label: E
options.text: Sensory loss from the lower premolars

questions.why: The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve leaves the skull through the foramen ovale. Stylohyoid instead receives a facial nerve branch after that nerve has left the stylomastoid foramen.

notes.A: Motor fibres from the mandibular nerve reach tensor tympani through a branch associated with the nerve to medial pterygoid.
notes.B: The mental branch of the inferior alveolar nerve carries sensation from the lower lip back to the mandibular division.
notes.C: The auriculotemporal nerve and other mandibular branches carry sensation from the temporomandibular joint.
notes.E: Inferior alveolar dental branches supply the lower premolars and carry information towards the mandibular division.

questions.stem: After tonsillectomy a patient loses general sensation and taste from the posterior third of the tongue. The injured nerve is a branch of the:
questions.why: The glossopharyngeal nerve gives lingual branches to the posterior third of the tongue and runs close to the tonsillar bed. Injury during removal of the tonsil can impair taste and general sensation there.

notes.B: Chorda tympani carries anterior tongue taste, while the lingual nerve provides general sensation in that region.
notes.C: The lingual nerve mainly supplies general sensation to the anterior tongue and floor of the mouth.
notes.D: The internal laryngeal branch of the vagus supplies the epiglottic region, farther posterior than the main glossopharyngeal territory.
notes.E: The hypoglossal nerve supplies most tongue muscles and does not carry the taste fibres described.

questions.stem: All of the following about the sciatic nerve are correct EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: It is the largest nerve in the body

options.label: B
options.text: It is formed by the dorsal rami of L4–S3

options.label: C
options.text: It passes through the greater sciatic foramen

options.label: D
options.text: It leaves the pelvis below piriformis

options.label: E
options.text: It is one of the two main nerves of the sacral plexus

questions.why: The sciatic nerve forms from contributions of the anterior rami of lumbar and sacral spinal nerves, usually L4 to S3. Posterior rami supply the intrinsic back and its overlying skin.

notes.A: The sciatic nerve is the body's largest peripheral nerve and contains tibial and common fibular components.
notes.C: The sciatic nerve passes out of the pelvis into the gluteal region through the greater sciatic foramen.
notes.D: The usual sciatic course is beneath piriformis, although the components may follow variant courses around or through the muscle.
notes.E: The sciatic nerve is a major branch of the sacral plexus and carries much of its output to the lower limb.

questions.stem: All of the following about the pudendal nerve are correct EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: It comes from the ventral rami of S2–S4

options.label: B
options.text: It accompanies the internal pudendal artery

options.label: C
options.text: It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen

options.label: D
options.text: It leaves the pelvis below both piriformis and coccygeus

options.label: E
options.text: It is the main sensory nerve of the external genitalia

questions.why: The pudendal nerve exits through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis and above the sacrospinous ligament beside coccygeus. It curves around the ischial spine to reach the perineum through the lesser foramen.

notes.A: The pudendal nerve forms from anterior rami of the second through fourth sacral spinal nerves.
notes.B: The nerve runs with the internal pudendal vessels around the ischial spine and within the pudendal canal.
notes.C: The greater sciatic foramen is the nerve's exit from the pelvis, while the lesser foramen provides its route into the perineum.
notes.E: Pudendal branches carry sensation from much of the external genital region, although other nerves also supply parts of the skin.

questions.stem: Which nerve leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen ABOVE piriformis?
questions.why: Piriformis divides the greater sciatic foramen into passages above and below the muscle. The superior gluteal nerve accompanies its vessels through the upper passage to supply gluteus medius and minimus.

notes.A: The sciatic nerve usually passes under piriformis into the deep gluteal region before descending towards the thigh.
notes.B: The pudendal nerve passes below piriformis and curves around the ischial spine before reaching the perineum.
notes.D: The lumbosacral trunk descends across the sacral ala to join the sacral plexus within the pelvis.
notes.E: The obturator nerve passes through the obturator canal to reach the medial compartment of the thigh.

questions.stem: The supraorbital foramen (notch) transmits:

options.label: D
options.text: The supraorbital nerve, a continuation of the frontal branch of CN V1

questions.why: The supraorbital nerve is a terminal branch of the frontal nerve from the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. It leaves the orbit at the supraorbital notch or foramen with accompanying vessels.

notes.A: The oculomotor nerve enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure to supply most extraocular muscles.
notes.B: The infraorbital nerve is a maxillary division branch that emerges below the orbit through the infraorbital foramen.
notes.C: The supratrochlear nerve is a more medial branch of the frontal nerve that crosses the orbital rim separately.
notes.E: The notch carries an ophthalmic sensory branch. Neither the oculomotor nerve nor a branch of the maxillary division uses it.

questions.stem: A student is knifed on the forearm and afterwards cannot ADDUCT his thumb. The knife has directly injured his:

notes.A: The median nerve supplies several thenar muscles important for opposition and palmar abduction of the thumb.
notes.B: Radial nerve branches supply the long thumb extensors and abductor pollicis longus in the posterior forearm.
notes.C: The deep ulnar branch innervates adductor pollicis, which provides thumb adduction and contributes to a strong pinch.

questions.why: Adduction draws the thumb towards the plane of the palm. The main muscle producing this action is adductor pollicis, which is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

questions.stem: To confirm ulnar nerve injury, he should check for loss of sensation over:

notes.A: The palmar thumb receives median nerve sensation, while much of its proximal dorsum receives superficial radial supply.
notes.B: The palmar tip of the little finger lies in the ulnar digital nerve territory with comparatively little overlap.
notes.C: Sensation at the palmar tip of the middle finger travels through a median digital branch.

questions.why: The ulnar nerve carries cutaneous sensation from the little finger, including its palmar surface. Sensory testing there helps distinguish an ulnar deficit from loss affecting principally the median nerve.

questions.stem: He should also look for the typical hand deformity of this nerve injury:

notes.A: Clawing is most marked in the ring and little fingers when their ulnar intrinsic muscles are paralysed.
notes.B: Wrist drop follows weakness of radial-innervated wrist extensors, especially with a radial nerve lesion proximal to their motor branches.
notes.C: Ape thumb posture reflects loss of median-innervated thenar function and impaired opposition rather than the usual ulnar pattern.

questions.why: Loss of ulnar interosseous and medial lumbrical function leaves the long finger muscles relatively unbalanced. In a typical distal ulnar lesion the ring and little fingers can hyperextend at the knuckles and flex at the interphalangeal joints.

questions.stem: After cutting the front of his wrist on glass, a student can still flex the distal interphalangeal joints of his four fingers and his thumb. So these muscles are uninjured:

notes.A: Flexor digitorum profundus inserts on the distal finger phalanges and bends the distal interphalangeal joints.
notes.B: Flexor pollicis longus inserts on the distal thumb phalanx and flexes its interphalangeal joint.
notes.C: Flexor carpi radialis acts at the wrist and attaches near the bases of the second and third metacarpals.

questions.why: Active flexion at the finger distal interphalangeal joints requires force transmission by flexor digitorum profundus. Flexion at the thumb interphalangeal joint likewise requires a functioning flexor pollicis longus muscle and tendon.

questions.stem: He therefore concludes that these nerves must be intact:

notes.A: It supplies the medial half of FDP.
notes.B: Its anterior interosseous branch supplies the lateral FDP and FPL.
notes.C: It supplies no forearm flexors.

questions.why: FDP has dual supply (median and ulnar); FPL is median (AIN).

questions.stem: He cannot flex the proximal interphalangeal joints of his four fingers. He has injured his:

notes.A: Flexor carpi radialis attaches at the metacarpal bases and flexes the wrist rather than the finger joints.
notes.B: Each superficialis tendon splits around profundus and inserts on the middle phalanx, allowing it to bend the proximal interphalangeal joint.
notes.C: Flexor carpi ulnaris inserts through the pisiform complex and contributes to wrist flexion and ulnar deviation.

questions.why: Flexor digitorum superficialis inserts on the middle phalanges and is the principal flexor of the proximal interphalangeal joints. Loss of isolated flexion at these joints can reflect injury to its tendons.

questions.stem: After a deep cut in the buttock, a man walks with the pelvis dropping on one side at each step (positive Trendelenburg sign). The damaged nerve is the:

notes.A: The nerve to obturator internus supplies that muscle and superior gemellus, which principally rotate the hip laterally.
notes.B: The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius and minimus, whose abduction torque stabilises the pelvis during walking.
notes.C: The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus, which is especially important for forceful hip extension.

questions.why: During single-leg stance, the hip abductors of the supporting limb hold the opposite side of the pelvis level. Weakness of gluteus medius and minimus after superior gluteal nerve injury lets the unsupported side drop.

questions.stem: After a fight, a man has weak knee extension from a femoral nerve lesion. The root values of the femoral nerve are:

notes.A: L1 supplies other lumbar plexus branches, including the ilioinguinal nerve, but is outside the usual femoral root range.
notes.B: The second through fourth lumbar anterior rami contribute to the femoral nerve through their posterior divisions.
notes.C: L5 contributes to the lumbosacral trunk. The femoral nerve receives a more cranial contribution from L2.

questions.why: The femoral nerve arises from the posterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2, L3 and L4. It supplies quadriceps femoris, so interruption of its motor fibres weakens knee extension.

questions.stem: Cutaneous nerves derived from the femoral nerve include the:

options.label: B
options.text: Anterior cutaneous nerves of the thigh

options.label: C
options.text: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh

notes.A: The saphenous nerve carries sensation from the medial leg and medial foot as the longest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve.
notes.B: Anterior cutaneous branches of the femoral nerve supply the skin over the front and medial side of the thigh.
notes.C: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh arises independently from the lumbar plexus and supplies anterolateral thigh skin.

questions.why: The femoral nerve gives direct cutaneous branches to the anterior thigh. Its long terminal sensory branch, the saphenous nerve, continues to supply skin along the medial leg and foot.

questions.stem: Muscles weakened by this femoral nerve lesion include:

notes.A: Quadratus lumborum receives segmental branches in the posterior abdominal wall and contributes to trunk side bending.
notes.B: Psoas muscles receive direct lumbar branches, while the femoral nerve supplies iliacus separately.
notes.C: Iliacus assists hip flexion, and the four quadriceps muscles extend the knee through the patella and its ligament.

questions.why: The femoral nerve supplies quadriceps in the anterior thigh and gives branches to iliacus in the pelvis. A lesion proximal to the relevant branches can weaken knee extension and reduce hip flexion.

questions.stem: During surgical drainage of an ischioanal abscess, the nerve at risk is the:

notes.A: Direct sacral branches may supply parts of the pelvic floor or sphincter. The named nerve crossing the fat towards the anus is the inferior rectal nerve.
notes.B: The nerve to obturator internus follows the tendon region towards the muscle and supplies superior gemellus along its course.
notes.C: The inferior rectal nerve passes medially across the fossa from the pudendal canal towards the anal sphincter and skin.

questions.why: The inferior rectal nerve branches from the pudendal nerve and crosses the fat of the ischioanal fossa with its vessels. It supplies perianal skin and contributes motor fibres to the external anal sphincter.

questions.stem: A malignant tumour is damaging a patient's glossopharyngeal nerve. He will have:

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of taste and general sensation over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue

options.label: B
options.text: Loss of taste and general sensation over the posterior third of the tongue

notes.A: The lingual nerve carries anterior general sensation, and chorda tympani carries taste from most of that region.
notes.B: Lingual branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve carry both sensory modalities from the posterior tongue.
notes.C: Protrusion depends on bilateral genioglossus activity, which is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.

questions.why: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue. The anterior tongue uses a different combination of nerves, and most tongue movement depends on the hypoglossal nerve.

questions.stem: A patient stabbed in the left posterior triangle may have damaged the accessory nerve. You would test it by asking him to:

options.label: A
options.text: Rotate the head to the left against resistance

options.label: B
options.text: Shrug the left shoulder against resistance

options.label: C
options.text: Report loss of skin sensation over the posterior triangle

notes.A: The right sternocleidomastoid rotates the head to the left. The left nerve has already supplied its sternocleidomastoid before reaching the triangle.
notes.B: Trapezius elevates the scapula during shoulder shrug and receives motor fibres from the ipsilateral accessory nerve.
notes.C: Cutaneous sensation over the triangle travels through cervical plexus branches. The accessory nerve chiefly provides motor output.

questions.why: In the posterior triangle, the spinal accessory nerve runs from sternocleidomastoid to trapezius. Weak elevation of the shoulder against resistance can reveal loss of trapezius function on the affected side.

questions.stem: Loss of general sensation over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue indicates damage to the:

options.label: A
options.text: Lingual branch of the mandibular nerve

notes.A: The lingual nerve arises from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve and supplies the anterior oral mucosa.
notes.B: Chorda tympani carries anterior tongue taste and parasympathetic fibres for salivary glands rather than general tongue sensation.
notes.C: Vagal sensory fibres supply the tongue near the epiglottis, at the posterior end of its sensory territory.

questions.why: The lingual nerve carries touch, pain and temperature from most of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Chorda tympani fibres use part of the same route to carry taste.

questions.stem: A woman has a medially directed squint of the right eye. This could be due to damage to the:

notes.A: Complete oculomotor palsy usually leaves the eye directed outwards and downwards, with possible ptosis and pupillary involvement.
notes.B: Trochlear palsy weakens superior oblique and usually produces vertical or torsional diplopia, especially on looking down.
notes.C: The right lateral rectus abducts the right eye, so a right abducens lesion can cause a convergent squint.

questions.why: The abducens nerve supplies lateral rectus. When that muscle weakens, the eye cannot abduct normally and may turn medially under the relatively unopposed pull of medial rectus.

questions.stem: After orbital injury damaging the oculomotor nerve, the signs present are:

options.label: A
options.text: Pupillary constriction and a medial squint

options.label: B
options.text: Pupillary dilatation and a lateral squint

options.label: C
options.text: Pupillary dilatation and a medial squint

notes.A: A small pupil suggests reduced sympathetic dilation, while a medial squint points towards weakness of lateral rectus.
notes.B: Loss of parasympathetic input can dilate the pupil, and preserved lateral rectus activity draws the eye laterally.
notes.C: A medial squint typically occurs when lateral rectus is weak, whereas the oculomotor lesion leaves lateral rectus innervated.

questions.why: A complete oculomotor lesion can disrupt parasympathetic constriction and weaken most extraocular muscles. The pupil becomes dilated, and lateral rectus and superior oblique pull the eye outwards and usually downwards.

questions.stem: The facial nerve supplies:

options.label: A
options.text: Taste buds on the posterior third of the tongue

notes.A: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste from the posterior third of the tongue and the circumvallate papillae.
notes.B: Most soft-palate muscles receive vagal motor fibres. Tensor veli palatini receives fibres from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
notes.C: The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve supplies muscles that help depress and shape the lower lip.

questions.why: Facial motor branches supply muscles of facial expression around the mouth, including the lower lip depressors. Taste over the posterior tongue and movement of the soft palate use different cranial pathways.

questions.stem: Cutaneous innervation of the body wall:

options.label: A
options.text: Skin above the 2nd rib and manubriosternal joint is supplied by the supraclavicular nerves (cervical plexus)

options.label: B
options.text: The dermatome above the 2nd rib is C4

options.label: C
options.text: Below the manubriosternal joint, the midline skin is supplied by anterior cutaneous branches of T2–L1

options.label: D
options.text: The lateral cutaneous branches of T12 and the iliohypogastric nerve supply skin of the buttock

options.label: E
options.text: The ilioinguinal nerve has no lateral cutaneous branch and so does not supply the buttock

notes.A: Supraclavicular nerves descend across the clavicle from the cervical plexus and supply skin over the upper anterior chest.
notes.B: The fourth cervical dermatome extends over the clavicle and upper thoracic skin, with overlap at adjacent segmental boundaries.
notes.C: Anterior cutaneous branches reach the skin near the midline, with thoracic supply above and iliohypogastric supply near the pubis.
notes.D: Lateral cutaneous branches of the subcostal and iliohypogastric nerves cross the iliac crest to supply upper buttock skin.
notes.E: The ilioinguinal nerve supplies the groin and adjacent upper medial thigh through its terminal cutaneous branches.

questions.why: Cutaneous supply changes from supraclavicular branches over the upper chest to segmental thoracic and upper lumbar branches more inferiorly. Some lower segmental nerves send lateral branches over the iliac crest onto the buttock.

questions.stem: Tongue muscles supplied by the hypoglossal nerve include:

notes.A: Palatoglossus receives motor fibres from the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus and elevates the back of the tongue.
notes.B: The superior and inferior longitudinal muscles receive hypoglossal motor fibres and shorten or curl the tongue.
notes.C: Styloglossus receives hypoglossal fibres and pulls the tongue upwards and backwards from its styloid attachment.
notes.D: The vertical muscle receives hypoglossal fibres and flattens or broadens the tongue during contraction.
notes.E: Hyoglossus is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve and depresses the side of the tongue.

questions.why: The hypoglossal nerve supplies the intrinsic muscles that change tongue shape and most extrinsic muscles that reposition it. Palatoglossus receives vagal innervation through the pharyngeal plexus.

questions.stem: Nerve supply of the tongue:

options.label: A
options.text: Proprioception from the tongue travels in the lingual nerve

options.label: B
options.text: General sensation of the anterior two-thirds is glossopharyngeal

options.label: C
options.text: General sensation of the posterior third is vagal

options.label: D
options.text: The vallate papillae are supplied by the chorda tympani

options.label: E
options.text: The cell bodies of chorda tympani taste fibres are in the trigeminal ganglion

notes.A: Probably via the hypoglossal nerve and cervical nerves; not the lingual.
notes.B: Lingual nerve.
notes.C: Glossopharyngeal.
notes.D: By the glossopharyngeal nerve.
notes.E: Geniculate ganglion.

questions.why: All five are false: general sensation of the anterior two-thirds is by the lingual nerve (V3) and of the posterior third by the glossopharyngeal, proprioception does not run in the lingual nerve, the vallate papillae are supplied by CN IX, and chorda tympani taste fibres have their cell bodies in the geniculate (not trigeminal) ganglion.

questions.stem: Cranial nerves supplying muscles derived from pharyngeal arch mesoderm include:

notes.A: The oculomotor nerve supplies extraocular muscles, which develop in a different mesodermal region from the pharyngeal arch muscles.
notes.B: The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve supplies muscles of the first arch, including those used in mastication.
notes.C: The facial nerve supplies second-arch muscles, including the muscles of facial expression and the stapedius.
notes.D: Glossopharyngeal motor fibres supply stylopharyngeus, the principal muscle derivative of the third pharyngeal arch.
notes.E: The hypoglossal nerve supplies tongue muscles formed chiefly from occipital somites, with palatoglossus supplied by the vagus.

questions.why: Most pharyngeal arch muscle groups retain a characteristic cranial motor supply. The trigeminal, facial and glossopharyngeal nerves serve the first three arch groups, while vagal branches serve the fourth and sixth.

questions.stem: Cutaneous innervation of the upper limb:

options.label: A
options.text: The lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm is a branch of the axillary nerve

options.label: B
options.text: The intercostobrachial nerve is a branch of the medial cord

options.label: C
options.text: The medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm is a branch of the median nerve

options.label: D
options.text: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm is the end of the musculocutaneous nerve

options.label: E
options.text: The posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm arises directly from the posterior cord

notes.A: The lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm arises from the radial nerve. The axillary nerve gives an upper lateral branch.
notes.B: The intercostobrachial nerve is usually the lateral cutaneous branch of the second intercostal nerve.
notes.C: The medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm arises directly from the medial cord and supplies medial forearm skin.
notes.E: The posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm branches from the radial nerve rather than directly from the posterior cord.
notes.D: After supplying the anterior arm muscles, the musculocutaneous nerve continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

questions.why: Cutaneous nerves to the upper limb may arise directly from the brachial plexus or as branches of its terminal nerves. The intercostobrachial nerve is an exception because it originates from a thoracic intercostal nerve.

questions.stem: Formation of the brachial plexus:

options.label: A
options.text: C7 alone forms the middle trunk

options.label: B
options.text: The lower two roots form the upper trunk

options.label: C
options.text: All posterior divisions join to form the posterior cord

options.label: D
options.text: The anterior division of the lower trunk continues as the medial cord

options.label: E
options.text: The anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks form the lateral cord

notes.B: The upper trunk forms from the fifth and sixth cervical roots, while the lowest pair forms the lower trunk.
notes.A: The seventh cervical anterior ramus continues as the middle trunk without uniting with a neighbouring root.
notes.C: The posterior divisions of all three trunks unite to form the posterior cord behind the axillary artery.
notes.D: The anterior division of the lower trunk continues into the medial cord, carrying chiefly C8 and T1 fibres.
notes.E: The anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks join to form the lateral cord.

questions.why: The brachial plexus normally reorganises anterior rami of C5 through T1 into three trunks, each with anterior and posterior divisions. Their divisions then converge into cords named for their position around the axillary artery.

questions.stem: Branches arising from the ROOTS of the brachial plexus include the:

notes.A: The nerve to subclavius arises from the upper trunk and descends to the muscle beneath the clavicle.
notes.B: The dorsal scapular nerve usually arises from the fifth cervical root and supplies the rhomboids and part of levator scapulae.
notes.C: The thoracodorsal nerve arises from the posterior cord and travels to latissimus dorsi.
notes.D: The long thoracic nerve usually receives fibres from the fifth through seventh cervical roots and supplies serratus anterior.

questions.why: The dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves branch from anterior rami before the trunks form. Their scapular targets differ from those of the nerves that arise farther along the plexus.

questions.stem: Branches arising from the TRUNKS of the brachial plexus include the:

notes.A: Supraclavicular nerves arise from the cervical plexus and supply skin over the clavicle, shoulder and upper chest.
notes.B: The suprascapular nerve arises from the upper trunk and supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
notes.C: The long thoracic nerve collects contributions directly from cervical roots before descending on serratus anterior.
notes.D: The thoracodorsal nerve arises from the posterior cord and supplies latissimus dorsi on the posterior axillary wall.
notes.E: The intercostobrachial nerve is usually a lateral cutaneous branch of the second intercostal nerve.

questions.why: Branches can leave the plexus before or after its trunks form. The suprascapular nerve leaves the upper trunk and runs towards the suprascapular notch to supply two scapular muscles.

questions.stem: A man in a motorbike accident is diagnosed with left Erb–Duchenne palsy because:

options.label: A
options.text: His face was twisted to the left

options.label: B
options.text: He could not abduct the left arm

options.label: D
options.text: His left arm was laterally rotated

notes.B: Weakness of supraspinatus and deltoid makes shoulder abduction difficult because both receive substantial upper plexus input.
notes.C: Wrist flexion can accompany the classical waiter's-tip posture, particularly when involvement extends to wrist extensors.
notes.D: Shoulder lateral rotators weaken, so the relatively unopposed internal rotators tend to turn the arm medially.
notes.E: Weak supination from biceps and supinator involvement allows the forearm to assume a pronated position.
notes.A: Facial expression depends on the facial nerve. An isolated upper brachial plexus injury affects the upper limb.

questions.why: Upper plexus injury affecting chiefly C5 and C6 weakens shoulder abduction and lateral rotation as well as elbow flexion and supination. The arm tends to rest adducted and internally rotated, with the forearm pronated.

questions.stem: After a shoulder injury, axillary nerve damage is suggested by:

options.label: B
options.text: Weak abduction of the right shoulder

options.label: C
options.text: Normal flexion of the right shoulder

options.label: D
options.text: Normal extension of the right shoulder

options.label: E
options.text: Numbness over the lower lateral arm

notes.C: Several muscles contribute to shoulder flexion, so preserved flexion alone does not establish axillary nerve damage.
notes.D: Extension also relies on muscles supplied by other nerves, so preserved extension is not a localising sign.
notes.E: The axillary cutaneous branch supplies the upper lateral arm. The lower lateral region receives a radial nerve branch.
notes.A: A sustained axillary motor lesion denervates deltoid and can flatten the normally rounded contour of the shoulder.
notes.B: Deltoid produces much of the force for shoulder abduction after supraspinatus initiates the movement.

questions.why: The axillary nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor and carries sensation over the upper lateral arm. Deltoid wasting and weak shoulder abduction therefore help localise dysfunction after a shoulder injury.

questions.stem: Radial nerve damage in the middle of the arm (spiral groove) causes:

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of sensation over the back of the arm

options.label: C
options.text: Sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand (lateral side)

options.label: E
options.text: Fixed lateral rotation of the arm

notes.A: The posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm usually arises before the radial nerve reaches the humeral groove.
notes.B: Most elbow extension is preserved if the triceps motor branches leave the nerve above the lesion.
notes.C: The superficial radial sensory branch supplies part of the dorsolateral hand, with the first dorsal web space a useful landmark.
notes.D: Loss of radial motor supply to the wrist extensors allows unopposed flexion, producing wrist drop.
notes.E: Shoulder rotation depends on muscles around the glenohumeral joint and is not fixed by a radial lesion in the arm.

questions.why: A radial nerve lesion at the humeral groove typically weakens wrist and finger extension and can impair dorsolateral hand sensation. Major triceps branches and the posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm often arise proximal to the lesion.

questions.stem: Ulnar nerve injury in the axilla causes:

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of sensation on the medial forearm

options.label: B
options.text: Loss of sensation of the medial 1½ fingers

options.label: C
options.text: Inability to extend the IP joints of the ring and little fingers

notes.A: Medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
notes.C: Paralysed medial lumbricals and interossei.
notes.D: Palmar interossei.
notes.E: Dorsal interossei are also paralysed.

questions.why: High ulnar injury numbs the medial one-and-a-half fingers and paralyses the interossei, so finger adduction and abduction are lost (B, D true); A is false (the medial forearm is the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm) and E is false (abduction is also lost). C is keyed false.

questions.stem: Intrinsic hand muscles supplied by the median nerve include:

notes.A: Adductor pollicis receives motor fibres from the deep branch of the ulnar nerve and contributes to pinch.
notes.B: The medial two lumbricals receive ulnar motor supply, while the lateral pair receive median supply.
notes.C: The superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis is usually supplied by the recurrent median branch.
notes.D: Abductor pollicis brevis receives recurrent median fibres and moves the thumb away from the plane of the palm.
notes.E: Opponens pollicis receives median motor fibres and rotates the first metacarpal during thumb opposition.

questions.why: The recurrent median branch supplies most thenar muscles, and median digital branches supply the lateral two lumbricals. The deep ulnar branch supplies adductor pollicis and the medial two lumbricals.

questions.stem: About the femoral nerve and vessels:

options.label: A
options.text: The femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral vein, inside the femoral sheath

options.label: B
options.text: The femoral artery lies medial to the femoral nerve

options.label: C
options.text: The femoral nerve occupies the lateral compartment of the sheath

options.label: D
options.text: The femoral artery lies at the midinguinal point

options.label: E
options.text: A femoral nerve block can be done just below the inguinal ligament

notes.A: The nerve lies lateral to the vessels, but the femoral sheath encloses the vessels and femoral canal.
notes.C: The sheath's lateral compartment contains the femoral artery. The femoral nerve lies farther laterally outside the sheath.
notes.B: The artery is medial to the femoral nerve and lateral to the femoral vein at the upper thigh.
notes.D: The midinguinal point is halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis and marks the artery.
notes.E: The femoral nerve is accessible below the ligament, where clinicians can identify it lateral to the artery for regional anaesthesia.

questions.why: Below the inguinal ligament the femoral nerve lies on iliacus lateral to the femoral artery and outside its sheath. The artery lies near the surface landmark halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis.

questions.stem: The root values of the femoral nerve include:

notes.A: Posterior rami supply the back and do not form the lumbar plexus, which is derived from anterior rami.
notes.B: The anterior ramus of L2 is the uppermost usual contribution to the femoral nerve.
notes.C: The anterior ramus of L3 contributes fibres to the femoral nerve through its posterior division.
notes.D: The anterior ramus of L4 provides the lowest usual root contribution to the femoral nerve.
notes.E: The anterior ramus of L5 contributes to the lumbosacral trunk rather than the femoral nerve.

questions.why: The femoral nerve forms in the lumbar plexus from posterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2, L3 and L4. It descends into the thigh between psoas major and iliacus.

questions.stem: Branches of the femoral nerve include:

options.label: A
options.text: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh

notes.A: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh arises directly from the lumbar plexus as a separate nerve.
notes.D: Adductor brevis normally receives motor fibres from the obturator nerve in the medial thigh.
notes.E: Gracilis receives obturator motor supply and contributes to hip adduction and knee flexion.
notes.B: The nerve to pectineus usually branches from the femoral nerve near the inguinal ligament.
notes.C: The saphenous nerve is the femoral nerve's long sensory branch to the medial leg and foot.

questions.why: Femoral nerve branches supply anterior thigh muscles and transmit sensation from the anterior thigh and medial leg. Several nearby muscles and cutaneous territories receive separate lumbar plexus branches.

questions.stem: About the obturator nerve:

options.label: A
options.text: It is a branch of the sacral plexus

options.label: B
options.text: It supplies the medial compartment of the thigh

options.label: C
options.text: It emerges below the lower border of piriformis

options.label: E
options.text: It supplies both the hip and knee joints
