notes.A: The obturator nerve forms from anterior divisions of lumbar anterior rami, usually L2 to L4.
notes.C: Its pelvic exit is the obturator canal. The passage beneath piriformis transmits branches of the sacral plexus.
notes.D: A cutaneous branch can supply a small patch of skin on the medial thigh, although the area is variable.
notes.B: Obturator motor branches supply most muscles in the medial compartment, including adductor longus and gracilis.
notes.E: The obturator nerve gives articular branches to the hip and can contribute sensory supply to the knee.

questions.why: The obturator nerve arises from the lumbar plexus and reaches the medial thigh through the obturator canal. It supplies several adductors and gives articular branches as well as a variable cutaneous branch.

questions.stem: Structures emerging through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis include the:

options.label: B
options.text: Posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh

notes.A: The inferior gluteal nerve and vessels pass below piriformis to reach the deep surface of gluteus maximus.
notes.B: The posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh leaves beneath piriformis and carries sensation from the posterior thigh.
notes.C: The pudendal nerve exits below piriformis before turning around the ischial spine into the perineum.
notes.D: The internal pudendal artery leaves alongside the pudendal nerve and returns through the lesser sciatic foramen.
notes.E: The nerve to obturator internus leaves through the lower passage and then reaches its muscle by the lesser foramen.

questions.why: Piriformis divides the greater sciatic foramen into two passages. Several sacral plexus branches and the inferior gluteal and internal pudendal vessels travel through the lower passage towards the buttock or perineum.

questions.stem: The sciatic nerve:

options.label: A
options.text: Is formed from the sacral plexus (L4–S3)

options.label: B
options.text: Has no cutaneous branches in the thigh

options.label: C
options.text: Supplies the hamstring part of adductor magnus

options.label: D
options.text: Is the most superficial neurovascular structure in the popliteal fossa (as the tibial nerve)

notes.A: The sciatic nerve gathers contributions from L4 through S3 in the sacral plexus.
notes.B: It gives muscular branches in the thigh. Skin over the posterior thigh is supplied chiefly by a separate cutaneous nerve.
notes.C: The tibial division supplies the hamstring part of adductor magnus, which contributes to hip extension.
notes.D: In the central popliteal bundle the tibial nerve lies closest to the surface, with the popliteal vein and artery deeper.

questions.why: The sciatic nerve carries lumbar and sacral fibres into the posterior thigh. Its tibial component supplies most hamstrings and continues towards the popliteal fossa, where the tibial nerve lies superficial to the central vessels.

questions.stem: Nerves supplying the anterior compartment of the leg:

options.label: C
options.text: Common fibular nerve (only via its branches)

notes.C: Directly it supplies none.
notes.D: Lateral compartment.
notes.E: Sensory.

questions.why: The anterior compartment of the leg is supplied by the deep fibular nerve (B true); the tibial supplies the posterior compartment, the superficial fibular the lateral compartment, and the saphenous is purely cutaneous, so the others are false.

questions.stem: Dermatomes correctly matched:

notes.A: The first cervical nerve usually lacks a distinct cutaneous dermatome. Other cervical and trigeminal nerves supply these regions.
notes.B: The sixth cervical dermatome commonly includes the thumb and lateral forearm, although its borders overlap adjacent segments.
notes.C: The umbilicus is the standard surface landmark for the tenth thoracic dermatome.
notes.D: The second thoracic dermatome includes the upper medial arm, supplied in part through the intercostobrachial nerve.
notes.E: The first lumbar dermatome reaches the groin near the inguinal ligament.

questions.why: Dermatomes map skin to spinal segments, with neighbouring territories overlapping. The thumb, upper medial arm, umbilicus and inguinal region are useful approximate landmarks for common segmental maps.

questions.stem: Spinal segments correctly matched with reflexes:

notes.D: The ankle reflex is mediated primarily by S1 through the tibial nerve to the plantarflexors.
notes.A: The biceps tendon reflex tests the musculocutaneous pathway, mainly through the fifth and sixth cervical segments.
notes.B: The radial nerve carries the triceps reflex, whose dominant segment is C7 with contribution commonly assigned to C8.
notes.C: The patellar tendon reflex tests mainly the third and fourth lumbar segments through the femoral nerve.
notes.E: The superficial abdominal responses use thoracic segments, with upper and lower quadrants involving different levels.

questions.why: Reflexes help localise dysfunction to the spinal segments and peripheral nerves that form their arcs. Tendon responses test stretch pathways, while stroking the abdominal skin elicits a superficial cutaneous response.

questions.stem: About the nerve supply of taste buds and papillae:

options.label: A
options.text: Filiform papillae have a sensory nerve supply (lingual nerve)

options.label: B
options.text: The vallate papillae are supplied by the lingual nerve

options.label: C
options.text: The fungiform papillae (taste) are supplied by the facial nerve

options.label: D
options.text: The vallate papillae are supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve

options.label: E
options.text: The fungiform papillae are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve

notes.A: Filiform papillae lack taste buds, but the lingual nerve carries general sensory information from their region.
notes.B: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the circumvallate papillae near the terminal sulcus.
notes.C: Taste from fungiform papillae reaches the facial nerve through its chorda tympani branch.
notes.E: The hypoglossal nerve supplies tongue muscles, while taste from fungiform papillae uses facial sensory fibres.
notes.D: Glossopharyngeal taste fibres supply the large vallate papillae just anterior to the terminal sulcus.

questions.why: General sensation and taste follow different routes in the anterior tongue. Fungiform taste fibres travel with chorda tympani, whereas circumvallate papillae receive glossopharyngeal fibres despite lying near the anterior side of the terminal sulcus.

questions.stem: Nerves providing sensory supply to the mouth include the:

options.label: E
options.text: Buccal branch of the facial nerve

notes.E: The facial buccal branch supplies muscles including buccinator. Cheek mucosal sensation travels mainly through the trigeminal buccal nerve.
notes.A: The greater palatine nerve supplies much of the hard palate and adjacent palatal gingiva.
notes.B: The nasopalatine nerve reaches the anterior hard palate through the incisive canal and supplies its mucosa.
notes.C: The inferior alveolar nerve supplies the lower teeth, with terminal branches reaching the chin and lower lip.
notes.D: Superior alveolar branches supply the maxillary teeth and related gingival tissues.

questions.why: Branches of the maxillary and mandibular divisions of the trigeminal nerve convey most general sensation from the palate, teeth and oral mucosa. The facial buccal branch instead supplies muscles around the cheek.

questions.stem: Which cranial nerve carries general somatic afferent (GSA) fibres?
questions.why: The trigeminal nerve carries the main general somatic afferent supply of the face, oral and nasal cavities and parts of the dura. These fibres convey modalities including touch, pain and temperature.

notes.A: The olfactory nerve carries smell from the olfactory epithelium as a specialised sensory modality.
notes.B: The oculomotor nerve supplies most orbital muscles and carries parasympathetic fibres to the ciliary ganglion.
notes.C: The trochlear nerve carries motor fibres to superior oblique, which contributes to eye depression and intorsion.
notes.E: The abducent nerve supplies lateral rectus, the muscle that moves the eye laterally.

questions.stem: Which cranial nerve carries special visceral efferent (branchiomotor) fibres?
questions.why: Branchial motor fibres of the facial nerve supply muscles derived mainly from the second pharyngeal arch. These include the muscles of facial expression, stapedius and the posterior belly of digastric.

notes.A: The optic nerve carries visual sensory information from the retina to central visual pathways.
notes.B: The oculomotor nerve supplies orbital muscles and carries parasympathetic fibres, using somatic and visceral motor components.
notes.C: The trochlear nerve supplies superior oblique, an extraocular muscle receiving somatic motor fibres.
notes.D: The abducent nerve activates lateral rectus through somatic motor fibres rather than an arch-derived motor pathway.

questions.stem: Oculomotor nerve lesions cause all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.why: The oculomotor nerve controls the upper eyelid elevator and most extraocular muscles. Loss of that control can cause ptosis and misalignment, while forward displacement of the globe generally points to an orbital process.

notes.A: A complete lesion weakens medial rectus, allowing relatively unopposed lateral rectus to turn the eye outwards.
notes.B: Ptosis occurs because levator palpebrae superioris loses its oculomotor motor supply.
notes.C: Asymmetrical weakness can misalign the eyes, producing diplopia when both eyes are open.
notes.D: The lesion can weaken adduction, elevation and depression because several extraocular muscles share oculomotor supply.

questions.stem: About trochlear nerve lesions:

options.label: A
options.text: The patient cannot see near objects

options.label: C
options.text: The patient has double vision on looking downward (e.g. reading, going downstairs)

options.label: E
options.text: The pupil is fixed and dilated

questions.why: The trochlear nerve supplies superior oblique, which helps depress the adducted eye and intort it. Weakness commonly causes vertical diplopia during tasks such as reading or going downstairs.

notes.A: Near focusing depends partly on the ciliary muscle and its oculomotor parasympathetic supply, rather than the trochlear nerve.
notes.B: Abduction depends on lateral rectus, which receives motor fibres from the abducent nerve.
notes.D: Superior rectus and inferior oblique contribute to upward gaze and receive oculomotor motor supply.
notes.E: A fixed dilated pupil can follow loss of oculomotor parasympathetic input to the sphincter of the pupil.

questions.stem: Which statement about facial nerve lesions is NOT correct?

options.label: A
options.text: A pontine lesion of the facial nerve may also paralyse lateral rectus

options.label: B
options.text: Paralysis of both VII and VIII suggests a lesion in the internal acoustic meatus

options.label: C
options.text: Damage to the facial nerve in the parotid gland causes loss of taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue

options.label: D
options.text: A lesion in the facial canal may cause hyperacusis

options.label: E
options.text: In an upper motor neuron lesion only the lower face is paralysed

questions.why: Chorda tympani leaves the facial nerve within the temporal bone before the main trunk enters the parotid gland. A lesion confined to the parotid segment therefore typically weakens facial expression while preserving anterior tongue taste.

notes.A: Facial fibres loop near the abducens nucleus in the pons, so a lesion there can affect lateral gaze and facial movement together.
notes.B: The facial and vestibulocochlear nerves share the internal acoustic meatus, where one lesion can affect both.
notes.D: A lesion upstream of the nerve to stapedius can cause hyperacusis by interrupting damping of ossicular motion.
notes.E: Bilateral cortical input usually preserves forehead movement after a unilateral upper motor neuron lesion, while the opposite lower face is weak.

questions.stem: All of the following are associated with vestibulocochlear nerve lesions EXCEPT:
questions.why: The vestibulocochlear nerve carries hearing and balance information. Its dysfunction can affect sound perception and vestibular responses, whereas Bell's palsy is an acute peripheral facial motor palsy without an identified cause.

notes.A: Asymmetric vestibular activity can cause vertigo, an illusory sense of movement.
notes.C: A vestibular imbalance can produce nystagmus through asymmetric input to the pathways controlling gaze.
notes.D: Cochlear or cochlear nerve dysfunction can produce tinnitus, the perception of sound without an external source.
notes.E: Damage to the cochlear division can impair sound transmission to the brain and cause sensorineural hearing loss.

questions.stem: Which nerve gives sensory supply to the middle ear cavity?
questions.why: The tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve enters the middle ear and contributes to the tympanic plexus on the promontory. This plexus provides sensation to the mucosa of the cavity.

notes.A: The facial nerve passes through its bony canal and gives motor fibres to stapedius. The tympanic plexus supplies the cavity mucosa.
notes.B: The auriculotemporal branch of the trigeminal nerve supplies part of the external ear and outer surface of the tympanic membrane.
notes.D: The vestibulocochlear nerve carries hearing and balance signals from receptors in the inner ear.
notes.E: The auricular branch of the vagus supplies parts of the external acoustic canal rather than the middle ear mucosa.

questions.stem: True or false: Damage to the median nerve after it passes between the heads of pronator teres causes weakness of pronation.
questions.why: The distal median nerve can lose its anterior interosseous branch to pronator quadratus. Branches to pronator teres usually leave earlier, so pronation weakens but remains possible.

notes.B: Pronator teres can still work, but loss of anterior interosseous supply weakens pronator quadratus and reduces overall pronation.

questions.stem: True or false: There are 8 anterior rami in the cervical region.
questions.why: There are eight pairs of cervical spinal nerves even though there are seven cervical vertebrae. Each spinal nerve divides into an anterior and a posterior ramus, yielding eight anterior rami on each side.

notes.B: The eighth cervical nerve emerges between the seventh cervical and first thoracic vertebrae and also has an anterior ramus.

questions.stem: True or false: If the radial nerve is cut where it pierces the lateral intermuscular septum, all posterior-arm muscles (except anconeus) are paralysed.
questions.why: The radial nerve supplies triceps in the posterior arm before traversing the lateral intermuscular septum. A distal lesion at the septum chiefly threatens motor branches to muscles in the forearm.

notes.A: Triceps receives branches proximal to the septum, so its motor supply is usually preserved after a lesion at that level.

questions.stem: True or false: Cutting the median nerve distal to the elbow causes profound weakness of MCP flexion of the 4th and 5th digits.
questions.why: The interossei and medial two lumbricals contribute strongly to flexion at the knuckles of the ring and little fingers. Their motor supply comes from the ulnar nerve, so they are spared by an isolated median lesion.

notes.A: Median injury can weaken long finger flexion, but the ulnar nerve supplies the intrinsic flexors of the ring and little finger knuckles.

questions.stem: True or false: Damage to the suprascapular nerve impairs lateral rotation of the arm.
questions.why: The suprascapular nerve supplies infraspinatus, which creates lateral rotation at the shoulder. Injury can weaken that action while the axillary nerve still supplies teres minor, another lateral rotator.

notes.B: Infraspinatus receives suprascapular motor fibres and contributes to externally rotating the humerus in the glenoid cavity.

questions.stem: True or false: The dorsal scapular nerve arises from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus.
questions.why: The dorsal scapular nerve usually leaves the anterior ramus of C5 before it joins C6 to form the upper trunk. Its principal targets are the rhomboids and part of levator scapulae.

notes.A: The upper trunk gives the suprascapular nerve and nerve to subclavius, whereas the dorsal scapular nerve generally arises more proximally.

questions.stem: True or false: The obturator nerve supplies the muscles of the posterior compartment of the thigh.
questions.why: The obturator nerve reaches the medial thigh through the obturator canal and supplies most adductors. The sciatic nerve supplies the hamstring muscles of the posterior thigh, mainly through its tibial division.

notes.A: Obturator branches supply medial thigh adductors, including adductor longus and gracilis, while sciatic branches supply the hamstrings.

questions.stem: True or false: The contents of the adductor (subsartorial, Hunter's) canal include the obturator nerve.
questions.why: The adductor canal carries the femoral vessels and saphenous nerve deep to sartorius. The main obturator nerve divides after reaching the medial thigh and distributes branches around adductor brevis.

notes.A: The main obturator nerve passes through the obturator canal and divides into branches around adductor brevis.

questions.stem: True or false: The root values of the femoral nerve are L2, L3 and L4.
questions.why: The femoral nerve forms from posterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2, L3 and L4. It reaches the thigh lateral to the femoral vessels after passing under the inguinal ligament.

notes.B: The femoral nerve receives fibres from the second, third and fourth lumbar anterior rami in the usual pattern.

questions.stem: True or false: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh supplies vastus lateralis.
questions.why: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh carries sensation from the anterolateral skin. Vastus lateralis is a quadriceps muscle in the anterior compartment and receives motor fibres from the femoral nerve.

notes.A: Vastus lateralis receives motor supply through a branch of the femoral nerve and contributes to extension of the knee.

questions.stem: True or false: Femoral nerve fibres supply the skin on the medial side of the leg and foot.
questions.why: The saphenous nerve is a cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve. It becomes superficial near the medial knee, then supplies skin along the medial leg and part of the medial foot.

notes.B: Femoral sensory fibres reach below the knee in the saphenous branch even though its main motor branches supply the thigh.

questions.stem: True or false: Below the manubriosternal joint, the ventral skin of the trunk is supplied by anterior cutaneous branches of T2 to S5.
questions.why: Cutaneous branches from thoracic spinal segments supply the anterior chest and abdomen, with L1 contributing near the groin and pubis. Sacral segments chiefly serve regions of the lower limb and perineum.

notes.A: The lower anterior abdomen receives lumbar as well as lower thoracic branches. Sacral dermatomes do not continue the anterior trunk series to the pubis.

questions.stem: True or false: The ilioinguinal nerve is a collateral branch of the iliohypogastric nerve.
questions.why: Both come from L1; Snell describes the ilioinguinal as its smaller collateral branch.

questions.stem: True or false: The collateral branches of the intercostal nerves supply the skin over the anterolateral chest wall.
questions.why: Intercostal nerves give named lateral and anterior cutaneous branches that reach the skin. Their collateral branches travel with small vessels along the border of the lower rib within the intercostal space.

notes.A: The lateral cutaneous branches supply skin on the side of the chest, while anterior cutaneous branches emerge near the sternum.

questions.stem: True or false: The first cervical nerve (C1) does not supply skin of the neck.
questions.why: The first cervical nerve chiefly supplies muscle and usually has no distinct cutaneous dermatome. Skin over the neck and scalp is supplied by other upper cervical branches, including branches from the second cervical nerve.

notes.B: The dorsal ramus of the first cervical nerve is the suboccipital nerve, which primarily supplies the deep suboccipital muscles.

questions.stem: True or false: The greater occipital nerve comes from the ventral rami of the cervical nerves.
questions.why: The greater occipital nerve arises from the medial branch of the second cervical posterior ramus. It ascends to supply posterior scalp, while the lesser occipital nerve comes from the cervical plexus.

notes.A: The cervical plexus uses anterior rami and gives the lesser occipital nerve. The greater occipital nerve comes from the posterior ramus of C2.

questions.stem: True or false: The abducent nerve can be seen passing through the cavernous sinus in the middle cranial fossa.
questions.why: The abducent nerve crosses the venous compartment of the cavernous sinus beside the internal carotid artery. The oculomotor, trochlear and upper trigeminal divisions instead run in the lateral wall.

notes.B: Unlike the nerves embedded in the lateral wall, the abducent nerve runs with the artery within the sinus proper.

questions.stem: The pelvic splanchnic nerves contain:
questions.why: Pelvic splanchnic nerves carry preganglionic parasympathetic fibres from sacral levels S2 to S4 to pelvic and distal bowel plexuses. They also provide a route for visceral afferents.

notes.A: Somatic afferents from pelvic floor skin or skeletal muscle chiefly run in somatic nerves, such as the pudendal nerve.
notes.B: Sympathetic fibres reach the pelvic plexus through hypogastric pathways and sacral splanchnic nerves, which are a separate group.
notes.D: Special visceral efferent fibres supply pharyngeal arch muscles through cranial nerves, rather than pelvic smooth muscle or glands.
notes.E: Special somatic afferent pathways carry visual, auditory or vestibular information through cranial nerves.

questions.stem: Parasympathetic stimulation in the female produces:

options.label: B
options.text: Engorgement of the erectile tissue of the vestibular bulbs

options.label: C
options.text: Engorgement of the greater vestibular glands

options.label: D
options.text: A decrease in size of the clitoris

questions.why: Parasympathetic activity promotes relaxation of smooth muscle and increased blood flow within genital erectile tissues. Filling of the vascular spaces produces engorgement of the vestibular bulbs and clitoral tissue.

notes.A: Genital arousal is associated with increased vaginal lubrication, including fluid movement across the vaginal wall.
notes.C: The greater vestibular glands secrete mucus. The adjacent vestibular bulbs contain the erectile tissue that engorges.
notes.D: Increased blood filling generally enlarges erectile tissue in the clitoris during arousal.
notes.E: Flaccidity follows reduced blood filling and detumescence, whereas the parasympathetic response promotes engorgement.

questions.stem: Regarding the parasympathetic nuclei of the brainstem, all are correct EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: The superior salivatory nucleus supplies the lacrimal gland

options.label: B
options.text: The superior salivatory nucleus supplies the submandibular gland

options.label: C
options.text: Lacrimal fibres from the superior salivatory nucleus relay in the pterygopalatine ganglion

options.label: D
options.text: The inferior salivatory nucleus supplies the parotid gland

options.label: E
options.text: The Edinger–Westphal nucleus supplies dilator pupillae

questions.why: Edinger–Westphal preganglionic fibres travel with the oculomotor nerve and synapse in the ciliary ganglion. Their targets promote pupillary constriction and accommodation, while the dilator pupillae receives sympathetic supply.

notes.A: The greater petrosal nerve carries facial preganglionic fibres from the superior salivatory region towards the lacrimal pathway.
notes.B: Superior salivatory fibres enter chorda tympani and travel with the lingual nerve to supply the submandibular gland after a ganglionic relay.
notes.C: Lacrimal secretomotor fibres synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion before reaching the gland on trigeminal branches.
notes.D: Parasympathetic fibres from the inferior salivatory nucleus reach the otic ganglion before supplying the parotid.

questions.stem: Nerves containing sympathetic fibres include the:

notes.A: The nerve of the pterygoid canal includes sympathetic fibres contributed by the deep petrosal nerve and parasympathetic fibres from the greater petrosal nerve.
notes.C: The lesser petrosal nerve principally conveys glossopharyngeal preganglionic parasympathetic fibres towards the otic ganglion to supply the parotid.
notes.B: The deep petrosal nerve carries postganglionic sympathetic fibres that have already relayed in the superior cervical ganglion.

questions.why: The deep petrosal nerve carries sympathetic fibres from the internal carotid plexus. It joins the greater petrosal nerve to form a mixed autonomic pathway through the pterygoid canal.

questions.stem: The parasympathetic supply to the heart, lungs, gut, liver and pancreas travels in the:

notes.C: Glossopharyngeal parasympathetic fibres relay in the otic ganglion to supply the parotid gland.
notes.A: Sacral spinal outflow gives pelvic parasympathetic fibres, while the named thoracic and upper abdominal organs mainly use the vagus.
notes.B: Vagal branches reach the heart and lungs, while oesophageal vagal pathways descend to upper abdominal organs.

questions.why: The vagus supplies parasympathetic fibres to thoracic organs and much of the abdominal digestive tract. The distal hindgut and pelvic organs instead receive parasympathetic fibres from sacral outflow.

questions.stem: The postganglionic parasympathetic pathway to the lacrimal gland includes the:

notes.A: The zygomatic nerve carries postganglionic fibres into the orbit after receiving them in the pterygopalatine fossa.
notes.B: A communication from the zygomaticotemporal branch transfers these fibres to the lacrimal nerve in the conventional pathway.
notes.C: The lacrimal nerve carries the postganglionic secretomotor fibres on the final segment of their route to the gland.

questions.why: Lacrimal secretomotor fibres synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion. They then use branches of the maxillary nerve and a communicating branch to reach the lacrimal nerve, which conveys them to the gland.

questions.stem: The pterygopalatine ganglion supplies all of the following EXCEPT the:
questions.why: The submandibular gland receives postganglionic fibres from the submandibular ganglion after facial preganglionic fibres travel through chorda tympani. The pterygopalatine ganglion instead relays fibres reaching lacrimal, nasal, palatal and pharyngeal targets.

notes.A: Postganglionic fibres reach the lacrimal gland via zygomatic and lacrimal branches after relaying in the pterygopalatine ganglion.
notes.B: Posterior nasal branches carry secretomotor fibres from the pterygopalatine ganglion to glands in the nasal mucosa.
notes.C: Branches of the palatine nerves carry postganglionic fibres from the pterygopalatine ganglion to glands in the palate.
notes.D: The pharyngeal branch carries postganglionic fibres towards glands in the mucosa of the nasopharynx.

questions.stem: Preganglionic fibres from the inferior salivatory nucleus supply the:
questions.why: Inferior salivatory preganglionic fibres leave in the glossopharyngeal nerve and continue through the tympanic plexus and lesser petrosal nerve. They synapse in the otic ganglion, whose output reaches the parotid gland.

notes.A: Lacrimal secretomotor fibres originate in the superior salivatory region and relay in the pterygopalatine ganglion.
notes.B: Chorda tympani carries facial parasympathetic fibres that relay in the submandibular ganglion and supply the submandibular gland.
notes.C: The sublingual gland receives facial parasympathetic input through chorda tympani with a submandibular ganglion relay.
notes.D: Minor lingual glands have regional parasympathetic pathways. The classical inferior salivatory and otic ganglion pathway supplies the parotid.

questions.stem: The suprarenal glands:

options.label: B
options.text: The right is in direct contact with the abdominal wall

options.label: D
options.text: The left is partly covered by peritoneum of the lesser sac

options.label: E
options.text: The right forms part of the stomach bed

notes.E: The stomach lies on the left, and the left suprarenal gland helps form its posterior bed.
notes.A: The right gland has a roughly pyramidal shape and caps the upper part of the right kidney.
notes.B: Renal fascia and fat surround the gland, and its posterior relation includes the diaphragm and intervening fascial tissue.
notes.C: The left gland is usually crescent shaped and extends down the upper medial side of the left kidney.
notes.D: Part of the left gland lies posterior to the peritoneal lining of the lesser sac in the stomach bed.

questions.why: The right adrenal gland is usually pyramidal and relates to the liver and inferior vena cava. The crescent-shaped left gland lies behind the upper stomach and partly relates to the lesser sac.

questions.stem: The tympanic membrane:

options.label: A
options.text: Is part of the inner ear

options.label: B
options.text: Forms the lateral wall of the middle ear

options.label: C
options.text: Forms the medial wall of the middle ear

questions.why: The tympanic membrane lies between the external acoustic canal and the air-filled tympanic cavity. It forms most of the lateral wall of the middle ear and transmits sound vibrations to the malleus.

notes.A: The inner ear contains the cochlea and vestibular labyrinth, which lie deeper than the external canal and tympanic cavity.
notes.C: The medial wall of the middle ear faces the labyrinth and contains the promontory and the oval and round windows.
notes.D: The membrane vibrates in response to sound pressure and transfers motion to the ossicular chain.
notes.E: Otoscopy allows the membrane to be examined at the medial end of the external acoustic canal.

questions.stem: The middle ear is separated from the middle cranial fossa by a thin plate of bone called the:
questions.why: The tegmen tympani is a thin plate of the temporal bone forming the roof of the tympanic cavity. It separates the middle ear from the dura and structures of the middle cranial fossa above.

notes.A: Tensor tympani is a muscle inserted on the malleus. Its canal lies below an anterior part of the bony roof.
notes.B: The separating layer is compact temporal bone. A fibrous fascial sheet does not form this cranial partition.
notes.D: A tympanic fascial label describes soft tissue rather than the defined temporal bone plate over the cavity.
notes.E: A border is a margin. The tegmen is the plate that spans the cavity and forms its roof.

questions.stem: Which part of the inner ear is the organ of hearing?
questions.why: The organ of Corti rests on the basilar membrane of the cochlear duct. Deflection of its hair cells during cochlear vibration converts mechanical energy into signals that are conveyed by the cochlear nerve.

notes.A: The anterior semicircular canal contains a duct whose ampulla senses angular acceleration in its plane.
notes.B: The lateral duct contains a receptor in its ampulla that signals rotation in a nearly horizontal plane.
notes.D: The utricle detects linear acceleration and head tilt through a macula oriented chiefly in the horizontal plane.
notes.E: The saccular macula detects linear acceleration and is oriented chiefly in a vertical plane.

questions.stem: Which of the following nerves does NOT supply the ear?
questions.why: The trochlear nerve supplies the superior oblique muscle in the orbit. The other listed pathways supply parts of the external or middle ear through sensory branches or through the facial motor branch to stapedius.

notes.A: The auriculotemporal nerve supplies parts of the auricle, external acoustic canal and lateral surface of the tympanic membrane.
notes.B: The facial nerve supplies stapedius, a small muscle that acts on the stapes within the middle ear.
notes.C: The auricular branch of the vagus supplies sensory fibres to part of the external acoustic canal and auricle.
notes.D: The glossopharyngeal tympanic branch supplies middle ear mucosa through the tympanic plexus.

questions.stem: Which fluid fills the membranous labyrinth?
questions.why: Endolymph fills the cochlear duct and the other compartments of the membranous labyrinth. It is rich in potassium compared with the perilymph that surrounds the membranous structures within the bony labyrinth.

notes.A: Perilymph is outside the membranous labyrinth and occupies the scala vestibuli and scala tympani in the cochlea.
notes.B: Cerebrospinal fluid occupies spaces around the central nervous system, while the membranous labyrinth contains its own inner fluid.
notes.D: The inner-ear fluid has a specialised ionic composition, maintained in the cochlear duct by processes including potassium secretion.
notes.E: Aqueous humour circulates in the anterior segment of the eye, where it contributes to intraocular pressure.

questions.stem: Which two cranial nerves have branches in the middle ear?
questions.why: The facial nerve gives a motor branch to stapedius, and chorda tympani crosses the tympanic cavity. The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the middle ear mucosa through its tympanic branch and plexus.

notes.A: The trochlear nerve supplies superior oblique and the cochlear division carries signals from the inner ear.
notes.B: The vestibulocochlear nerve serves inner-ear receptors, while the abducent nerve supplies lateral rectus in the orbit.
notes.D: The nasociliary nerve provides orbital and nasal sensation, while the trochlear nerve supplies an extraocular muscle.
notes.E: Facial branches reach the middle ear, but the optic nerve carries visual signals from the retina.

questions.stem: The middle ear connects to the nasopharynx through the:
questions.why: The pharyngotympanic tube extends from the anterior wall of the middle ear to the lateral nasopharynx. Its opening allows ventilation and helps balance pressure across the tympanic membrane.

notes.A: The nasolacrimal duct carries tears into the inferior nasal meatus from the lacrimal sac.
notes.C: The uterine tube connects the uterine cavity to a fimbrial opening near the ovary and belongs to the reproductive tract.
notes.D: The palatoglossal fold is a boundary of the opening from the oral cavity to the oropharynx.
notes.E: The nasolabial fold is a surface crease between the cheek and lip, lateral to the nose.

questions.stem: The two muscles of the middle ear are:
questions.why: Tensor tympani pulls on the malleus and receives mandibular trigeminal motor fibres. Stapedius acts on the stapes and receives facial motor fibres, providing a second way to regulate ossicular movement.

notes.A: Stapedius belongs to the middle ear, while tensor veli palatini tenses the soft palate and helps open the auditory tube.
notes.B: Tensor palati refers to the soft-palate tensor. The tensor attached to the malleus is tensor tympani.
notes.C: The specific tympanic tensor is the muscle attached to the malleus. “Tympanic muscle” alone does not name the pair precisely.
notes.E: Levator veli palatini raises the soft palate during swallowing. Stapedius acts on an ossicle inside the tympanic cavity.

questions.stem: Damage to the vestibulocochlear nerve can cause:

notes.A: Cochlear nerve dysfunction can reduce sensorineural hearing and may produce tinnitus on the affected side.
notes.B: Unequal vestibular input can drive involuntary rhythmic eye movement through the gaze-stabilising reflex pathways.
notes.C: A sudden imbalance in vestibular signals can create an apparent sensation that the person or surroundings are moving.

questions.why: The cochlear division carries hearing signals, while the vestibular division carries information about head motion and orientation. Damage can therefore cause hearing symptoms or disturb gaze and balance, depending on the fibres involved.

questions.stem: About the tongue:

options.label: A
options.text: The vallate papillae lie just in front of the sulcus terminalis

options.label: B
options.text: Filiform papillae are more numerous at the edges

options.label: C
options.text: Filiform papillae have no taste buds

options.label: E
options.text: There are more taste buds around the sulcus than at the tip

notes.B: Filiform papillae cover much of the presulcal dorsum. Fungiform papillae are more characteristic of the tip and margins.
notes.E: The vallate region near the sulcus has many taste buds along the walls of its trenches, while each fungiform papilla near the tip usually has few.
notes.A: Vallate papillae form a row on the anterior side of the V-shaped terminal sulcus.
notes.C: Filiform papillae provide friction mechanically and do not contain taste buds in the normal tongue.
notes.D: Fungiform papillae have rounded tops and can carry taste buds, often on their upper surface.

questions.why: The oral tongue has several types of papillae. Filiform papillae provide a widespread mechanical surface, while fungiform and vallate papillae contribute to taste and occur in distinct patterns.

questions.stem: About development of the tongue:

options.label: A
options.text: The tongue muscles come from the occipital myotomes

options.label: B
options.text: The mucosa of the anterior two-thirds comes from the lateral lingual swellings (1st arch)

options.label: C
options.text: The mucosa of the posterior third comes from the tuberculum impar

options.label: D
options.text: 2nd arch tissue is not represented in the adult mucosa

options.label: E
options.text: The hypobranchial eminence (4th arch part) gives the mucosa near the vallecula and epiglottis

notes.C: The tuberculum impar is a median first-arch swelling associated with the anterior tongue. The posterior third forms from the hypobranchial eminence.
notes.D: Later arch tissue overgrows the second-arch swelling, leaving no substantial second-arch territory in the adult tongue mucosa.
notes.A: Occipital myotomes contribute most tongue muscles and are accompanied by the hypoglossal nerve during development.
notes.B: Paired first-arch lateral lingual swellings enlarge and merge to form most of the mucosa of the oral tongue.
notes.E: The caudal fourth-arch region contributes mucosa near the epiglottis, where vagal sensory supply is retained.

questions.why: The anterior tongue mucosa develops chiefly from first-arch lateral swellings. The posterior mucosa develops mainly from the hypobranchial eminence, whereas most tongue muscles are formed by migrating occipital myotomes.

questions.stem: Features of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue include:

notes.D: Vallate papillae form a row just anterior to the sulcus even though they receive glossopharyngeal innervation.
notes.E: A vallecula is a mucosal recess between the pharyngeal tongue and epiglottis, behind the terminal sulcus.
notes.A: Filiform papillae cover much of the anterior dorsum and provide a textured surface for moving food.
notes.B: The terminal sulcus forms the V-shaped posterior boundary of the oral part of the tongue.
notes.C: Minor lingual glands are present anteriorly, including mixed glands on the underside near the tip.

questions.why: The terminal sulcus marks the boundary between oral and pharyngeal tongue. Most oral papillae lie in front of it, including the vallate row, while the valleculae lie between the tongue base and epiglottis.

questions.stem: Lingual papillae containing taste buds include the:

notes.A: Filiform papillae are slender mechanical structures that increase friction and lack the sensory cells of taste buds.
notes.B: Fungiform papillae are scattered on the anterior tongue and can contain taste buds on their exposed surfaces.
notes.C: Vallate papillae contain taste buds chiefly along their lateral walls facing the surrounding trenches.
notes.D: The posterolateral foliate folds can contain taste buds within the epithelium of the grooves.

questions.why: Taste buds occur in fungiform, vallate and foliate papillae, where their sensory cells contact afferent fibres. The numerous keratinised filiform papillae instead help the tongue grip and move food.

questions.stem: About the olfactory pathway, which statement is WRONG?

options.label: A
options.text: The olfactory cortex is part of the primary sensory cortex

options.label: B
options.text: There is no thalamic relay in the main olfactory pathway

options.label: C
options.text: A unilateral olfactory cortex lesion seldom causes complete anosmia

options.label: D
options.text: The main projection cells of the olfactory bulb are mitral cells

options.label: E
options.text: The olfactory tract ends as medial and lateral olfactory striae

questions.why: The olfactory (piriform) cortex is in the temporal lobe, separate from the primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus).

notes.B: True: it reaches cortex directly.
notes.C: True: bilateral connections.
notes.D: True.
notes.E: True.

questions.stem: About the external acoustic meatus:

options.label: A
options.text: Its outer third is bony and inner two-thirds cartilaginous

options.label: B
options.text: Its outer third has no hairs

options.label: C
options.text: Its inner bony two-thirds has hair follicles

options.label: D
options.text: Its inner two-thirds has ceruminous glands

options.label: E
options.text: Its outer third is cartilaginous and inner two-thirds bony

questions.why: The external acoustic canal has a lateral cartilaginous third followed by a medial bony two-thirds. Hairs and ceruminous glands are features of the thicker skin of the outer segment.

notes.A: Cartilage supports the lateral canal, while the temporal bone forms the deeper portion nearest the tympanic membrane.
notes.B: The lateral cartilaginous portion has thicker skin with hair follicles that help trap debris.
notes.C: The medial bony portion has thin skin closely applied to bone and normally lacks hair follicles.
notes.D: Ceruminous glands lie in the outer cartilaginous skin and contribute secretions that form earwax.

questions.stem: A student falls off a motorcycle, injuring a nerve in his axillary region and breaking bones in his coxal, femoral, acromial and crural regions. In order, these regions are the:
questions.why: The terms identify surface regions from proximal limb landmarks to the lower leg. Axillary denotes the armpit, coxal the hip, femoral the thigh, acromial the shoulder tip and crural the leg below the knee.

notes.B: The thigh is femoral and the shoulder tip is acromial, so neither matches the first two regions named.
notes.C: The shoulder tip is acromial, whereas the first region is the axilla under the shoulder joint.
notes.D: The crural region is the leg between knee and ankle, which is the last region in the sequence.
notes.E: Coxal correctly refers to the hip, but the sequence begins with the axilla and ends with the leg.

questions.stem: The L1 vertebra is a key abdominal landmark. The horizontal plane through L1 is the:

notes.A: Addison’s transpyloric plane usually crosses the body or lower border of the first lumbar vertebra.
notes.B: The subcostal plane passes through the inferior points of the costal margins and lies near the third lumbar vertebra.
notes.C: The transumbilical plane passes through the umbilicus, which usually overlies a lower and more variable lumbar level.

questions.why: The transpyloric plane is conventionally drawn at about the first lumbar vertebra. It helps describe the positions of upper abdominal structures, though the pylorus and other organs shift with posture and filling.

questions.stem: The surface level of L1 is found by drawing a line:

options.label: A
options.text: Through the lowest points of the costal margins

options.label: B
options.text: Through the highest points of the iliac crests

options.label: C
options.text: Halfway between the jugular notch and the upper border of the pubic symphysis

notes.A: The lower points of the costal margins define the subcostal plane, which typically lies near the third lumbar vertebra.
notes.B: A line joining the highest iliac crests lies near the fourth lumbar spinous level or the interval below it.
notes.C: The midpoint between these two midline landmarks defines the surface level of the transpyloric plane.

questions.why: Addison’s plane is located on the anterior body surface halfway from the jugular notch to the upper border of the pubic symphysis. It corresponds approximately to the first lumbar vertebra.

questions.stem: Structures lying on the transpyloric (L1) plane include:

options.label: A
options.text: The tips of the 9th costal cartilages

options.label: C
options.text: The origin of the superior mesenteric artery

notes.B: The fundus commonly projects near the right ninth costal cartilage where the lateral rectus border meets the costal margin.
notes.A: The tips of the ninth costal cartilages are the anterior costal landmarks for this horizontal plane.
notes.C: The superior mesenteric artery originates from the front of the abdominal aorta near the first lumbar level.

questions.why: Addison’s transpyloric plane lies near the first lumbar vertebra. Classically it meets the ninth costal cartilages and approximates the gallbladder fundus and superior mesenteric artery origin, with individual variation.

questions.stem: Structures wholly or partly covered by the ribs include the:

notes.A: The right lobe lies under the right dome of the diaphragm, with much of the liver deep to the lower right ribs.
notes.B: The fundus and upper body of the stomach lie beneath the left costal margin and left hemidiaphragm.
notes.C: The spleen typically lies deep to the ninth through eleventh left ribs, with its long axis near the tenth.
notes.D: The higher left kidney has posterior relations to the eleventh and twelfth ribs, with intervening diaphragm superiorly.
notes.E: The right kidney usually lies lower, but its upper posterior region still relates to the twelfth rib.

questions.why: The lower thoracic cage overlaps upper abdominal organs. The diaphragm separates several of them from the chest, while posterior lower ribs also overlie the upper parts of the retroperitoneal kidneys.

questions.stem: In dividing the abdomen into 9 regions, which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The horizontal planes are the transpyloric and intertubercular planes

options.label: B
options.text: The vertical planes are the left and right midsternal lines

options.label: C
options.text: The transpyloric plane lies midway between the suprasternal notch and the umbilicus

options.label: D
options.text: The hypogastrium lies largely under the costal margins

options.label: E
options.text: The vertical planes pass through the midinguinal points

questions.why: Usual scheme: subcostal and transtubercular planes, with midclavicular lines through the midinguinal points.

notes.A: Usually subcostal and transtubercular.
notes.B: Midclavicular lines.
notes.C: Between the suprasternal notch and the pubic symphysis.
notes.D: That is the epigastrium.

questions.stem: All of the following about the transpyloric plane are correct EXCEPT:

options.label: B
options.text: It passes through the fundus of the gallbladder

options.label: C
options.text: It passes through the 9th costal cartilages

options.label: D
options.text: It passes through the lower border of L1

options.label: E
options.text: It lies below the subcostal plane

questions.why: The transpyloric plane is higher than the subcostal plane. It is conventionally near the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra, while the subcostal plane is nearer the third lumbar vertebra.

notes.A: The pylorus often lies on or near this plane in the supine individual, although its position changes with gastric filling.
notes.B: The gallbladder fundus usually lies near the right ninth costal cartilage at the level of the transpyloric plane.
notes.C: The ninth costal cartilage tips are landmarks where the transpyloric plane meets the costal margin.
notes.D: The conventional vertebral reference is the lower border of the first lumbar vertebral body.

questions.stem: Lines dividing the abdomen into nine regions include the:

notes.B: The transpyloric plane at approximately L1 can replace the subcostal plane as the upper transverse boundary.
notes.C: The intercristal plane joins the highest iliac crest points and is a different surface landmark from the intertubercular plane used in the grid.
notes.A: The subcostal plane is a common upper boundary and passes through the lowest points of the costal margins.
notes.D: The intertubercular plane passes through the iliac tubercles and separates the middle abdominal regions from the lower regions.
notes.E: Paired midclavicular planes form the vertical divisions and continue inferiorly towards the midinguinal points.

questions.why: Two sagittal and two transverse planes divide the anterior abdomen into nine regions. The superior transverse plane may be subcostal or transpyloric, depending on the convention used, while the lower plane passes through the iliac tubercles.

questions.stem: Surface lines of the anterior abdominal wall:

options.label: A
options.text: The midclavicular line extended downward reaches the midinguinal point

options.label: B
options.text: The transpyloric plane lies midway between the suprasternal notch and the top of the pubic symphysis

options.label: D
options.text: The subcostal plane passes through the 10th costal cartilages

options.label: E
options.text: The intercristal plane joins the highest points of the iliac crests

notes.C: Both iliac tubercles are joined by the same horizontal plane, which is a transverse rather than vertical landmark.
notes.A: The midclavicular plane is conventionally extended to the point halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis.
notes.B: The transpyloric plane lies halfway between the jugular notch and the upper border of the pubic symphysis.
notes.D: The lowest points of the tenth costal cartilages define the subcostal plane near the third lumbar vertebra.
notes.E: The intercristal line joins the highest points of the iliac crests, near the fourth lumbar level.

questions.why: Abdominal surface planes use palpable landmarks to describe the positions of deeper organs. The intertubercular and intercristal planes are transverse, while the paired midclavicular planes descend vertically.

questions.stem: True or false: Surgical access to thoracic structures involves some kind of thoracotomy.
questions.why: Opening the chest wall to reach the lungs, heart or mediastinum is a thoracotomy, most often made through an intercostal space.

questions.stem: True or false: A plane from the 2nd costal cartilage (sternal angle) to the lower border of T4 divides the mediastinum into superior and inferior parts.
questions.why: The conventional transverse thoracic plane extends from the sternal angle, where the second costal cartilages attach, to the disc between the fourth and fifth thoracic vertebrae. It separates superior and inferior mediastinal regions.

notes.B: The lower border of T4 is adjacent to the T4–T5 disc, the posterior landmark of this division.

questions.stem: A patient has an inguinal hernia, lumbar kidney pain and perineal haemorrhoids. These regions are, respectively:

options.label: A
options.text: Groin, loin, between the anus and external genitalia

questions.why: Inguinal refers to the groin and lumbar refers here to the loin. The perineum is the pelvic outlet region around the external genitalia and anus, including the interval between them.

notes.B: The groin is inguinal. The loin is lumbar, rather than the second and third regions listed here.
notes.C: The first two labels are accurate, but the perineum includes both the anal and external genital regions.
notes.D: The loin correctly identifies the lumbar region, while the groin belongs first with the inguinal lesion.
notes.E: The inguinal region is specifically the groin, and the perineum includes the anal region as well as external genital structures.

questions.stem: Functions of the female reproductive system include:

options.label: B
options.text: Provision of a site for fertilization and implantation

options.label: C
options.text: Nourishment and development of the preimplantation embryo

notes.E: The kidneys filter blood and excrete nitrogenous wastes such as urea in the urine.
notes.A: Ovarian follicles contain developing oocytes and produce hormones that regulate the reproductive cycle.
notes.B: Fertilisation usually occurs in the uterine tube, whereas implantation occurs in the uterine endometrium.
notes.C: Tubal and uterine secretions support early development as the conceptus travels towards the implantation site.
notes.D: The tube provides a route for sperm to reach the oocyte and transports the oocyte or early embryo towards the uterus.

questions.why: The ovaries produce oocytes and reproductive hormones. The uterine tubes transport gametes and support fertilisation and early cleavage, while the uterus provides the endometrium in which the blastocyst can implant.

questions.stem: Functions of the muscular system include:

options.label: B
options.text: Is responsible for locomotion and facial expression

notes.E: Bone matrix stores calcium and phosphate in mineral crystals. Skeletal muscle is primarily a contractile tissue.
notes.A: Muscles acting across the upper-limb joints allow the hands to manipulate tools and other objects.
notes.B: Limb muscles move the body, while the muscles of facial expression pull on skin to change facial appearance.
notes.C: Sustained activity in postural muscles helps support body position against gravity even during quiet standing.
notes.D: Contraction releases heat as chemical energy is converted to work, and shivering increases heat production.

questions.why: Contraction of skeletal muscle produces force for movement, expression and posture. Muscle metabolism also releases heat, while the mineralised skeleton provides the major long-term calcium and phosphate store.

questions.stem: “Dysphagia” “dysphonia” and “dyspnoea” refer to conditions affecting the:
questions.why: Dysphagia means difficulty swallowing, dysphonia means altered voice, and dyspnoea means difficult or uncomfortable breathing. Pharynx, larynx and lungs are the best corresponding sites among the choices, although the symptoms have wider causes.

notes.B: The larynx is central to phonation, so it corresponds to dysphonia, the second symptom in the sequence.
notes.C: The pharynx can be involved in swallowing difficulty, while a change in voice is more directly linked to the larynx.
notes.D: Middle ear dysfunction primarily affects hearing or pressure sensation. Dysphagia describes difficulty moving material from the mouth towards the stomach.
notes.E: The lungs can contribute to breathlessness, which is the last symptom. Dysphagia relates to the act of swallowing.

questions.stem: Two of the fingers on Theresa’s right hand are fused together by a web of skin. Ten-year old Joseph has a small streak of white hair on top of his old although the rest of his hair is black. Both Theresa and Joseph exhibit:
questions.why: Anatomical variation means a difference in physical form between individuals. A skin web between digits and a local area of differently pigmented hair are structural findings whose significance depends on clinical context.

notes.A: A difference in physical form alone does not establish a disease or indicate whether it has functional effects.
notes.B: Digit webbing may be congenital, but the examples give too little information to classify either finding as a serious defect.
notes.D: Tinnitus is a perception of sound, and albinism affects melanin production more broadly than an isolated white streak.
notes.E: Agenesis is failure of a structure to form. Both examples describe structures that are present with a difference in form or colour.

questions.stem: Hepatitis and glomerulonephritis are inflammations of the
questions.why: Hepatitis is inflammation of liver tissue. Glomerulonephritis refers to inflammation involving renal glomeruli, the capillary structures that filter blood at the beginning of each nephron.

notes.A: The gallbladder stores bile and its inflammation is called cholecystitis, a different process from glomerulonephritis.
notes.B: The glomeruli are in the kidney and correspond to the second term, while hepatitis refers to the liver first.
notes.D: The liver is the organ affected in hepatitis, and the gallbladder lacks the glomerular structures named in the second term.
notes.E: Urinary bladder inflammation is cystitis, while gallbladder inflammation is cholecystitis.

questions.stem: Oophorectomy and hysterectomy refer to surgical removal of the
questions.why: Oophorectomy is removal of an ovary, and hysterectomy is removal of the uterus. These are distinct operations because the ovaries may be retained when a hysterectomy is performed.

notes.A: The hymen is tissue at the vaginal opening and is anatomically separate from the uterus removed at hysterectomy.
notes.B: Removal of a uterine fibroid while retaining the uterus is called myomectomy.
notes.D: Removal of the uterus is hysterectomy, which is the second term. Oophorectomy refers to the ovary first.
notes.E: A hydatidiform mole is abnormal gestational tissue. Its removal is distinct from the definition of hysterectomy.

questions.stem: About inflammatory conditions:

options.label: A
options.text: Arthritis is the inflammation or degeneration of the joints

options.label: B
options.text: Osteoarthritis is a degenerative condition that involves the articular cartilages and bones

options.label: C
options.text: Gout is joint inflammation caused by a deposition of urate salts in the synovial membranes

options.label: D
options.text: Orchitis is the inflammation of the epididymis and vas deferens

options.label: E
options.text: Colitis is the inflammation of the cones of the eye

notes.D: Orchitis is inflammation of the testis. Inflammation of the epididymis is termed epididymitis.
notes.E: Colitis is inflammation of the colon and has no anatomical connection to the cone cells of the retina.
notes.A: Arthritis covers a range of joint disorders that may feature synovial inflammation, articular degeneration or both.
notes.B: Osteoarthritis affects the whole joint, including progressive articular cartilage loss and changes in the underlying bone.
notes.C: Gout occurs when monosodium urate crystals accumulate in joint tissues and provoke an inflammatory response.

questions.why: Arthritis describes joint disease and includes inflammatory and degenerative forms. Gout reflects the inflammatory response to urate crystals, while other inflammation terms identify different organs by their anatomical roots.

questions.stem: Cholecystitis and Cystitis refer to inflammation of the:
questions.why: Cholecystitis refers to inflammation of the bile-storing gallbladder. In urinary clinical terminology, cystitis refers to inflammation of the urinary bladder, the reservoir for urine.

notes.A: The urinary bladder corresponds to cystitis, while inflammation of a uterine tube is termed salpingitis.
notes.B: The gallbladder matches the first term, while inflammation of the testis is called orchitis.
notes.D: The testis is affected in orchitis and the uterine tube in salpingitis. Both terms refer to reproductive organs.
notes.E: Inflammation of the liver is hepatitis. Cholecystitis specifically involves the gallbladder.

questions.stem: Functions of the urinary system include:

options.label: C
options.text: Regulates water content of the body

options.label: D
options.text: Regulates various salts retained and or excreted

options.label: E
options.text: Deamination of proteins and the production of urea

notes.E: The liver converts much of the nitrogen from amino acid metabolism into urea, which the kidneys then excrete.
notes.A: Urea and other nitrogenous wastes leave the bloodstream and are eliminated in the urine.
notes.B: The kidneys reabsorb and generate bicarbonate and excrete acid, helping regulate blood pH.
notes.C: The kidneys change urine volume and concentration to conserve water or remove a surplus.
notes.D: Tubular transport adjusts sodium, potassium and other electrolyte losses according to physiological demand.

questions.why: The kidneys remove metabolic wastes and adjust the amount of water, electrolytes and acid excreted in urine. These processes help maintain the internal environment as intake and metabolism vary.

questions.stem: Functions of the cardiovascular system include:

options.label: A
options.text: Transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide

options.label: B
options.text: Transport of nutrients and waste products

options.label: D
options.text: Deamination of proteins and the production of urea

notes.C: Bile acts in the digestive tract and is produced by the liver. The circulation mainly transports materials between organs.
notes.D: Hepatocytes carry out the urea cycle, while blood carries the resulting urea to the kidneys.
notes.A: Blood carries oxygen from lungs to tissues and returns carbon dioxide to the lungs for exhalation.
notes.B: Circulation delivers absorbed nutrients to tissues and brings waste products to organs that process or excrete them.

questions.why: The cardiovascular system moves blood between lungs, digestive organs, tissues and excretory organs. It therefore transports useful materials to cells and carries wastes away for elimination or processing.

questions.stem: Functions of the nervous system include:

options.label: A
options.text: Responds to internal and external changes

options.label: B
options.text: Regulates processes such as growth and reproduction

options.label: C
options.text: Transport of hormones and regulation of water content of the body

options.label: D
options.text: Maintenance of the extracellular fluid volume

notes.C: Cardiovascular.
notes.D: Kidneys.

questions.why: The nervous system responds to internal and external changes and, through the hypothalamus, helps regulate growth and reproduction (A, B true); hormone transport and maintenance of extracellular fluid volume are roles of other systems, so C and D are false.

questions.stem: The nervous system:

options.label: A
options.text: Can be divided into 2 principal parts; central nervous system and peripheral nervous system

options.label: B
options.text: The peripheral nervous system consists of the cranial and spinal nerves

options.label: C
options.text: The central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord which is the integrating and command centre

options.label: D
options.text: There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 35 pairs of spinal nerves

notes.D: There are twelve pairs of cranial nerves and thirty-one pairs of spinal nerves in the conventional count.
notes.A: The standard anatomical division recognises central structures and peripheral nerves and ganglia linking them to the body.
notes.B: Cranial and spinal nerves account for much of the peripheral system, along with their branches and associated ganglia.
notes.C: The brain and spinal cord process signals and coordinate motor, autonomic and other responses.

questions.why: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system and integrate incoming information. Peripheral nerves and associated ganglia connect those central structures to receptors, muscles and glands.

questions.stem: Long bones are a site of:

notes.A: Yellow marrow contains adipocytes that store lipid within the medullary cavities of many adult long bones.
notes.B: Thyroid hormones are secreted by follicular cells of the thyroid gland, outside the skeletal system.
notes.C: Chondrocytes proliferate and make cartilage at growth plates of immature long bones, before the tissue is replaced by bone.
notes.D: Red marrow produces blood cells, including at some proximal long-bone sites in adults.
notes.E: The mineralised matrix of long bones stores calcium and phosphate as part of the body's skeletal reserve.

questions.why: Long bones store mineral in their matrix and contain marrow for blood cell formation or fat storage. In growing bones, cartilage at the epiphyseal plates also provides a template for longitudinal growth.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman stumbles slightly and breaks her hip. X-ray shows that the compact and spongy bone throughout her spine is very thin. Her condition is:

options.label: B
options.text: One in which bone resorption outweighs bone deposition

options.label: C
options.text: Particularly common in postmenopausal women because of oestrogen deficiency

options.label: D
options.text: Due to inadequate mineralization of bone

notes.A: Osteomyelitis is an infection of bone and would require findings supporting infection in addition to fragility.
notes.B: Bone mass falls when resorption exceeds the formation of new bone over successive remodelling cycles.
notes.C: After menopause, reduced oestrogen can increase bone resorption and accelerate loss of bone mass.
notes.D: Defective mineralisation of bone matrix characterises osteomalacia, while osteoporosis reduces bone mass and disrupts architecture.
notes.E: Rickets involves impaired mineralisation at growing epiphyseal plates in children and does not explain this adult pattern.

questions.why: A low-energy fracture and generalised thinning of bone suggest osteoporosis. Loss of bone quantity and architecture weakens the skeleton even when the remaining matrix is appropriately mineralised.

questions.stem: Cartilage differs from bone in that:

options.label: A
options.text: Cartilage contains much more water than bone and is more resilient

options.label: B
options.text: Cartilage is especially strong in resisting shear (bending and twisting) forces

options.label: C
options.text: Neither contains capillaries, so nutrients diffuse through both matrices

options.label: D
options.text: Cartilage can grow faster than bone in the growing skeleton

options.label: E
options.text: Cartilage regenerates faster than bone when damaged in adults

notes.A: Water bound within the cartilage matrix helps it regain shape after compression and distribute loads.
notes.B: Cartilage is particularly adapted to withstand compression, while marked shear can injure the tissue.
notes.C: Cartilage relies on diffusion for nutrition, but bone has vessels in its canals and marrow.
notes.D: Cartilage can expand through division of chondrocytes within its matrix, enabling rapid growth at developing skeletal sites.
notes.E: Adult cartilage has limited repair capacity because it lacks a direct vascular supply and contains relatively few cells.

questions.why: Cartilage has a hydrated matrix that can deform under load and lacks its own blood vessels. Bone has a vascular, mineralised matrix, providing greater stiffness and generally faster repair than adult articular cartilage.

questions.stem: The organic components (mainly collagen) of bone matrix provide:

options.label: B
options.text: Hardness and the ability to resist twisting

options.label: C
options.text: The ability to resist twisting and flexibility

options.label: E
options.text: Tensile strength and the ability to resist twisting

notes.A: Hardness comes from the inorganic hydroxyapatite.
notes.B: Hardness is mineral, not organic.
notes.C: Collagen gives bone flexibility and resistance to twisting.
notes.D: Collagen fibres resist stretching and give some flexibility.
notes.E: Both come from the collagen framework.

questions.why: Collagen (organic) gives tensile strength and flexibility; calcium hydroxyapatite (inorganic) gives hardness and resistance to compression.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old baby has a "soft spot" on the head, identified as a fontanelle. Concerning fontanelles:

options.label: A
options.text: The diamond-shaped anterior fontanelle normally closes by about 18–24 months

options.label: B
options.text: Fontanelles accommodate growth of the brain

options.label: C
options.text: Premature fusion of sutures (craniosynostosis) can deform the skull

options.label: D
options.text: Fontanelles allow the foetal skull to be moulded during birth

options.label: E
options.text: The site of the anterior fontanelle later becomes the lambda

notes.A: The diamond-shaped anterior fontanelle is usually closed by the end of the second year, with variation between infants.
notes.B: Open sutures and fontanelles allow skull expansion as the infant's brain increases in size.
notes.C: If a suture fuses early, skull growth is restricted in one direction and can produce an altered head shape.
notes.D: The flexible gaps allow the cranial bones to shift slightly relative to each other during birth.
notes.E: The anterior fontanelle marks the future bregma. Lambda marks the junction at the posterior fontanelle.

questions.why: Fontanelles are flexible connective tissue gaps between developing skull bones. They allow the head to mould during delivery and leave room for brain growth before the adult suture landmarks form.

questions.stem: Features of the cervical vertebrae include:

options.label: A
options.text: A short, bifid spinous process that projects anteriorly

options.label: B
options.text: A large, roughly triangular vertebral foramen

options.label: C
options.text: A foramen in the transverse process (foramen transversarium)

options.label: D
options.text: C7 is the vertebra prominens, used as a landmark for counting vertebrae

options.label: E
options.text: No intervertebral disc between C1 and C2

notes.A: Typical bifid spinous processes project backwards from the vertebral arch, away from the body.
notes.B: A relatively broad triangular vertebral foramen accommodates the cervical spinal cord and its coverings.
notes.C: Each transverse process has a transverse foramen, although the structures passing through it vary with level.
notes.D: The seventh cervical vertebra usually has a long palpable spine and is conventionally called the vertebra prominens.
notes.E: The atlas and axis articulate through synovial joints and have no intervertebral disc between them.

questions.why: Typical cervical vertebrae have relatively large triangular vertebral foramina and transverse foramina. Their spinous processes project posteriorly, and the atlas, axis and seventh cervical vertebra have distinctive features.

questions.stem: Diagnostic features of thoracic vertebrae include:

options.label: A
options.text: They all articulate with ribs and have long, slender, downward-sloping spines

options.label: B
options.text: Rib facets and massive vertebral bodies

options.label: C
options.text: A foramen in each transverse process

options.label: D
options.text: No facets for articulation with ribs

options.label: E
options.text: No complete neural arch and no transverse processes

notes.A: Costal facets on bodies and transverse processes, and long spines.
notes.B: Massive bodies are lumbar; thoracic bodies are medium-sized and heart-shaped.
notes.C: Only cervical vertebrae have foramina transversaria.
notes.D: Rib facets are THE feature of thoracic vertebrae.
notes.E: That describes none of the typical vertebrae.

questions.why: Every thoracic vertebra carries costal facets; the bodies are heart-shaped and the spines long and sloping.

questions.stem: Concerning the lumbar vertebrae:

options.label: A
options.text: The lumbar discs bear the greatest strain and herniate most often

options.label: D
options.text: They lack facets for articulation with ribs

options.label: E
options.text: They have rib facets on their transverse processes

notes.A: Lumbar discs transmit considerable load, and lower lumbar levels are common sites of disc herniation.
notes.B: Lumbar vertebral bodies are broad and roughly kidney shaped when viewed from above.
notes.C: Transverse foramina are cervical landmarks. Typical lumbar transverse processes have no such opening.
notes.D: Lumbar vertebrae lack the costal facets that allow thoracic vertebrae to articulate with the ribs.
notes.E: Costal facets on transverse processes represent a thoracic feature where the process articulates with a rib tubercle.

questions.why: Lumbar vertebrae support a substantial load through large bodies and intervertebral discs. Their processes lack the transverse foramina of the cervical region and the costal articular facets of the thoracic region.

questions.stem: Concerning the ribs:

options.label: A
options.text: The first 8 pairs are true (vertebrosternal) ribs

options.label: B
options.text: The costal cartilages of ribs 8–10 join the cartilage of the rib above

options.label: C
options.text: The last two pairs (floating ribs) are short and do not reach the sternum

options.label: D
options.text: The first 7 pairs are vertebrochondral ribs

options.label: E
options.text: A typical rib has a head, neck, tubercle, angle and shaft

notes.A: Seven pairs are vertebrosternal. The eighth joins the costal margin through another cartilage rather than reaching the sternum directly.
notes.B: The cartilages of ribs eight through ten join the cartilage above to help form the costal margin.
notes.C: Ribs eleven and twelve are short floating ribs with anterior ends that lack attachment to the sternum.
notes.D: Vertebrochondral ribs reach the sternum indirectly through other costal cartilage. The first seven have direct attachments.
notes.E: A typical rib has a head and neck near the vertebra, a tubercle, an angle and a curved shaft.

questions.why: The first seven rib pairs reach the sternum through their own cartilages. Ribs eight through ten generally join the costal margin indirectly, and the two lowest pairs have no anterior sternal attachment.

questions.stem: The side to which a scapula belongs can be worked out from:

options.label: A
options.text: Its concave costal surface, which faces anteriorly

options.label: B
options.text: The spine on the posterior surface, which extends laterally as the acromion

options.label: C
options.text: The acromion and glenoid cavity, which are at the upper lateral part

options.label: D
options.text: The supraspinous and infraspinous fossae, which are on the dorsal surface

options.label: E
options.text: The supraspinous and infraspinous fossae, which are on the costal surface

notes.A: The subscapular fossa is the broad concavity on the anterior surface that rests against the rib cage.
notes.B: The posterior spine extends laterally to become the acromion, which overhangs the shoulder joint.
notes.C: The glenoid cavity faces laterally near the upper part of the bone, and the acromion projects above it.
notes.D: The spine divides the dorsal surface into a smaller supraspinous fossa and a larger infraspinous fossa.
notes.E: The costal surface contains the subscapular fossa. The fossae above and below the spine lie posteriorly.

questions.why: Side a scapula by facing its smooth concave surface towards the thorax and placing the spine posteriorly. The glenoid cavity then points laterally on the side to which the bone belongs.

questions.stem: Features of the humerus include:

options.label: A
options.text: It articulates with the scapula at the shoulder

options.label: B
options.text: It has a shaft and two ends

options.label: C
options.text: Its proximal end has the condyle and the medial and lateral epicondyles

options.label: D
options.text: Its proximal end has the head, anatomical neck and greater and lesser tubercles

options.label: E
options.text: Its distal end has the two tubercles and the epicondyles

notes.A: The humeral head articulates with the scapular glenoid cavity at the glenohumeral joint.
notes.B: The shaft unites the expanded proximal and distal ends and provides attachment surfaces for arm muscles.
notes.C: The capitulum, trochlea and flanking epicondyles are features of the distal end near the elbow.
notes.D: The anatomical neck surrounds the humeral head, and the greater and lesser tubercles lie nearby for tendon attachments.
notes.E: The distal end has epicondyles, whereas the greater and lesser tubercles are landmarks of the proximal end.

questions.why: The humeral head and tubercles form the proximal end at the shoulder. The shaft extends to the articular condyle and epicondyles distally, where the humerus meets the forearm bones.

questions.stem: The femur:

options.label: A
options.text: Is the longest and heaviest bone of the body

options.label: B
options.text: Transmits weight from the hip bone to the tibia when standing

options.label: C
options.text: Has a head, a neck and greater and lesser tubercles at its upper end

options.label: D
options.text: Has two condyles and two trochanters at its lower end

notes.A: The femur is normally the longest and heaviest bone in the human skeleton.
notes.B: Load passes from the acetabulum to the femoral head and shaft, then through the condyles to the tibia.
notes.C: The proximal femoral projections are the greater and lesser trochanters. The named greater and lesser tubercles belong to the humerus.
notes.D: The distal femur has two condyles and adjacent epicondyles. Its trochanters lie near the proximal neck.
notes.E: The femur has a long shaft and expanded ends, which place it in the long-bone category.

questions.why: The femur is the major weight-bearing long bone of the thigh. Its proximal head articulates with the pelvis, and its distal condyles transmit forces to the tibia at the knee.

questions.stem: The bones of the skull include:

notes.A: The sphenoid and ethmoid are irregular bones with complex contours around several cranial or facial spaces.
notes.B: The frontal and parietal bones form broad protective plates in the cranial vault and are classified as flat bones.
notes.C: Short bones are exemplified by carpals and most tarsals rather than the standard skull bones.
notes.D: Long bones have a shaft and two ends, a pattern characteristic of much of the appendicular skeleton.
notes.E: Sesamoid bones develop within tendons, as the patella does, and are not a standard skull bone category.

questions.why: The skull includes broad plates protecting the brain and more complex bones forming the cranial base and face. Those shapes give common examples of flat and irregular bones.

questions.stem: Irregular bones are found in the:

notes.A: Vertebrae have complex bodies and processes, while bones such as the sphenoid have similarly irregular outlines.
notes.B: The tibia and fibula are long bones, and most carpals of the wrist are short bones.
notes.C: The humerus is a long bone. Some skull bones are irregular, but the arm does not supply the matching example.
notes.D: Several skull bones are irregular, while the carpals are conventionally classified as short bones apart from special cases.
notes.E: The vertebral column contains irregular bones, but the standard shape category for most wrist bones is short.

questions.why: Irregular bones have complex shapes that do not fit the long, short or flat categories. Vertebrae and several bones of the cranial base and face are examples.

questions.stem: Short bones are found in the:

notes.A: The framework of the leg between knee and ankle consists of tibia and fibula, both long bones.
notes.B: The humerus is the long bone of the anatomical arm between shoulder and elbow.
notes.C: Vertebrae are irregular bones because their processes and arches produce complex shapes.
