notes.D: Most carpal bones are compact short bones forming the wrist at the proximal end of the hand.
notes.E: The tarsus contains several short bones, including the cuboid and cuneiforms, around the ankle and hindfoot.

questions.why: Short bones have broadly similar length, width and thickness. Most carpals and tarsals are conventionally placed in this category, providing stability and limited movement in the wrist and foot.

questions.stem: The skeleton with the highest number of separate bones is that of:

notes.A: Early in fetal development much of the skeleton is still cartilaginous and ossification centres have yet to appear.
notes.B: A newborn has multiple separate skeletal elements that later fuse, giving the highest conventional count among these choices.
notes.C: By ten years some elements, such as separate parts of the mandible, have already united.
notes.D: An adult skeleton usually has about 206 named bones after the normal developmental fusions.
notes.E: The higher conventional number of separate elements in the newborn provides a matching choice.

questions.why: At birth, several skeletal elements remain separate that later unite during growth. Fusion of parts of the skull, pelvis and vertebral column helps reduce the conventional count of separate bones by adulthood.

questions.stem: Which order correctly names: a hole through a bone; a narrow slit; a wide depression; an open (uncovered) channel along a bone; a mucous-membrane-lined cavity within a bone?
questions.why: These labels distinguish different surface features. A foramen is a hole, a fissure a narrow slit, and a fossa a depression. An open channel is a groove, while a pneumatic sinus is a lined cavity.

notes.B: A sinus is a cavity within bone, while an elongated open channel on its surface is a groove.
notes.C: A fossa is a depression and a foramen passes through bone, so the first and third labels are reversed.
notes.D: A fissure describes a narrow slit. The wide depression in the sequence is a fossa.
notes.E: A complete hole through bone is a foramen, whereas a narrow cleft is called a fissure.

questions.stem: The prominent bony knobs on each side of the ankle joint are the:

options.label: A
options.text: Styloid processes of the tibia and fibula

options.label: B
options.text: Medial malleolus of the fibula and lateral malleolus of the tibia

options.label: C
options.text: Medial malleolus of the tibia and lateral malleolus of the fibula

options.label: D
options.text: Epicondyles of the tibia and fibula

options.label: E
options.text: Head of the fibula and tuberosity of the tibia

questions.why: The two malleoli are the distal projections of the lower-leg bones that frame the ankle. The tibial projection is medial, while the fibular projection is lateral and usually extends farther down.

notes.A: Styloid names a slender pointed process elsewhere. The ankle projections of the distal tibia and fibula are the malleoli.
notes.B: The tibia lies medially and gives the medial malleolus. The fibula forms the lateral projection.
notes.D: Epicondyles are projections near a condyle. The bony sides of the ankle are named the malleoli.
notes.E: The fibular head and tibial tuberosity are proximal landmarks near the knee, far above the ankle.

questions.stem: All the following are carpal bones EXCEPT the:
questions.why: The cuboid belongs to the tarsus on the lateral side of the foot. The trapezium and trapezoid are in the distal carpal row, while the triquetral and pisiform are on the ulnar side of the wrist.

notes.A: The trapezium is the distal carpal that articulates with the base of the first metacarpal.
notes.B: The trapezoid lies in the distal carpal row near the base of the second metacarpal.
notes.C: The triquetral is a bone in the proximal carpal row on the ulnar side of the wrist.
notes.D: The pisiform is a small sesamoid carpal within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon.

questions.stem: A technician says that the pubis supports body weight when sitting and that the cuboid is the bone of the heel. He is wrong; the correct bones are the:
questions.why: The ischial tuberosities are the weight-bearing prominences of the pelvis in sitting. In the foot, the plantar surface of the calcaneus forms the bony support of the heel.

notes.A: The acetabulum is the hip socket, and the cuboid lies lateral and anterior to the principal heel bone.
notes.B: The calcaneus is the heel bone, but the iliac blade is the upper part of the hip bone rather than the sitting prominence.
notes.D: The ischium provides the sitting prominence, but the navicular lies in the medial midfoot.
notes.E: The talus receives load at the ankle, while the coccyx forms the terminal portion of the spine.

questions.stem: Which group of features belongs to the proximal end of the humerus?

options.label: A
options.text: Greater trochanter, lesser tubercle and intertrochanteric crest

options.label: B
options.text: Lesser tubercle, greater tubercle and intercondylar fossa

options.label: C
options.text: Lesser trochanter, greater trochanter and bicipital groove

options.label: D
options.text: Greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity and intertrochanteric crest

options.label: E
options.text: Greater tubercle, lesser tubercle and intertubercular (bicipital) groove

questions.why: The greater and lesser tubercles lie near the humeral head and provide tendon attachment sites. Between them the intertubercular groove carries the tendon of the long head of biceps.

notes.A: The greater trochanter and intertrochanteric crest are proximal femoral landmarks. The lesser tubercle is on the humerus.
notes.B: Both tubercles belong to the proximal humerus, but the intercondylar fossa separates the distal femoral condyles.
notes.C: Both trochanters lie on the proximal femur, although the bicipital groove belongs to the humerus.
notes.D: Tuberosity can be used for the humeral tubercles, but the intertrochanteric crest joins the two femoral trochanters.

questions.stem: Concerning the curvatures of the vertebral column:

options.label: A
options.text: The thoracic and lumbar curvatures are the primary curvatures present at birth

options.label: B
options.text: The thoracic and sacral curvatures are convex posteriorly, so a newborn spine arches like a four-legged animal

options.label: C
options.text: The pelvic and lumbar curvatures are secondary curvatures

options.label: D
options.text: The cervical and lumbar curvatures are convex posteriorly

options.label: E
options.text: The sacral curvature places the weight of the upper body over the lower limbs

notes.A: The thoracic and sacral curves are primary. The lumbar curve becomes distinct during later postural development.
notes.B: The thoracic and sacral segments are convex posteriorly, corresponding to the general curve present at birth.
notes.C: Cervical and lumbar curvatures are the secondary curves. The sacral curve is present earlier.
notes.D: Cervical and lumbar lordoses are convex anteriorly, opposite the thoracic and sacral kyphoses.
notes.E: Lumbar lordosis helps position trunk weight over the legs in standing. The sacral curve retains a primary posterior convexity.

questions.why: The thoracic and sacral curves retain the posterior convexity of the early spine. Cervical and lumbar curves develop in the opposite direction as the infant gains head control and adopts an upright posture.

questions.stem: The sternum:

options.label: A
options.text: Its xiphoid process stays largely cartilaginous until about age 40

options.label: B
options.text: Is a bony plate anterior to the heart

options.label: C
options.text: Is an irregular bone with three parts

options.label: D
options.text: The 2nd costal cartilage joins it at the sternal angle, a landmark for counting ribs

options.label: E
options.text: The first 7 costal cartilages articulate directly with it

notes.A: The xiphoid process ossifies relatively late, often around mid-adulthood, with substantial variation between individuals.
notes.C: Although it has three named subdivisions, the sternum is classified as a flat bone.
notes.D: The second costal cartilage joins the sternum at its angle, allowing other rib levels to be counted from it.
notes.E: Each of the first seven ribs has a costal cartilage that reaches the sternum directly.
notes.B: The sternum lies anterior to the mediastinum and protects the underlying heart and nearby structures.

questions.why: The sternum forms the flat anterior midline plate of the thoracic cage. Its manubrium, body and xiphoid process provide attachments for costal cartilages, and the manubriosternal angle marks the second rib level.

questions.stem: The ribs:

options.label: B
options.text: The first seven are true ribs

notes.A: The usual total is twelve pairs, corresponding to the twelve levels of the thoracic vertebral column.
notes.B: Ribs one to seven are true ribs because their cartilages connect them directly to the sternum.
notes.C: The eighth pair also lacks an independent sternal attachment, so the non-true group starts at rib eight.
notes.D: Ribs eleven and twelve are floating. The tenth generally joins the costal margin through its cartilage.
notes.E: The last two ribs terminate anteriorly without attaching to the sternum or another costal cartilage.

questions.why: Humans usually have twelve rib pairs. The first seven attach directly to the sternum by their own costal cartilages. The remaining pairs attach indirectly or, for the last two, end without an anterior attachment.

questions.stem: The skull:

options.label: A
options.text: The opening that joins the cranial cavity to the vertebral canal is the foramen magnum

options.label: B
options.text: The foramen magnum lies in the occipital bone

options.label: C
options.text: The occipital bone joins the two parietal bones at the sagittal suture

options.label: D
options.text: The lambdoid suture separates the parietal bones from the frontal bone

options.label: E
options.text: The parietal bones meet each other at the coronal suture

notes.A: The foramen magnum permits continuity of the lower brainstem and spinal cord across the skull base.
notes.B: The basilar, lateral and squamous parts of the occipital bone enclose the foramen magnum.
notes.C: The lambdoid suture joins the occipital and parietal bones. The sagittal suture runs between the two parietals.
notes.D: The lambdoid suture lies posteriorly and separates the parietal bones from the occipital bone.
notes.E: The coronal suture joins the frontal bone to the parietals, which meet each other at the sagittal suture.

questions.why: The foramen magnum is the large skull-base opening connecting the cranial cavity with the vertebral canal. It lies within the occipital bone, which meets the parietals posteriorly at the lambdoid suture.

questions.stem: Lumbar vertebrae are identified by:

options.label: D
options.text: Their thick, posteriorly directed, hatchet-shaped spines

notes.A: The broad kidney-shaped lumbar body provides a substantial surface for transferring load to the disc below.
notes.B: The lumbar transverse processes are conspicuous lateral projections, with their length varying by vertebral level.
notes.C: Transverse foramina perforate cervical transverse processes. The corresponding lumbar processes are solid.
notes.D: A typical lumbar spinous process is thick, blunt and directed posteriorly rather than markedly inferiorly.
notes.E: Lumbar vertebrae lack the costal articular facets involved in the rib articulations of the thoracic region.

questions.why: Typical lumbar vertebrae have large bodies for load bearing and short, thick spinous processes. Their transverse processes extend laterally and lack the foramina or rib facets characteristic of other regions.

questions.stem: The clavicle:

options.label: A
options.text: Is a curved long bone with medial and lateral ends

options.label: B
options.text: Runs horizontally across the upper thorax and is the collar bone

options.label: C
options.text: Acts as a strut holding the scapula and arm away from the thorax

options.label: E
options.text: Its lateral end is rounded and articulates with the sternum

notes.C: Its strut function keeps the scapula and arm lateral to the chest and transmits upper-limb forces medially.
notes.D: The medial sternal end is relatively bulky. The lateral acromial end is the flattened end.
notes.E: The lateral end articulates with the acromion, while the rounded medial end articulates with the manubrium.
notes.A: The clavicle is a curved long bone with a shaft linking a sternal end to an acromial end.
notes.B: The collarbone has a roughly horizontal course between the superior sternum and shoulder tip.

questions.why: The clavicle is an S-shaped long bone spanning the upper thorax. Its bulky medial end joins the sternum, while its flattened lateral end joins the acromion and helps hold the shoulder laterally.

questions.stem: The hip bone:

options.label: A
options.text: (os coxae, innominate bone) articulates with the sacrum

options.label: B
options.text: Is formed by the ilium, ischium and pubis

options.label: C
options.text: With the sacrum and coccyx forms the bony pelvis

options.label: D
options.text: Is an irregular bone whose acetabulum articulates with the femur

options.label: E
options.text: Meets its partner at the pubic symphysis, a disc of elastic cartilage

notes.A: The ilium articulates with the sacrum at the sacroiliac joint to transmit load between trunk and lower limbs.
notes.B: The three components join around the acetabulum, whose developmental cartilage later ossifies.
notes.E: The pubic symphysis contains a fibrocartilaginous disc between articular surfaces, rather than elastic cartilage.
notes.C: The two hip bones, sacrum and coccyx together form the bony pelvis.
notes.D: The hip bone is irregular and its acetabulum receives the head of the femur.

questions.why: The hip bone forms from the fused ilium, ischium and pubis around the acetabulum. It joins the sacrum behind and the opposite pubis in front to help complete the pelvic ring.

questions.stem: The bony pelvis:

options.label: A
options.text: Consists of the two hip bones, the sacrum and the coccyx

options.label: B
options.text: In the female is wider, shallower and lighter, adapted for childbirth

options.label: C
options.text: Has a pelvic inlet and a pelvic outlet

options.label: D
options.text: Its outlet is bounded by the pubic arch in front, the ischial tuberosities at the sides and the coccyx behind

options.label: E
options.text: Is a useful guide to sex identification

notes.A: The hip bones form the lateral walls, while the sacrum and coccyx complete the posterior part of the bony pelvis.
notes.B: On average the female pelvis is wider and shallower, with a wider subpubic angle that accommodates childbirth.
notes.C: The inlet lies at the pelvic brim. The outlet is the lower opening of the bony pelvis.
notes.D: The pubic arch, ischial tuberosities and coccyx are anterior, lateral and posterior landmarks of the outlet respectively.
notes.E: Pelvic features such as the subpubic angle and sciatic notch help estimate skeletal sex, with individual overlap.

questions.why: The two hip bones join the sacrum and coccyx to form the bony pelvis. Its inlet and outlet bound the lesser pelvis, and their proportions are clinically important in childbirth.

questions.stem: The coronal suture joins:
questions.why: The coronal suture extends across the skull vault and joins the frontal bone to the paired parietal bones. It forms the anterior boundary of the parietal region on each side.

notes.B: The squamous suture joins the temporal squama to the adjacent parietal bone on the lateral skull.
notes.C: The temporal bones lie on opposite sides of the skull and do not meet each other at a midline suture.
notes.D: The parietal bones meet in the midline at the sagittal suture, which runs backwards from the coronal suture.
notes.E: The occipitomastoid suture is the junction between the temporal and occipital bones near the skull base.

questions.stem: Which group lists only parts of the sternum?
questions.why: The sternum consists of a manubrium superiorly, an elongated body in the middle and a xiphoid process inferiorly. The second costal cartilage marks the junction between the manubrium and body.

notes.B: The xiphoid and body belong to the sternum. Intervertebral discs lie between vertebral bodies in the spine.
notes.C: Costal cartilage connects ribs to the sternum, while the malleus is an auditory ossicle in the middle ear.
notes.D: The manubrium belongs to the sternum, but the incus is a middle-ear bone and elastic cartilage is a tissue.
notes.E: The xiphoid and manubrium are sternal parts. The vomer helps form the bony nasal septum.

questions.stem: Which group contains a bone that is NOT part of the skull?
questions.why: The patella lies in the quadriceps tendon at the front of the knee and is the largest sesamoid bone. The palatine and occipital bones in its group both belong to the skull.

notes.A: The parietal forms part of the vault, while the ethmoid and vomer contribute to the nasal region of the skull.
notes.B: The frontal and temporal bones contribute to the cranium, and the maxilla forms much of the upper jaw.
notes.C: The nasal, zygomatic and lacrimal bones are facial bones contributing to the nose, cheek or medial orbital wall.
notes.E: The mandible forms the lower jaw, and the malleus and incus are small bones of the middle ear.

questions.stem: The sagittal suture joins:
questions.why: The sagittal suture runs in the midline between the right and left parietal bones. It meets the coronal suture at bregma and the lambdoid suture at lambda.

notes.A: The lambdoid suture joins the occipital bone to the parietal bones at the back of the vault.
notes.B: The squamous suture joins the squamous temporal bone to the parietal bone on the lateral skull.
notes.C: The temporal bones lie on opposite sides of the skull and have no shared suture.
notes.E: The occipitomastoid suture joins the mastoid part of the temporal bone to the occipital bone.

questions.stem: Which group consists only of carpal bones?
questions.why: The lunate and scaphoid are in the proximal carpal row. The capitate is in the distal row, centrally aligned with the third metacarpal.

notes.B: The cuboid is a tarsal bone in the lateral foot. The hamate and triquetral are carpals.
notes.C: The calcaneus and tarsal navicular are in the foot. Only the capitate is a carpal here.
notes.D: The talus and cuneiforms are tarsals. The pisiform is a carpal in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris.
notes.E: The trapezium and trapezoid are distal carpals, whereas the cuboid is in the lateral midfoot.

questions.stem: Which group consists only of tarsal bones?
questions.why: The medial cuneiform, navicular and cuboid are tarsals in the midfoot. The medial cuneiform lies in front of the navicular, and the cuboid is lateral.

notes.B: The talus and cuboid are tarsals. The hamate is a distal carpal on the ulnar side of the wrist.
notes.C: The calcaneus and navicular are tarsals. The capitate is in the distal carpal row of the wrist.
notes.D: The navicular and cuneiforms belong to the foot. The pisiform is a carpal on the palmar side of the triquetral.
notes.E: The cuboid and talus are tarsals. The trapezium is a carpal at the base of the thumb.

questions.stem: After it closes in the second year of life, the site of the anterior fontanelle is called the:
questions.why: The anterior fontanelle is at the junction of the frontal and parietal bones. Once it closes, the point where the sagittal and coronal sutures meet is bregma.

notes.A: Lambda is the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures at the former posterior fontanelle.
notes.B: Pterion is the lateral junction of the frontal, parietal, squamous temporal and greater wing of sphenoid.
notes.D: Asterion is the posterolateral junction of the lambdoid, parietomastoid and occipitomastoid sutures.
notes.E: Inion is the prominent midline point on the external occipital protuberance, below lambda.

questions.stem: The upper (pectineal) edge of the superior pubic ramus forms the:
questions.why: The sharp superior ridge of the superior pubic ramus is the pecten pubis, also called the pectineal line. It forms part of the pelvic brim.

notes.A: The iliopubic eminence is the elevation where the ilium and pubis meet, at the lateral end of the pectineal line.
notes.B: The pubic tubercle is a projection near the medial end of the pectineal line and gives attachment to the inguinal ligament.
notes.D: The anterior inferior iliac spine is on the ilium above the acetabulum and gives origin to the straight head of rectus femoris.
notes.E: The acetabulum is the socket for the femoral head. The pubis contributes to it, and its pectineal line lies medial to the socket.

questions.stem: All of the following form boundaries of the pelvic inlet EXCEPT the:

options.label: C
options.text: Anterior border of the ala of the sacrum

questions.why: The inferior pubic ramus joins the ischial ramus and forms part of the pubic arch at the outlet. The pelvic inlet is bounded by the pelvic brim above it.

notes.B: The sacral promontory is the anterior lip of the first sacral vertebral body and marks the posterior midline of the inlet.
notes.C: The anterior margin of each sacral ala is part of the posterior pelvic brim, lateral to the promontory.
notes.D: The arcuate line is the ridge on the internal surface of the ilium connecting the sacral and pubic parts of the brim.
notes.E: The pecten pubis is the sharp superior ridge of the superior pubic ramus and forms the anterolateral brim.

questions.stem: In the anatomical position, which of the following lie in the same vertical (coronal) plane?

options.label: B
options.text: Anterior superior iliac spines and the front of the pubic symphysis

options.label: C
options.text: Posterior superior iliac spines and the ischial tuberosities

options.label: D
options.text: Ischial spines and the posterior border of the obturator foramen

options.label: E
options.text: Superior pubic rami and the greater sciatic notch

questions.why: The two anterior superior iliac spines and the anterior surface of the pubic symphysis lie in the anterior pelvic plane. This reference plane is vertical in the anatomical position.

notes.A: The promontory is posterior within the pelvis. The pubic tubercles are anterior, near the symphysis.
notes.C: The posterior superior iliac spines locate the posterior iliac region. The ischial tuberosities are inferior weight-bearing landmarks in sitting.
notes.D: The ischial spines project posteromedially between the sciatic notches. The obturator foramen is anteroinferior to them.
notes.E: The superior pubic rami form the anterior pelvic brim. The greater sciatic notch is at the posterior margin of each hip bone.

questions.stem: The occipital condyles articulate with the:
questions.why: The occipital condyles articulate with the superior articular facets of the atlas. The paired atlanto-occipital joints allow flexion and extension of the head for nodding.

notes.A: The axis is C2. It articulates with the atlas at the atlanto-axial joints, below the occipital condyles.
notes.C: The vertebra prominens usually refers to C7, whose palpable spinous process is at the base of the neck.
notes.D: The transverse processes lie lateral to the atlantal lateral masses. The condyles meet the superior articular facets on those masses.
notes.E: The dens is the projection of C2 around which the atlas rotates. It articulates with the anterior arch of C1.

questions.stem: How many unpaired bones are in the cranium (neurocranium)?
questions.why: Four neurocranial bones are unpaired in the adult skull. They are the frontal, occipital, sphenoid and ethmoid. The parietal and temporal bones form the two pairs.

notes.A: A count of two misses two unpaired bones. The sphenoid and ethmoid must be included with the frontal and occipital.
notes.B: The ethmoid is also a single neurocranial bone, alongside the frontal, occipital and sphenoid bones.
notes.D: Only four bones are unpaired. Each parietal belongs to a pair and is excluded from this count.
notes.E: Both the temporal and parietal bones occur as left and right pairs. Neither pair increases the count of unpaired bones.

questions.stem: The adult facial skeleton has two unpaired bones: the vomer and the:
questions.why: The mandible is the single lower jaw bone and the vomer forms the posteroinferior portion of the nasal septum. They are the two unpaired adult facial bones.

notes.A: There are two maxillae. They meet at the midline and together form the upper jaw.
notes.B: Each zygomatic bone forms the cheek prominence and part of the lateral wall and floor of its orbit.
notes.C: There is a lacrimal bone in each medial orbital wall, where it contributes to the fossa for the lacrimal sac.
notes.E: The two palatine bones meet in the posterior hard palate. Each also forms part of the lateral nasal wall.

questions.stem: A student falls on her outstretched hand and is tender in the anatomical snuffbox. The carpal bone in the snuffbox floor most often fractured is the:

notes.A: The lunate is in the central proximal carpal row and lies ulnar to the scaphoid.
notes.B: The scaphoid is a radial-sided proximal carpal and forms part of the snuffbox floor.
notes.C: The triquetral is on the ulnar side of the proximal carpal row, away from the radial-sided snuffbox.

questions.why: The scaphoid lies in the floor of the anatomical snuffbox. Local tenderness after a fall on an outstretched hand raises suspicion of a scaphoid fracture.

questions.stem: About the ribs:

options.label: A
options.text: The upper seven are true ribs

options.label: B
options.text: The 9th rib is a typical rib

options.label: C
options.text: The 10th rib is a floating rib

notes.B: The ninth rib has the standard head, neck, tubercle and shaft of a typical rib.
notes.C: The tenth normally attaches indirectly to the sternum via the costal margin, although its anterior attachment can vary.
notes.A: Each true rib is connected to the sternum directly by its own costal cartilage.

questions.why: Ribs one to seven have individual costal cartilages attaching to the sternum. The ninth is a typical rib, and the eleventh and twelfth are conventionally classed as floating.

questions.stem: Features of typical cervical vertebrae:

options.label: A
options.text: The body is small and heart-shaped

options.label: B
options.text: The transverse processes have anterior and posterior roots (tubercles)

options.label: C
options.text: The spines are long and slope downward

notes.A: The typical cervical body is small and transversely broad. A heart-shaped body is more characteristic of a typical thoracic vertebra.
notes.C: Typical cervical spinous processes are short and commonly bifid. Long, downsloping spines are characteristic of mid-thoracic vertebrae.
notes.B: The anterior and posterior roots border the transverse foramen. They continue laterally to the anterior and posterior tubercles.

questions.why: Typical cervical vertebrae have small bodies that are wider transversely, transverse processes with anterior and posterior components, and short spinous processes that are usually bifid.

questions.stem: Features of the proximal end of the ulna:

notes.B: The radial tuberosity is on the proximal radius, distal to its neck, and receives the biceps tendon.
notes.A: The radial notch is on the lateral side of the proximal ulna and forms part of the proximal radioulnar joint.
notes.C: The coronoid process is the anterior projection of the proximal ulna and forms the inferior margin of the trochlear notch.

questions.why: At the proximal ulna, the radial notch articulates with the radial head and the coronoid process forms the lower lip of the trochlear notch.

questions.stem: Bones articulating with the talus include the:

notes.A: The cuboid articulates with the calcaneus at the lateral part of the transverse tarsal joint.
notes.B: The medial malleolus of the tibia articulates with the medial facet of the talar body at the ankle.
notes.C: The calcaneus is inferior to the talus and articulates with it at the subtalar and talocalcaneonavicular joints.

questions.why: The talus articulates with the tibia and fibula at the ankle, the calcaneus inferiorly and the navicular anteriorly. The cuboid lies lateral to the navicular.

questions.stem: Bones visible on the lateral view of the skull (norma lateralis) include:

notes.B: The lesser wing forms part of the boundary between the anterior and middle cranial fossae and lies near the orbital apex.
notes.A: The frontal process of the maxilla is visible between the nasal bone and the frontal bone beside the medial orbit.
notes.C: The greater wing is visible in the temporal fossa and contributes to the pterion and lateral orbital wall.

questions.why: The frontal process of the maxilla and the greater wing of the sphenoid are exposed on the side of the skull. The lesser wing is mainly intracranial and orbital.

questions.stem: Sutures associated with the hard palate include the:

notes.D: The mandible forms the lower jaw. The bony hard palate consists of the maxillae and palatine bones.
notes.A: The intermaxillary part of the median palatine suture joins the palatine processes of the two maxillae.
notes.B: The interpalatine part of the median palatine suture joins the two horizontal plates posteriorly.
notes.C: The palatomaxillary suture forms the transverse junction between the palatine processes and the horizontal plates.

questions.why: The median hard palate joins the paired maxillary processes in front and the paired palatine plates behind. The transverse palatine suture separates these maxillary and palatine parts.

questions.stem: In caudal anaesthesia, the needle passes through all of the following EXCEPT the:
questions.why: Caudal anaesthesia delivers local anaesthetic into the sacral epidural space through the sacral hiatus. The spinal dura remains intact because the target is outside the dural sac.

notes.A: The needle passes through the skin over the lower sacrum before reaching the tissues covering the hiatus.
notes.B: The superficial fascia is between the skin and the deeper tissues over the sacral hiatus.
notes.C: The sacral hiatus is the inferior opening of the sacral canal and provides access to the caudal epidural space.
notes.E: The sacrococcygeal ligament covers the hiatus and lies superficial to the caudal epidural space.

questions.stem: True or false: Only two metacarpal bones articulate with the capitate.
questions.why: The capitate has its main articulation with the third metacarpal and typically has smaller articular surfaces for the bases of the second and fourth metacarpals.

notes.A: This count omits a usual contact. The capitate can articulate with the second, third and fourth metacarpal bases.

questions.stem: True or false: The costal margin is formed by the costal cartilages of the 7th to 11th ribs.
questions.why: The continuous costal margin runs along the cartilages of ribs seven to ten. The eleventh rib is floating and its cartilage ends in the abdominal wall.

notes.A: The eleventh costal cartilage has a free anterior end and does not join the cartilage above it.

questions.stem: True or false: The lower two ribs have no tubercles and no synovial joint with the transverse processes.
questions.why: Ribs eleven and twelve lack tubercles, so they have no costotransverse joints. Their heads still articulate with the bodies of the corresponding thoracic vertebrae.

notes.B: A costotransverse joint requires a rib tubercle. Ribs eleven and twelve lack one, although their heads retain costovertebral joints.

questions.stem: About the appendicular skeleton:

options.label: A
options.text: Each upper extremity (upper limb) consists of a proximal humerus within the arm

options.label: B
options.text: Each upper extremity has an ulna and tibia within the forearm

options.label: C
options.text: The carpal bones are wrist bones and the metacarpal and phalangeal bones are bones of the hand

options.label: D
options.text: Each lower extremity (lower limb) consists of a proximal tibia within the thigh

options.label: E
options.text: Metatarsal bones form the ankle whereas tarsal and phalangeal bones form the skeleton of the foot

notes.B: The radius and ulna are the forearm bones. The tibia is the medial bone of the leg.
notes.D: The femur is in the thigh. The tibia is the medial weight-bearing bone below the knee.
notes.E: Tarsals form the proximal foot and the talus participates in the ankle joint. Metatarsals and phalanges are more distal.
notes.A: The humerus forms the skeleton of the arm and extends between the shoulder and elbow joints.
notes.C: Carpals are the wrist bones, metacarpals form the palm, and phalanges provide the skeleton of the digits.

questions.why: The arm contains the humerus, the forearm contains the radius and ulna, and the wrist contains the carpals. In the lower limb, the femur lies in the thigh.

questions.stem: About the radius:

options.label: A
options.text: It is the longer and more lateral bone of the forearm

options.label: B
options.text: It articulates with the carpus proximally and the ulna medially

options.label: C
options.text: The proximal end consists of a head, neck and tuberosity

options.label: D
options.text: The distal end is expanded and bears a pointed process known as the styloid process

options.label: E
options.text: The styloid process is located laterally and distally

notes.A: The radius is lateral in anatomical position. The ulna is the longer of the two forearm bones.
notes.B: The radius meets the carpus distally. At its proximal end it meets the capitulum and radial notch of the ulna.
notes.C: The head, neck and radial tuberosity are proximal. The tuberosity receives the biceps brachii tendon.
notes.D: The broad distal radius bears the radial styloid process near the scaphoid side of the wrist.
notes.E: The radial styloid projects from the distal lateral radius on the thumb side of the wrist.

questions.why: The radius is the lateral forearm bone in anatomical position. Its proximal head articulates at the elbow, and its broad distal end articulates with the proximal carpal row.

questions.stem: About the bony girdles:

options.label: A
options.text: The pelvic girdle is formed by 2 hip bones united anteriorly by the symphysis pubis

options.label: B
options.text: The hip bones are united posteriorly by the lumbar vertebrae

options.label: C
options.text: The pelvic girdle protects the lower viscera within the pelvic cavity

options.label: D
options.text: The primary function of the pectoral girdle is to provide attachment for the muscles that move the upper limb

options.label: E
options.text: The scapulae, clavicles and sternum constitute the pectoral girdle

notes.B: The posterior connections are the sacroiliac joints. They link the ilia to the sacrum below the lumbar spine.
notes.E: The sternum is axial. It meets the clavicles at the sternoclavicular joints and is outside the pectoral girdle.
notes.A: The two pubic bodies meet anteriorly at the pubic symphysis, a fibrocartilaginous joint.
notes.C: The bony pelvic ring encloses the pelvic cavity and provides protection for its viscera.
notes.D: The scapula and clavicle provide attachments for muscles that position the shoulder girdle and move the upper limb.

questions.why: The pelvic girdle consists of two hip bones, joined to each other anteriorly and to the sacrum posteriorly. The pectoral girdle consists of the clavicles and scapulae.

questions.stem: The tibia:

options.label: A
options.text: Is located on the anterior and medial side of the leg

options.label: B
options.text: Its larger expanded end is distal

options.label: C
options.text: The proximal end bears a prologation that is medial

options.label: D
options.text: The distal end bears a prologation that is medial

options.label: E
options.text: It is a short, irregular bone

notes.B: The larger expansion is proximal, where the tibial condyles support the femoral condyles at the knee.
notes.C: The medial malleolus is a distal projection. Proximally the tibial plateau has medial and lateral condyles.
notes.D: The medial malleolus projects inferiorly from the medial side of the distal tibia and forms the medial ankle prominence.
notes.E: The tibia is a long bone with a shaft, a proximal epiphysis and a distal epiphysis.
notes.A: The tibia lies medial to the fibula, and its anterior border is palpable subcutaneously as the shin.

questions.why: The tibia is the large anteromedial bone of the leg. Its broad proximal end forms the tibial plateau, and the distal end projects medially as the medial malleolus.

questions.stem: Kyphosis is:

options.label: A
options.text: An exaggerated inward curvature of the lumbar region of the spine just above the sacrum

options.label: B
options.text: An abnormal lateral curvature of the vertebral column

options.label: D
options.text: Also known as “swayback” and is particularly common in aged women as a result of spinal fractures that follow osteoporosis

notes.A: Exaggeration of the inward lumbar curve is lumbar hyperlordosis. The thoracic kyphotic curve is convex posteriorly.
notes.B: Lateral spinal curvature with vertebral rotation is scoliosis. Kyphosis describes curvature in the sagittal plane.
notes.D: Osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures can increase thoracic kyphosis. Swayback is a term for a different postural pattern.
notes.C: Excess posterior convexity of the thoracic spine is the usual finding meant by clinical kyphosis.
notes.E: Hunchback is an older term for the rounded back seen in pronounced thoracic hyperkyphosis.

questions.why: The thoracic spine normally has a kyphotic curve with posterior convexity. Excessive curvature in this direction is hyperkyphosis, often called simply kyphosis in clinical usage.

questions.stem: The calvaria:

options.label: A
options.text: Is also known as the skullcap

options.label: B
options.text: Consists of the occipital, parietal and frontal bones

options.label: C
options.text: Consists of the occipital, parietal, maxillary, temporal and frontal bones

options.label: D
options.text: Bears fibrous areas known as fontanelles in the infant

options.label: E
options.text: Consists of the occipital, palatine and frontal bones

notes.C: Maxilla is facial.
notes.E: Palatine is facial.

questions.why: The calvaria (skullcap) is formed by the frontal, parietal and occipital bones and shows fontanelles in the infant (A, B, D true); C and E are false because they wrongly include facial bones (maxilla, palatine).

questions.stem: Sex differences in the skeleton:

options.label: A
options.text: The mandible is larger and more robust in the male

options.label: B
options.text: Male bones are heavier with prominent bone markings

options.label: C
options.text: The female pelvis is broader with a heart-shaped inlet and relatively deep for childbearing

notes.C: The female inlet is typically wider and rounder or more oval. A heart-shaped inlet is more characteristic of the male pelvis.
notes.A: Adult males have, on average, a larger and more robust mandible. Individual mandibular measurements can overlap between sexes.
notes.B: Male skeletons are generally more robust and often have more prominent muscle attachment markings. The comparison is population-level.

questions.why: Adult male skeletons have greater average robusticity, whereas the female pelvis tends to have a broader, shallower cavity and a wider, rounder or more oval inlet. Individual traits overlap.

questions.stem: Functions of the skeletal system include:

options.label: A
options.text: Support and attachment of muscles only

options.label: C
options.text: Protection, production of blood cells and filtration of blood

notes.A: The skeleton also protects organs, stores minerals and houses blood-forming marrow, so support and muscle attachment are only two roles.
notes.B: Bones act as levers and red marrow produces B lymphocytes and progenitors of T lymphocytes. T cells mature in the thymus.
notes.C: Protection and blood cell production are skeletal functions, but blood filtration is classically a function of the spleen and kidneys.
notes.D: Red marrow supports haematopoiesis, bone matrix stores calcium, and the skeleton supports the body.
notes.E: Calcium and phosphate are stored mainly as hydroxyapatite crystals in the mineralised bone matrix.

questions.why: The skeleton supports and protects the body, acts as a lever system for movement, stores minerals and houses marrow for blood cell production, including lymphocyte lineages.

questions.stem: The sacrum:

options.label: A
options.text: Is located on the posterior aspect of the pelvis

options.label: C
options.text: Articulates with L5 superiorly and the coccyx inferiorly

options.label: D
options.text: Its alae articulate with the two hip bones

options.label: E
options.text: Consists of six sacral vertebrae and four anterior foramina

notes.D: Its lateral auricular surfaces meet the hip bones.
notes.E: Five fused vertebrae.

questions.why: The sacrum is a curved triangular bone at the back of the pelvis, articulating with L5 above, the coccyx below and the hip bones at its alae (A-D true); E is false because it has five fused vertebrae and four pairs of anterior foramina.

questions.stem: The patella:

options.label: A
options.text: Is a sesamoid bone that articulates with the femur, tibia and fibula

options.label: C
options.text: Enclosed in the tendon that secures the anterior muscles of the thigh to the tibia

options.label: D
options.text: Has an apex that is directed superiorly and a base that is inferior

notes.A: The patella articulates with the femoral trochlea. It is connected to the tibia by the patellar ligament and has no fibular articulation.
notes.C: The patella is embedded in the quadriceps tendon, and the patellar ligament continues to the tibial tuberosity.
notes.D: The base of the patella is broad and superior. Its pointed apex is inferior and gives attachment to the patellar ligament.
notes.E: The patella is classed as a sesamoid bone because it develops within the quadriceps tendon.
notes.B: The patella lies in front of the knee joint and provides anterior bony protection.

questions.why: The patella is a sesamoid bone within the quadriceps tendon. It protects the front of the knee and holds the extensor tendon away from the joint axis, increasing leverage.

questions.stem: The foot:

options.label: A
options.text: Consists of the tarsals, metacarpals and phalanges

options.label: B
options.text: Consists of tarsal bones with the calcaneus being the largest

options.label: C
options.text: Has 3 arches; medial longitudinal arch, lateral longitudinal arch and intermediate arch

options.label: D
options.text: It has 7 tarsal bones, 5 metatarsal bones and 12 phalanges

options.label: E
options.text: It has 3 cuneiforms superior, inferior and intermediate cuneiforms

notes.A: The foot has metatarsals between its tarsals and phalanges. Metacarpals form part of the hand.
notes.C: The two longitudinal arches are medial and lateral. The remaining arch is the transverse arch.
notes.D: There are fourteen phalanges because the great toe has two and the other four toes have three each.
notes.E: The cuneiforms are named medial, intermediate and lateral according to their positions across the midfoot.
notes.B: The calcaneus is the largest tarsal. It forms the heel and receives the calcaneal tendon posteriorly.

questions.why: Each foot contains seven tarsals, five metatarsals and fourteen phalanges. The calcaneus is the largest tarsal and provides the bony framework of the heel.

questions.stem: The ulna:

options.label: A
options.text: The ulna is the longer and more lateral bone of the forearm

options.label: B
options.text: It articulates with the humerus proximally and the radius laterally

options.label: C
options.text: The proximal end includes the olecranon, the trochlear notch and the radial notch

options.label: D
options.text: The distal end includes the head and the styloid process

options.label: E
options.text: The ulna is the shorter and more medial bone of the forearm

notes.A: The ulna is the longer forearm bone and lies on the medial side in anatomical position.
notes.B: The trochlear notch meets the humeral trochlea. The proximal radial notch is lateral, where it meets the radial head.
notes.C: These are proximal landmarks. The olecranon forms the upper lip of the trochlear notch, and the radial notch lies laterally.
notes.D: The head and styloid are distal on the ulna. The radial head, by comparison, is proximal.
notes.E: The ulna is medial but longer than the radius, largely because of its prominent proximal olecranon.

questions.why: The ulna is the longer medial forearm bone. Its proximal trochlear notch forms the main hinge with the humerus, while its small distal end has a head and styloid.

questions.stem: Concerning the intervertebral disc:

options.label: A
options.text: It is a hyaline cartilage pad with an inner gelatinous core and an outer fibrous ring

options.label: B
options.text: It is an elastic cartilage pad with an inner annulus fibrosus and an outer nucleus pulposus

options.label: C
options.text: It is a fibrocartilage pad that absorbs shock and allows the spine to bend

options.label: D
options.text: The discs together make up about half the height of the vertebral column

options.label: E
options.text: A "slipped disc" is protrusion of the nucleus pulposus through a tear in the annulus fibrosus, most often in the lumbar region

notes.A: Thin hyaline cartilage endplates separate the disc from the vertebral bodies. The annulus itself is fibrous with fibrocartilaginous layers.
notes.B: The nucleus pulposus is central and the annulus fibrosus is peripheral. The disc contains no elastic cartilage.
notes.C: The fibrocartilaginous annulus surrounds a hydrated nucleus that distributes loads while allowing movement between vertebrae.
notes.D: The intervertebral discs together account for roughly one-quarter of the length of the vertebral column.
notes.E: Disc herniation involves displacement of disc material through a weakened or torn annulus. The lumbar region is the most common site.

questions.why: The disc has an outer annulus fibrosus surrounding the gelatinous nucleus pulposus. This arrangement spreads compressive loads and permits small movements between adjacent vertebral bodies.

questions.stem: Immovable joints (synarthroses) are found in the:

notes.A: Foetal sutures and fontanelles allow the bones to move (moulding at birth).
notes.B: Infant sutures still allow growth and slight movement.
notes.C: Adult sutures are immovable fibrous joints.
notes.D: Intervertebral and facet joints are movable.
notes.E: Its joints are movable.

questions.why: Sutures become truly immovable only in the adult skull.

questions.stem: The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is a:
questions.why: The first carpometacarpal joint is saddle-shaped. Its reciprocally concave and convex surfaces allow two main axes of motion, and combined movements bring the thumb into opposition.

notes.A: Plane joints allow predominantly gliding between relatively flat surfaces. The trapezium and first metacarpal have reciprocal curvatures.
notes.B: A hinge joint allows mainly flexion and extension around one axis. The thumb base also permits abduction and adduction.
notes.D: An ellipsoid joint has an oval convex surface in an elliptical depression. At the thumb base each surface has reciprocal curvatures.
notes.E: A pivot joint allows rotation around one main axis, as at the proximal radioulnar joint. The thumb base permits motion about two axes.

questions.stem: Articulations found on the thoracic cage include:

options.label: A
options.text: Joints of the heads of the ribs

notes.A: A joint of the head of a rib connects the rib head to one or more thoracic vertebral bodies.
notes.B: A costotransverse joint is between the rib tubercle and a transverse process. Ribs eleven and twelve lack these joints.
notes.C: Costovertebral articulations connect ribs to vertebrae. The term can collectively include the rib-head and costotransverse articulations.
notes.D: Interchondral joints connect neighbouring costal cartilages, particularly those forming the costal margin.
notes.E: Costochondral joints are synchondroses between the anterior ends of the bony ribs and their own costal cartilages.

questions.why: Ribs articulate with thoracic vertebrae posteriorly. Anteriorly the bony ribs meet their own costal cartilages, and some adjacent costal cartilages also articulate with one another.

questions.stem: About the manubriosternal joint:

options.label: A
options.text: It is a symphysis (secondary cartilaginous joint)

options.label: B
options.text: Its articular surfaces are covered by fibrocartilage

options.label: D
options.text: It contains a synovial cavity in most people

options.label: E
options.text: It lies at the level of the 1st rib

notes.B: Hyaline cartilage covers the adjacent bony surfaces. A separate fibrocartilaginous layer unites them.
notes.D: A synovial cavity is not the usual arrangement. The bones are normally united by intervening cartilage.
notes.E: The second costal cartilage articulates at the level of the sternal angle. The first meets the manubrium more superiorly.
notes.A: The joint is usually a secondary cartilaginous joint because fibrocartilage unites the manubrium and sternal body.
notes.C: Fibrocartilage is interposed between the hyaline-covered joint surfaces, as expected in a symphysis.

questions.why: The manubriosternal joint is usually a symphysis with a fibrocartilaginous disc between hyaline-covered surfaces. It forms the sternal angle, the landmark for the second costal cartilage.

questions.stem: Types of fibrous joint include:

notes.A: A ginglymus is a synovial hinge joint, such as the humeroulnar articulation at the elbow.
notes.B: A syndesmosis uses a ligament or interosseous membrane to join bones, as at the distal tibiofibular joint.
notes.C: A suture is a fibrous joint that joins adjacent skull bones by short connective tissue fibres.

questions.why: In fibrous joints, dense connective tissue links the participating structures. Sutures join skull bones, syndesmoses link bones by a ligament or membrane, and gomphoses anchor teeth.

questions.stem: Types of cartilaginous joint include:

notes.A: A saddle joint has a synovial cavity and reciprocally curved surfaces, as at the first carpometacarpal joint.
notes.B: An epiphyseal plate is a temporary hyaline cartilage synchondrosis that permits longitudinal bone growth.
notes.C: At the joint between adjacent vertebral bodies, the fibrocartilaginous disc provides the connection characteristic of a symphysis.

questions.why: A synchondrosis uses hyaline cartilage, as in a growing epiphyseal plate. A symphysis uses fibrocartilage between the bony surfaces, as at the joint between vertebral bodies.

questions.stem: Types of synovial joint include:

notes.A: A synchondrosis connects bones by hyaline cartilage and lacks a synovial cavity.
notes.B: A gomphosis is fibrous. The periodontal ligament anchors the root of a tooth in its alveolar socket.
notes.C: A pivot joint is a uniaxial synovial joint, with rotation around the long axis of one component.

questions.why: A pivot joint has a synovial cavity and permits rotation about one axis. At the proximal radioulnar joint, the radial head turns within the annular ligament.

questions.stem: Factors that help keep the patella from dislocating laterally include:

options.label: A
options.text: The forward prominence of the LATERAL femoral condyle

options.label: B
options.text: Tension in the medial patellar retinaculum

options.label: C
options.text: The lower horizontal fibres of vastus medialis

options.label: D
options.text: The oblique (lateral) pull of the quadriceps

notes.D: The lateral component of the quadriceps line of pull tends to displace the patella laterally, increasing the demand on medial restraints.
notes.A: The prominent lateral trochlear ridge forms a bony buttress to lateral patellar translation as the patella enters the groove.
notes.B: The medial retinacular tissues, including the medial patellofemoral ligament, resist lateral patellar translation, especially near extension.
notes.C: The distal oblique fibres of vastus medialis provide a medial pull that contributes to dynamic patellar tracking.

questions.why: The lateral trochlear ridge provides a bony restraint to lateral patellar translation. Medial retinacular structures and the medial pull of distal vastus medialis also help keep the patella centred.

questions.stem: About inversion and eversion of the foot:

options.label: A
options.text: In inversion the medial border of the foot is raised

options.label: B
options.text: The fully inverted foot is also plantarflexed

options.label: C
options.text: Inversion and eversion occur at the ankle joint

options.label: D
options.text: Tibialis anterior can invert the foot

options.label: E
options.text: All invertors and evertors attach to the forefoot

notes.B: Inversion usually combines with plantarflexion and adduction (supination).
notes.C: At the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints.
notes.E: Fibularis brevis attaches to the 5th metatarsal base; tibialis posterior mainly to the navicular.

questions.why: Inversion raises the medial border and combines with plantarflexion, and tibialis anterior is an invertor (A, B, D true). C is false (inversion/eversion occur at the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints, not the ankle) and E is false (several invertors/evertors attach to the midfoot, not only the forefoot).

questions.stem: Structures supporting the medial longitudinal arch include:

notes.B: Fibularis longus crosses the sole to the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal, helping support the first ray and arch.
notes.A: The plantar aponeurosis acts as a tie from the calcaneus to the forefoot. Toe extension tensions it during push-off.
notes.C: Flexor hallucis longus runs under the medial foot and provides dynamic longitudinal support as its tendon is tensioned.
notes.D: Tibialis anterior inserts on the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal base, where its tendon helps support the medial arch.
notes.E: Tibialis posterior attaches prominently to the navicular and helps lift and stabilise the medial longitudinal arch.

questions.why: The plantar aponeurosis provides passive tension along the medial arch. Tendons crossing the plantar and medial foot give dynamic support, including posterior tibial and long toe-flexor contributions.

questions.stem: True or false: An ellipsoid (condyloid) synovial joint does not allow rotation.
questions.why: An ellipsoid joint is biaxial, allowing flexion and extension plus abduction and adduction. Circumduction combines these movements, while independent axial rotation is not a primary movement.

notes.B: Circumduction is possible by combining the two axes of motion. It does not require independent rotation around the long axis.

questions.stem: True or false: The part of the shoulder joint capsule that allows the greatest range of movement lies anteriorly.
questions.why: The inferior part of the glenohumeral capsule forms the lax axillary recess with the arm at the side. The fold unfolds during abduction and accommodates elevation of the humerus.

notes.A: The axillary recess lies below the joint. The anterior capsule has ligamentous thickenings that help restrain translation.

questions.stem: True or false: The iliotibial tract keeps the knee in the hyperextended position.
questions.why: The iliotibial tract transmits tension from tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus to the lateral tibia. This tension helps stabilise the knee near extension during weight-bearing.

notes.A: The tract helps support an extended knee. Lateral stabilisation does not require movement beyond the normal extension range.

questions.stem: True or false: The upper NINE costal cartilages articulate with the sternum at sternocostal joints.
questions.why: The first seven costal cartilages attach directly to the sternum at sternocostal joints. The eighth and ninth reach it indirectly through the interchondral connections of the costal margin.

notes.A: The eighth and ninth cartilages join the costal margin via the cartilages above them and have no direct sternal articulation.

questions.stem: True or false: The first sternocostal joint is a primary cartilaginous joint.
questions.why: The first costal cartilage joins the manubrium in a synchondrosis, a primary cartilaginous joint. The second to seventh sternocostal joints are generally classified as plane synovial joints.

notes.B: The first sternocostal connection is continuous through hyaline cartilage and lacks the joint cavity typical of the lower sternocostal articulations.
